title: Minimum-Width Drawing of Trees with Sized Vertices
comment: Accepted at the 34th International Symposium on Graph Drawing and Network Visualization (GD 2026)
summary: Trees arise in many applications and computing nice tree layouts is a classical problem in information visualization. In many practical settings, vertices need to be represented as rectangles with a given width and height rather than as points. When an order over the children of each vertex is given, polynomial-time algorithms are known that produce drawings adhering to various drawing conventions. However, in many applications, the order of children carries no semantic meaning, and choosing it well can significantly reduce the drawing's width. In this paper, we study the problem \textsc{Min-Width Tree Drawing with Reordering} (\textsc{MWD}): given a rooted tree whose vertices have prescribed widths, find a sibling order at each internal vertex that minimizes the width of the resulting layered drawing. We show that the problem is \textsf{NP}-complete, even on binary trees with unit-width vertices. We present a mixed integer linear program that solves \textsc{MWD} exactly on moderately sized instances, and a heuristic that is fast and delivers good results in practice. We evaluate both approaches against a baseline on synthetic and real-world datasets, where reordering reduces drawing width by a median of $\approx20\%$ and by up to $\approx55\%$ on individual instances. The heuristic computes its layouts in under a second and, when the MILP proves optimality, it stays within $25\%$ of the optimal width in three-quarters of all instances.

AI.tldr: NP-complete to minimize the width of layered tree drawings by reordering children; MILP solves moderate instances exactly, and a fast heuristic provides near-optimal layouts.
AI.motivation: To reduce the width of layered tree drawings when child order has no semantic meaning, by optimally reordering siblings under width-constrained vertex rectangles.
AI.method: Proves NP-completeness for MWD; formulates a mixed integer linear program (MILP) to solve MWD exactly on moderately sized instances; develops a fast heuristic for practical use; evaluates on synthetic and real datasets against a baseline.
AI.result: Reordering reduces drawing width with a median improvement of about 20% and up to 55% on some instances; the heuristic runs in under a second; when MILP proves optimal, the heuristic achieves within 25% of optimal width in ~75% of instances.
AI.conclusion: Reordering siblings without semantic meaning yields substantial width reductions in layered tree drawings; the proposed MILP provides exact solutions for moderate sizes and the heuristic offers fast, practical performance with strong empirical results.

title: Tight UGC Thresholds for Geometric Stabbing Problems
summary:
Many geometric stabbing problems admit natural covering LPs in which each constraint is a union of consecutive traces on ordered candidate sets. We prove a transfer theorem showing that every fixed finite, bounded-arity integrality-gap instance of this form yields a matching hardness ratio under the Unique Games Conjecture. Using the strict-CSP framework of Kumar, Manokaran, Tulsiani, and Vishnoi [SODA 2011], we construct the required connected local distributions by randomized rounding and a full-support perturbation. Given a fractional vector $x$ on a block, the rounding selects candidate $i$ with marginal probability $x_i$ and hits each consecutive trace $T$ with probability $\min\{1,x(T)\}$.
  We obtain three tight UGC thresholds. First, for every fixed $d\ge 2$, stabbing arbitrary-size axis-parallel $d$-cubes with coordinate hyperplanes has threshold $d$. For $d=2$, the hardness holds for arbitrary-size squares and establishes threshold $2$ for rectangle and square stabbing, matching the $2$-approximation of Gaur, Ibaraki, and Krishnamurti [ESA 2000]. Second, stabbing horizontal segments with horizontal and vertical lines has threshold $e/(e-1)$, matching the $e/(e-1)$-approximation of Kovaleva and Spieksma [ESA 2004]. Third, separated $d$-interval transversal has threshold $d$ for every fixed $d\ge 2$, closing under UGC the gap left by the $d$-approximation of Ben-David, Grant, Ma, and Sharpe [CCCG 2012].

AI.tldr: UGC-hardness transfer for a broad class of geometric stabbing problems; gives three tight thresholds: axis-aligned d-cubes by coordinate hyperplanes; stabbing horizontal segments with horizontal/vertical lines; separated d-interval transversal.
AI.motivation: Understand the limits of approximation for stabbing/covering problems by linking LP integrality gaps to Unique Games Conjecture hardness; provide a unified transfer framework for problems expressible as LPs with unions of consecutive traces.
AI.method: Use the strict-CSP framework (Kumar–Manokaran–Tulsiani–Vishnoi). Construct connected local distributions via randomized rounding and full-support perturbation. For a fractional x on a block, rounding picks i with probability x_i and hits each trace T with probability min{1, x(T)} to maintain marginal and correlation structure.
AI.result: Three tight UGC thresholds are obtained: (1) axis-parallel d-cubes stabbed by coordinate hyperplanes have threshold d for any fixed d≥2 (and for d=2 this includes arbitrary-size squares, matching the 2-approximation for rectangle/square stabbing); (2) stabbing horizontal segments with horizontal and vertical lines has threshold e/(e−1) (matching Kovaleva–Spieksma’s e/(e−1) approximation); (3) separated d-interval transversal has threshold d for every fixed d≥2 (closing the gap left by the d-approximation of Ben‑David et al.).
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a general transfer principle from bounded-arity integrality-gap instances to UGC-hardness for a broad family of stabbing problems, and proves three tight thresholds that match the best-known approximation guarantees in natural geometries, thus closing several open gaps under UGC.

title: It's Not Just More Demos: Counterfactual Action Sensitivity Coverage for Data-Efficient Robust Robot Imitation
comment: Workshop paper accepted at the RSS 2026 Workshop on Data-Centric Robotics: What Data Do Robots Really Need?
summary: Visuomotor imitation learning has demonstrated success for manipulation tasks. However, the trained policies remain brittle to visual `nuisances', with even minor task-preserving variations such as lighting, distractions or changes in colour result in heavy degradation of the trained policy's performance. While increasing data diversity can improve robustness, it is unclear which additional demonstrations are informative for a particular trained policy. We propose Counterfactual Nuisance Behaviour Cloning (CFNBC), an offline data-selection framework for targeted robustness repair. Starting from a nominal policy trained on `clean' demonstrations, CFNBC generates paired clean and nuisance observations that preserve the expert action, then measures \emph{action drift}: the change in the policy's predicted action under a nuisance that should not alter the desired behaviour. This provides a policy-specific sensitivity signal for selecting a compact, response-diverse repair set from a larger candidate pool, without requiring rollout success labels or online policy execution. We show in MuJoCo bimanual cube transfer and SimplerEnv cube stacking that action drift correlates with nuisance-induced failure, and that response-guided repair with only $20$--$30$ selected candidates substantially outperforms matched-budget random selection while approaching the performance of much larger random repair budgets. These results support a data-centric view of robustness repair: the most useful data are not necessarily the most numerous, visually diverse, or obviously difficult, but the examples that cover fragile response modes of the current policy.

AI.tldr: CFNBC is an offline data-selection framework for targeted robustness repair in visuomotor imitation, using action drift to pick a compact set of nuisance-containing demonstrations that reveal fragile policy responses, improving robustness with few data.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor imitation policies degrade under visual nuisances (lighting, color, distractions). Merely increasing data diversity is not necessarily informative; need data that probes fragile response modes of the current policy.
AI.method: From a nominal policy trained on clean data, CFNBC creates paired clean/nuisance observations preserving the expert action, computes action drift (change in predicted action under nuisance), and selects a compact, response-diverse repair set from a larger candidate pool in an offline manner without rollout labels or online execution.
AI.result: Action drift correlates with nuisance-induced failure. Repair with 20–30 selected candidates substantially outperforms matched-budget random selection and approaches the performance of much larger random budgets in MuJoCo bimanual cube transfer and SimplerEnv cube stacking.
AI.conclusion: Data-centric robustness repair is effective when selecting data that cover fragile response modes of the current policy; the most useful data are those that reveal how the policy responds to nuisances, not merely the most numerous or obviously difficult examples.

title: Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability
summary: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

AI.tldr: Recursive weight-sharing transformers offer a parameter-efficient, compute-focused surrogate modeling approach for small engineering datasets. Three variants are evaluated (Tiny Recursive Model, Depth Recursive Transformer, Simple Recursive Transformer) and validated on thermo-mechanical reliability of advanced packages and a Laplace PDE iterative solver, showing favorable trade-offs between accuracy, parameter count, and FLOPs under resource constraints.
AI.motivation: Engineering surrogates operate on small, low-dimensional datasets where large transformers overfit and incur high memory/compute. A compute-centric, parameter-efficient architecture is needed; hardware-aware evaluation of recursive transformers can guide architecture selection in resource-constrained design spaces.
AI.method: Hardware-aware comparison of three recursive transformer paradigms with weight sharing: Tiny Recursive Model, Depth Recursive Transformer, and Simple Recursive Transformer. Evaluate predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, and FLOPs on two tasks: (1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis under costly FEA across a DOE sweep for advanced semiconductor packages, and (2) a Laplace PDE iterative solver for capacitance field. Derive practical design guidelines.
AI.result: Recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling. The study yields actionable guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource constraints.
AI.conclusion: For small-data engineering surrogates, weight-sharing recursive transformers offer a favorable balance of accuracy and efficiency. Among the three variants, practitioners can choose based on resource limits and task characteristics to optimize recall/MRR with reduced parameters and FLOPs.

title: Theatre Chapbooks At Scale: A Statistical Comparative Analysis of Typography
summary: We propose a statistical methodology that quantifies the similarity of typefaces between printed historical books. This provides a tool that accelerates philological analysis. Using character prototypes derived from clustering and aligning automatically extracted character images, the method defines a typeface distance between any two books. To produce actionable outputs, we develop an a contrario statistical framework to interpret the significance of the computed typeface distances. We apply the method to the philological study of 17 th -century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks in a quantity that exceeds the capabilities of systematic visual inspection by human experts. Our method enables the automatic comparison of Roman and Italic types extracted from different books. After validation by human experts, our method has led to new printer attributions being discovered, and former printer attributions being revised. This success strongly suggests that our method has the potential to enable digital bibliography on a larger scale than was previously possible.

AI.tldr: Statistical pipeline to quantify typeface similarity across books using clustering-based character prototypes and an a contrario significance test; enables automatic printer attribution for historical typography.
AI.motivation: Fill a gap in philology by providing a scalable, quantitative tool to compare typefaces across historical books, surpassing subjective visual inspection.
AI.method: Extract character images; cluster and align to form character prototypes; compute typeface distance between books; interpret distances with an a contrario statistical framework; apply to 17th-century Spanish chapbooks; distinguish Roman vs Italic; perform automatic cross-book comparisons; validate with human experts.
AI.result: Validated by experts; new printer attributions discovered; some attributions revised; demonstrates potential to scale digital bibliography in philology.
AI.conclusion: Shows feasibility and value of quantitative typography analysis for philology; scalable approach with generalization potential; future work could broaden types, datasets, and robustness.

title: Multi-Head Attention Residuals
summary: Transformers propagate information across depth through a single additive residual stream: every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by letting each sublayer attend, through a learned softmax. However, that read uses a single query shared across the entire width, so every feature subspace must read the depth history through one distribution. The cost of this forced compromise grows with how much the subspaces disagree about which layers to read, and disagreement grows with model width. We introduce Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR): the routing query is reshaped into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H = 1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM- and code-heavy, MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B (-0.061, -0.149, and -0.140). It achieves the best result among four methods in every setting, with the gain increasing from 100M to the larger scales. The head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob: validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H = 4 or H = 8 across scales. We adopt H = 8 for large-scale models; over-splitting beyond this point (H = 16) consistently gives back part of the gain. A direct probe of the trained queries confirms that learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. Fused Triton routing kernels increase attention-residual training throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of the baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training, yielding improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

AI.tldr: MHAR introduces H-headed per-subspace routing for attention residuals, enabling independent depth-wise reads by subspaces. It yields validation-loss improvements over a standard Transformer across 100M, 350M, and 1B scales, with optimum H around 4–8, and provides throughput gains via fused kernels and effective delta-residual conversion for 8B models.
AI.motivation: In standard attention residuals, a single shared query across the full feature width forces all subspaces to read the depth history through one distribution. As model width grows, subspaces disagree more about which layers to attend to, degrading learning efficiency. MHAR aims to relax this constraint by giving each subspace its own routing head to read from depth history.
AI.method: Replace the single routing query with H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The resulting read is block-diagonal. The reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute. H=1 recovers baseline attention residuals. Train from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus (STEM/code-heavy). Compare four methods; perform ablations over H. Speeds up training with fused Triton kernels. Use delta attention residuals to enable 8B mid-training.
AI.result: MHAR outperforms the standard Transformer on validation loss at 100M, 350M, and 1B steps (-0.061, -0.149, -0.140). It is the best among four methods in all settings, with gains growing with scale. Validation loss is U-shaped in H, with a flat optimum at H=4 or H=8; H=8 is adopted for large models; H=16 reduces gains. Direct probes show learned subspace disagreement is the driver. Throughput for attention-residual training increases with fused kernels to 0.55–0.88x baseline. An 8B mid-training delta-residual conversion yields improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.
AI.conclusion: MHAR provides a practical and scalable enhancement to attention residuals by enabling per-subspace, depth-wise routing that reduces cross-subspace disagreement. It delivers consistent validation gains across scales, offers guidance on the optimal number of heads (roughly 4–8), and yields notable training-speedups. The improvement is driven by learned subspace disagreement and is compatible with large-scale training via efficient routing kernels and delta residuals.

title: Simulation of Surgical Suturing Using Position-Based Dynamics and the Material Point Method for Robot Reinforcement Learning
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures, accepted for the IEEE RAS/EMBS 11th International Conference on Biomedical Robotics and Biomechatronics (BioRob 2026)
summary: Recent advances in robotics research have created a strong demand for high-performance simulators. Surgical robotics simulation faces unique challenges due to the need to model diverse objects, such as rigid instruments, soft tissue, and fluids. While many studies simulate sutures or soft tissue independently, only a few have considered the complete soft-tissue suturing scenario, including the contact between sutures and deformable tissue during suture insertion. Building on previous work, this paper presents a novel suturing simulation environment using sutures modelled by position-based dynamics (PBD) and soft bodies modelled by the material point method (MPM) while considering two-way contact with frictional and drag forces. We introduce a contact coupling method between the PBD suture and the MPM soft tissue, enabling visually plausible suture-tissue interactions. The simulator is optimized for GPU execution with parallel scenes using multiple CUDA streams, and we present a Reinforcement Learning (RL) environment for autonomous suturing sub-tasks, including needle insertion, driving, and extraction. Using ML-Agents, RL agents trained in the simulator show stable learning and achieve 80% and 68% success rates in needle insertion and extraction, respectively, under the strictest distance threshold.

AI.tldr: Novel integration of position-based dynamics (PBD) sutures with material point method (MPM) soft tissue to simulate two-way contact with friction and drag, optimized for GPU, plus an RL environment for autonomous suturing tasks achieving 80% needle insertion and 68% extraction success under strict distance thresholds.
AI.motivation: Need for high-fidelity, interactive surgical simulators that capture complex suturing with deformable tissue and realistic contact dynamics to train RL-driven autonomous sub-tasks.
AI.method: Model sutures with PBD; model soft tissue with MPM; implement contact coupling between PBD suture and MPM tissue with friction/drag; GPU-accelerated parallel scenes via CUDA streams; provide RL environment via ML-Agents; evaluate with RL agents on needle insertion, driving, extraction.
AI.result: Demonstrates visually plausible suture-tissue interactions; stable RL learning; 80% insertion, 68% extraction success under strict distance threshold.
AI.conclusion: Integrates two advanced numerical methods to simulate complete suturing with contact; supports RL-based autonomous sub-tasks; potential for realistic training tools and extension to broader tasks.

title: Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning
summary: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

AI.tldr: Introduces Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and CMCDR to address decision-level shifts in modality contributions in multimodal continual learning; provides replay-based and replay-free regularization to preserve prior modality structure; validated on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual VQA.
AI.motivation: Current MMCL focuses on cross-modal alignment or semantic similarity but overlooks stability of each modality's contribution and their interactions across tasks, leading to drift in decision-level contributions and forgetting.
AI.method: Define MCD score combining contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under modality-subset interventions. Theoretical and empirical analyses show why existing MMCL methods fail to mitigate this drift. Propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR) to preserve prior-task modality contribution structure. Two variants: (1) replay-based CMCDR with diagnostic probes on stored old samples to constrain old-task contributions; (2) replay-free CMCDR that distills old-task contribution responses from the frozen model using current-task samples.
AI.result: CMCDR improves retention of modality-contribution structure across tasks and is validated on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering, demonstrating generality and effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Preserving modality contribution structure via CMCDR mitigates decision-level drift in MMCL, addressing a previously overlooked source of forgetting and enabling more robust continual multimodal learning across task sequences.

title: OVEarth-Bench: Evaluating Category Breadth and Query Diversity for Open-Vocabulary Earth Observation
summary: Open-vocabulary Earth observation (EO) aims to localize geospatial concepts specified in natural language rather than a fixed label set. Existing benchmarks, however, usually cover narrow category vocabularies or limited query forms. To fill this gap, we introduce OVEarth-Bench, which extends existing evaluation in two directions: category breadth, through broad hierarchical category coverage with positive and negative expressions, and query diversity, through vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries. The benchmark supports mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. We evaluate a broad set of general and EO-specific methods. The evaluation reveals that: (1) the performance of current methods remains limited, while broader category coverage yields more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; and (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest methods. These findings provide guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and highlight the importance of developing more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation. Our data and evaluation package are released at https://earth-insights.github.io/OVEarth-bench.

AI.tldr: A new open-vocabulary evaluation benchmark for Earth observation, OVEarth-Bench, expands category breadth and query diversity to better assess zero-shot localization using mask/box tasks. It reveals current methods remain limited, MLLM-based approaches perform best overall, and EO-specific models underperform; emphasizes need for larger, more realistic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing EO benchmarks cover narrow vocabularies and limited query forms, hindering evaluation of open-vocabulary, language-guided localization. A broad, realistic benchmark with diverse queries and hierarchical categories is needed to guide future method development and fair comparison.
AI.method: Introduce OVEarth-Bench with broad hierarchical category coverage, including positive and negative expressions; support mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol; include vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries; evaluate a wide range of general and EO-specific methods.
AI.result: Evaluation shows: (1) broader category coverage yields more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform compared to general models and rarely match the top methods.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and underscores the need for more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation; data and evaluation package released at the project site.

title: KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/flagos-ai/KernelGenBench
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

AI.tldr: KernelGenBench provides a unified benchmark to evaluate LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and hardware. It introduces two sub-benchmarks (MS and MC) and reports that agent-based generation outperforms pure LLM sampling, but cross-platform degradation and high generation cost limit practicality.
AI.motivation: There is no comprehensive, standardized benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM- and agent-generated kernels across multiple operator sources and heterogeneous hardware; a unified benchmark is needed to assess portability, efficiency, and practical costs.
AI.method: KernelGenBench_MS (Multi-Source) evaluates 210 operators from three sources beyond PyTorch-centric tasks; KernelGenBench_MC (Multi-Chip) evaluates a 110-operator subset across six heterogeneous hardware platforms. Large-scale evaluation uses over 15 billion tokens. Comparisons include agent-based generation vs pure LLM sampling vs cuBLAS baselines. Key metrics include success rate, performance portability across hardware, cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E), and token-cost per operator (AKO ~5.11–5.19 million tokens).
AI.result: Agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling; cuBLAS operators pose the greatest challenge across methods; generation performance varies notably across hardware, with substantial cross-platform degradation; autonomous kernel generation is highly cost-intensive, averaging ~5.11M tokens per successful operator (AKO4all ~5.19M).
AI.conclusion: KernelGenBench provides a rigorous framework to quantify portability and cost of LLM-/agent-generated kernels, highlighting substantial cross-platform gaps and the need to optimize agent strategies and efficiency. The benchmark invites future work on improving portability, reducing token costs, and expanding operator sources.

title: Corrigible Assistance in One Round: Pragmatic-Pedagogic Best Response
comment: World Symposium on the Algorithmic Foundations of Robotics (WAFR) 2026
summary: Assistance games formalize human-robot collaboration under asymmetric information: the human knows the goal, while the robot must infer it from observation and interaction in order to assist effectively. In general, computing optimal assistance game strategies online is intractable, since exact solutions require planning in a POMDP. We identify a class of assistance games in which pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning resolves goal uncertainty in a single time step, rendering the full-horizon game exactly solvable by a tractable best-response procedure. Within this class, we show that mainstream inverse optimal control exhibits an inference ceiling that hinders alignment, while pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning overcomes this barrier by immediately disambiguating goals through actions that look equivalent under task execution alone. Finally, we validate our theoretical results and proposed method on a simple collaborative block-building example.

AI.tldr: A tractable subclass of assistance games uses pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning to disambiguate goals in one step, enabling exact full-horizon planning via a best-response; it reveals an inference ceiling in inverse IRL and validates on a simple block-building task.
AI.motivation: Human-robot collaboration with asymmetric information where the human has goal knowledge and the robot must infer it; general solutions are intractable due to POMDP complexity, necessitating scalable approaches.
AI.method: The authors define a subclass of assistance games where goal uncertainty is resolved in a single time step through pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning. They show that within this subclass, the full-horizon problem reduces to a tractable best-response solution. They contrast this with mainstream inverse optimal control, which suffers from an inference ceiling, and argue that pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning eliminates this barrier by producing goal-disambiguating actions. A simple collaborative block-building experiment validates the theory and method.
AI.result: In the identified subclass, the full-horizon game is exactly solvable via a tractable best-response procedure. Pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning yields immediate goal disambiguation, overcoming the inference ceiling seen in standard inverse IRL. The approach is validated on a simple block-building task, demonstrating practical applicability.
AI.conclusion: Pragmatic-pedagogic reasoning enables immediate goal inference and tractable planning in assistance games with asymmetric information, addressing inference limitations of inverse optimal control and offering a viable solution for real-time human-robot collaboration.

title: DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series
summary: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

AI.tldr: DoTime is an open-source generator for multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, featuring continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with a positivity guard, regime-switching (generalizing interrupted time series), non-stationary dynamics via switching parameters, and deterministic ramp/sinusoidal intervention profiles; includes evaluation suites with ground-truth interventional and counterfactual data, baselines and evaluation harness; demonstrates interventional priors improve direction-accuracy over observational models.
AI.motivation: Address limitations in causal inference benchmarks for time series by providing scalable, theoretically grounded interventional and counterfactual evaluation, enabling reliable benchmarking in healthcare, policy, and climate applications.
AI.method: A generator (dotime) that produces multivariate temporal structural causal models with interventions, continuous-time windows, regime-switching dynamics, non-stationarity, and deterministic intervention shapes; ships with frozen evaluation suites, ground-truth data, and baseline implementations; 100,000 trajectories across eight identification structures; supports interventional prior training.
AI.result: Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, interventional prior-fitted networks show a positive direction-accuracy gap over observational models across all structures, trajectory lengths, seeds (three seeds per arm); the evaluation suites provide paired interventional trajectories and shared-noise counterfactuals with exact ground truth.
AI.conclusion: DoTime provides a scalable, theory-grounded benchmark and priors for causal foundation-model research in time-series, enabling falsifiable claims about the benefits of interventional training and supporting robust evaluation across diverse identification structures.

title: VETO: Towards Protecting Images From Frontier AI Editing
summary: The rise of powerful, accessible image-editing models such as FLUX.2 has brought high-fidelity editing within broad reach. Their capabilities now extend beyond localized modifications to extracting and recontextualizing objects and identities in entirely new scenes. By allowing prompt and generation tokens to attend directly to reference-image tokens, modern models blur the boundary between conventional editing and text-to-image synthesis. This expanded generative freedom also broadens the space of potential misuse, as harmful transformations are no longer confined to a predictable set of localized edits. Existing anti-edit defenses are designed to disrupt the semantic bottleneck of the reference-image encoding in legacy diffusion pipelines. However, newer editors distill reference information through joint-attention blocks, thereby often circumventing these protections. We therefore introduce VETO, a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts this inner mechanism through which modern models read the source image. Additionally, as existing editing benchmarks leave comprehensive recontextualizations largely untested, we introduce VetoBench, which evaluates defenses not only on conventional localized edits but also on broader contextual shifts. Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.

AI.tldr: Introduces VETO, a subtle anti-edit cloak, and VetoBench to defend against non-local, context-level edits in modern image-editing models; shows superior protection across editors and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Powerful image-editing models enable broad, non-local transformations by reading reference images via joint-attention, creating potential for malicious recontextualizations. Existing defenses target legacy pipelines and often fail against newer editors.
AI.method: Proposes VETO, an anti-edit cloak that disrupts how models read the source image, and VetoBench, a comprehensive benchmark assessing defenses on both conventional edits and broader contextual shifts. Evaluation spans two editing models and three benchmarks.
AI.result: VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses, delivering a stronger protection–fidelity trade-off across the tested editors and benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: VETO and VetoBench advance defense strategies against contemporary editing threats by targeting inner reference-reading mechanisms and broadening evaluation scope to non-local recontextualizations.

title: RadHarmony: Radiological Data Handling in the Era of Agentic AI
summary: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. We present RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets, with a primary focus on chest radiographs and early support for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, and supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, with an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration and verification. To lower the barrier for integrating new datasets, RadHarmony introduces an AI-agent skill that guides the full integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing. We demonstrate the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. The code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/f10409/RadHarmony.

AI.tldr: RadHarmony is an open-source Python library that unifies heterogeneous radiology datasets (primarily chest radiographs) with a single API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting data, including images, labels, masks, boxes, and radiology report text; it uses 24 public datasets, MONAI map-style wrapping, optional on-disk caching, visualization, and an AI-agent for end-to-end integration; demonstrated by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT on combined chest X-ray datasets.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous radiology datasets impede DL progress due to varied file formats, schemas, and annotations; need a unified, extensible, and reproducible data-loading pipeline.
AI.method: Aggregate metadata from 24 public datasets into a unified tabular format; wrap MONAI map-style datasets with optional on-disk caching; provide a single interface to classification, segmentation, bounding boxes, and report text; offer interactive dataset visualization for exploration; introduce an AI-agent skill to guide end-to-end integration (from inspection to code generation and testing); demonstrate by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT on three chest X-ray datasets with no dataset-specific code.
AI.result: Empirical demonstration via pretraining RadHarmony-ViT on heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets without dataset-specific code; code and pretrained weights are available at the project repository.
AI.conclusion: RadHarmony enables seamless integration and augmentation of heterogeneous radiology datasets, enabling reproducible DL workflows and lowering integration barriers, with open-source tooling and AI-assisted workflow generation.

title: Failure Detection for Surgical Robot Imitation Policies via Flow-Matching World Modeling
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Imitation learning has shown increasing promise for autonomous robotic surgery, yet safe deployment remains challenging due to the safety-critical nature of surgical tasks and the complexity and variability of surgical environments. Failure detection is therefore an essential safeguard, but its development remains difficult due to the challenges of scarce failure data, highly variable manipulation dynamics, and the need to balance missed detections against disruptive false alarms. To address these challenges, we introduce FoMo-FD (Flow-Matching World Model for Failure Detection), a failure detection method that learns nominal short-horizon visual dynamics with an action-conditioned flow-matching world model. FoMo-FD scores the inverse-transport nonconformity of observed endpoint latents, enabling window-level detection of visual-action inconsistencies without requiring failure demonstrations. Detection thresholds are obtained by conformal calibration on successful executions, yielding task-specific alarms without assuming future failure types. We evaluate FoMo-FD on four surgically relevant manipulation tasks with twenty failure modes across simulation and real-world experiments using the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK). Results show that FoMo-FD outperforms observation-level anomaly baselines and a prediction-error variant of the same world model, with the wrist-camera view achieving the strongest performance, including a 96.6% failure detection rate (FDR) at a 1.3% false alarm rate (FAR).

AI.tldr: FoMo-FD uses an action-conditioned flow-matching world model to detect surgical failures by measuring inverse-transport nonconformity of visual latents, calibrated with conformal methods on success data, enabling window-level failure detection without failure examples.
AI.motivation: Safe deployment of imitation-learning-based surgical robots is hindered by scarce failure data, variable dynamics, and the need to minimize missed detections while avoiding excessive false alarms.
AI.method: Train a nominal short-horizon, action-conditioned flow-matching world model; compute inverse-transport nonconformity of observed endpoint latents; apply conformal calibration on successful runs to set task-specific alarms without failure-type supervision; evaluate on four manipulation tasks with twenty failure modes in simulation and dVRK real-world data; use wrist-camera view.
AI.result: Outperforms observation-level anomaly baselines and a prediction-error variant; achieves high detection performance, e.g., 96.6% failure detection rate at 1.3% false alarm rate; robust across views with wrist-camera yielding strongest results; no need for failure demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: FoMo-FD provides a robust, calibration-based failure detection framework for imitation-learned robotic surgery, capable of detecting failures without failure examples and with low false alarms, suitable for real-world deployment.

title: PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective
summary: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

AI.tldr: PlatformBid introduces a platform-centric benchmark for auto-bidding in integrated SSP/DSP/Ad Exchange ecosystems, defines three realistic competition settings, evaluates a broad spectrum of auto-bidding methods (classical controls, RL, generative), and proposes BidFlow, a flow-matching-based auto-bidding method. Online deployment on Kuaishou reports a +0.68% improvement in target cost, supporting offline-online consistency.
AI.motivation: Traditional auto-bidding research focuses on DSP-side objectives (e.g., advertiser conversions) while modern platforms internally unify SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange. There is a lack of platform-centric benchmarks and evaluation frameworks to optimize total platform revenue, motivating a unified benchmark and new algorithms.
AI.method: Define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse strategies, and (3) promotional competition with budget surges during events. Systematically evaluate a wide range of existing auto-bidding methods (classical control, RL-based, generative). Propose BidFlow, a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching that yields expressive policy representations to handle dynamic competition. Validate offline and online (Kuaishou) to demonstrate offline-online consistency.
AI.result: PlatformBid provides the first comprehensive, platform-centric benchmark for auto-bidding research. It enables systematic comparison across three realistic settings and method families. The BidFlow method demonstrates strong expressive policy representation for dynamic competition. Online experiments on Kuaishou report a +0.68% improvement in target cost, indicating deployment viability and alignment with offline evaluations.
AI.conclusion: PlatformBid establishes a unified, platform-centric evaluation framework for auto-bidding in integrated ad platforms and introduces BidFlow as a competitive, flow-matching-based policy. The results suggest promising directions for platform-aware auto-bidding research and practical deployment, with potential for cross-platform generalization and further multi-objective optimization.

title: Bunraku: Turning a Single Illustration into an Editable Live2D Character
summary: Live2D is the dominant 2D character-animation format for anime characters and virtual avatars, representing each character as a stack of RGBA layers driven by per-layer mesh deformation. Despite its wide use in virtual streaming, mobile games, and interactive characters, authoring a Live2D model still demands weeks of manual layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, and keyframing, and no prior generative method produces such a structured asset end-to-end. We present the first system that, from a single illustration, generates all the structured information a Live2D runtime consumes: ordered RGBA layers, a deformation mesh per layer, and the parameter-driven keypose vertex offsets that make the character move. Stage 1 casts layered decomposition as a layered diffusion process under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, producing an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 builds a content-conforming triangle mesh for each layer from its alpha channel alone, then predicts the keypose displacement field of all layers jointly: every vertex of every layer is one token, self-attention spans layer boundaries, and each displacement is factorised into a bounded direction and a log-magnitude. Joint rather than independent prediction is what makes the result a coherent character instead of separately plausible parts, and is our largest gain; scaling the network 112x yields none. On 50 held-out characters, under true generation with no teacher forcing, Stage 2 attains a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Because a layer's mesh derives from its alpha channel, a clothing layer can be re-textured from a natural-language instruction while the mesh and predicted animation are reused byte-for-byte. We further contribute Live2D-Bench, the first standardized benchmark for the task, and an 8,884-model Live2D corpus with layer and animation supervision.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end system that converts a single illustration into fully structured Live2D assets by jointly predicting layered RGBA stacks, per-layer meshes, and keypose vertex offsets, with a diffusion-based Stage 1 and a joint, cross-layer Stage 2, plus a standardized benchmark and a large corpus.
AI.motivation: Automate the labor-intensive Live2D authoring workflow (layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, keyframing) and deliver a single-generated asset pipeline, addressing the lack of end-to-end generative methods for structured Live2D assets.
AI.method: Stage 1: layered diffusion under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy to produce an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2: construct a content-conforming triangle mesh per layer from the alpha channel and jointly predict the keypose displacement field for all layers; each vertex is a token, cross-layer self-attention, and displacement factorized into a bounded direction and a log-magnitude. Joint prediction yields coherence; network scale up to 112x shows diminishing returns. Evaluation on 50 held-out characters using true generation (no teacher forcing) yields per-vertex direction cosine metrics (median 0.828).
AI.result: Proposes Live2D-Bench as a standardized benchmark and provides an 8,884-model Live2D corpus with layer and animation supervision. Demonstrates that the joint, cross-layer generation produces coherent, reusable assets where a layer’s mesh derives from its alpha, enabling re-texturing of clothing while preserving mesh and animation.
AI.conclusion: First end-to-end system to generate all Live2D runtime assets from a single image, showing substantial coherence and reusability benefits; joint prediction across layers is key, and the work supplies benchmarks and data to drive future research.

title: Asymmetric Collapse in Model Merging: When Refusal Over- writes Recognition
comment: Accepted into COLM AIW, waiting decision for AdvML-Frontiers x CoTMA and HAIPS
summary: Model merging is often used to combine capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. We study this question through a controlled case study using two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on two complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. We merge the two fine-tunes using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES, and evaluate the merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Across all four methods, attack resistance transfers significantly more than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Weight-space measurements suggest that this asymmetry is not caused by strongly opposing task-vector directions: the two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011). Instead, the refusal fine-tune induces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates. These results show that standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale.

AI.tldr: Merging two safety-related finetunes on Gemma-3-1B-IT with four standard methods preserves jailbreak refusal far more than CARES accuracy, indicating an asymmetry driven by task-vector magnitudes rather than directions; the result collapses multi-safety behavior into broad refusal.
AI.motivation: To determine whether standard model merging preserves multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously and to identify factors causing potential loss of one behavior when merging distinct safety objectives.
AI.method: Finetune two models on complementary safety objectives (CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal). Merge using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES. Evaluate merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance (jailbreak refusal), and benign compliance. Analyze per-layer task-vector magnitudes and cosine similarity between task vectors.
AI.result: Merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal across methods, while CARES accuracy drops to at most 12.9%. The task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity ~0.011). Refusal updates dominate due to larger per-layer magnitudes in the adversarial-refusal fine-tune, making magnitude-sensitive methods favor refusal updates. Overall, standard merging collapses safety recognition into broad refusal when safety task vectors differ substantially in scale.
AI.conclusion: Standard model merging can collapse multi-safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ in scale, not direction. This highlights the need for scale-aware or vector-normalized merging approaches to preserve multiple safety behaviors.

title: Cross-Embodiment Transfer via Behavior-Aligned Representations
summary: Recent progress in large-scale imitation learning for robot manipulation has been driven by leveraging datasets across a wide range of robot embodiments. However, achieving significant cross-embodiment transfer is often still challenging. In this work, we study the role of using behavior-aligned representations (e.g., object bounding boxes, language motions, end-effector traces of robot motion) in vision-language-action (VLA) models to promote cross-embodiment transfer. We hypothesize that by possessing invariances across embodiments while being predictive of robot actions, these representations can help unify large-scale cross-embodiment data to enhance transfer. To assess our hypothesis, we develop a simulation-based benchmark designed to assess transfer with diverse cross-embodiment data to new embodiments. Using this benchmark, we compare different representations and ways of incorporating them. We identify that end-effector traces can be particularly beneficial for transfer, representations are generally more useful with larger prior datasets, and can be used to benefit from action-free data. We also demonstrate that they can enhance sim-to-real cross-embodiment transfer, improving task completion progress of real robot policies pre-trained on simulation data by 28%. We provide videos of our evaluations at our website: https://ajaysridhar.com/barx/.

AI.tldr: Behavior-aligned representations (e.g., end-effector traces) improve cross-embodiment transfer in vision-language-action models, demonstrated via a new simulation benchmark and 28% sim-to-real gains.
AI.motivation: Cross-embodiment transfer in large-scale imitation learning remains challenging; representations invariant across embodiments yet predictive of actions may unify heterogeneous data.
AI.method: Develop a simulation-based benchmark to evaluate cross-embodiment transfer; compare representations (object bounding boxes, language motions, end-effector traces) and integration approaches; assess benefits with varying data scales and action-free data; test sim-to-real transfer.
AI.result: End-effector traces most beneficial for transfer; representations more effective with larger pretraining datasets; can leverage action-free data; improved sim-to-real task progress by 28% for real policies pre-trained in simulation.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-aligned representations, particularly end-effector traces, facilitate cross-embodiment transfer in VLA models and can enhance sim-to-real transfer; dataset scale and action-free data further boost benefits.

title: Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding
summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification. We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end functional reconstruction approach converts MHA/GQA to MLA to preserve cache efficiency without retraining, improving speculative-decoding draft-token acceptance across diverse configurations; the method optimizes MLA attention to replicate the post-output-projection response on calibration data, converter-agnostic and verifier-free.
AI.motivation: Direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion introduces attention-function errors due to low-rank factorization and RoPE handling, reducing agreement with drafts and hurting speculative-decoding acceptance. A converter-agnostic, post-conversion optimization aimed at reproducing the original post-output-projection response can preserve cache and inference graph while improving acceptance without retraining.
AI.method: End-to-end (E2E) functional reconstruction: optimize each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of the original MHA/GQA on calibration hidden states. Converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure that preserves cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor supervision.
AI.result: Evaluated 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations across four Llama/Qwen pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point tolerance, Functional Reconstruction improved acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, left 26 unchanged, and materially decreased one.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a converter-agnostic, training-free path to boost MLA draft acceptance by aligning post-output-projection responses, preserving cache and inference graphs; broad empirical support across diverse configurations; code is publicly available.

title: Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation for Unpaired Cross-Modal Medical Classification
summary: Cross-modal knowledge distillation can transfer diagnostic knowledge from a strong but costly teacher modality to a cheaper and more deployable student modality. In medical image analysis, however, the two modalities are often unpaired: they are collected from different patient cohorts and occupy geometrically incompatible feature spaces. This makes instance-level distillation invalid and direct feature matching unreliable. To address these challenges, we propose Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation (SSCD), which compares teacher and student representations through a shared discrete codebook. Each image is represented as a distribution over a common, modality-agnostic vocabulary, and knowledge is transferred by aligning these distributions across modalities, both globally and class-conditionally, without requiring paired samples or directly comparable raw features. The codebook is evolved online by exponential moving average and kept diverse through entropy regularization and dead-code restart. At inference, all teacher-side and codebook modules are discarded, leaving only the student encoder and classifier. On two heterogeneous unpaired settings, OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification, SSCD improves the student from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1 and from 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1, respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines on both settings. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/DillanImans/SSCD-unpaired-distillation

AI.tldr: SSCD introduces a shared discrete codebook to distill knowledge across unpaired medical image modalities. It represents images as distributions over a common vocabulary and aligns teacher-student representations globally and class-conditionally, without paired samples. The codebook is updated online via EMA and regularized for diversity, and only the student remains at inference.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal distillation in medical imaging is hindered by unpaired data and incompatible feature spaces between modalities. Traditional instance-level distillation and feature matching fail under these conditions, necessitating a modality-agnostic, discrete representation to bridge modalities.
AI.method: A shared discrete codebook (vocabulary) across modalities. Each image is encoded as a distribution over the codebook. Knowledge is transferred by aligning these distributions globally and per class, without needing paired samples. The codebook evolves online with exponential moving average and is kept diverse through entropy regularization and dead-code restart. Inference uses only the student encoder and classifier; teacher and codebook modules are discarded.
AI.result: On two unpaired settings, OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest X-ray pneumonia classification, SSCD improves macro-F1 from 64.5 to 70.2 and from 73.8 to 76.3, respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines.
AI.conclusion: SSCD provides an effective framework for unpaired cross-modal knowledge distillation in medical imaging, achieving substantial performance gains while maintaining a lightweight inference pipeline. The approach is validated on two heterogeneous tasks and code/models are publicly available.

title: Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion
summary: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

AI.tldr: A training-free inference-time framework that fuses a generalist LLM with a domain-specific model by per-token Jensen-Shannon divergence-based routing; improves performance on scientific benchmarks across Qwen and Llama families.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between broad reasoning and specialized domain knowledge without fine-tuning, enabling adaptive, inference-time policy composition.
AI.method: At each generation step, compute the next-token distribution from both the generalist and the domain specialist. Measure their disagreement using Jensen-Shannon divergence. If divergence exceeds a threshold, route the token generation to the generalist; otherwise, use the specialist. No training is required; the framework acts as a dynamic switch between models, akin to draft-and-verify with a learned roulette of policies.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench shows Divergence Decoding outperforms both the standalone specialist and the generalist across Qwen and Llama families, and even surpasses most single-model baselines.
AI.conclusion: Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free mechanism for inference-time collaboration and capability fusion across diverse LLMs. It demonstrates the viability of adaptive model routing to leverage complementary strengths; future work should examine latency, threshold calibration, and broader domain generalization.

title: A Systems Engineering Framework for Vision-Language-Enabled UAV Triage and Disaster Response
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures. Author accepted manuscript of AIAA Paper 2026-4010, published in the AIAA AVIATION 2026 Forum
summary: Recent advances in Vision Language Models (VLMs) have created new opportunities for disaster response, where responders must interpret large volumes of sensor data under time pressure. Current VLM applications include social media monitoring for situational awareness, generation of draft action plans, and translation of technical alerts into public-facing messages. While these efforts can accelerate information flow, they remain largely limited to decision-support roles. Such approaches can increase operator burden because humans must still translate outputs into coordinated actions across teams and robotic assets. This study explores the viability of embedding VLMs as coordination agents within the human-UAV loop. The proposed architecture integrates natural language interaction, mission-level task coordination, software-in-the-loop implementation, and communication aligned with the Incident Command System (ICS). Rather than functioning solely as advisory tools, VLMs facilitate communication between human operators, mission control logic, and UAV task execution. The framework was developed using a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach, with use case and block definition diagrams representing system roles, internal structure, and component interactions. Three key elements, the VLM Coordinator Agent, UAV Mission Control, and Task Allocator, were implemented within an integrated simulation and control environment. A preliminary human-factors evaluation with seven participants showed reduced perceived workload across mental demand, effort, and frustration, along with high ratings for AI trust and communication clarity. By integrating MBSE, software-in-the-loop testing, and human-factors evaluation, this work advances scalable human-autonomy teaming for high-stakes disaster response, with broader implications for aerospace autonomy and civil safety.

AI.tldr: Embedding VLMs as coordination agents in human-UAV disaster response, using MBSE design, software-in-the-loop testing, and ICS-aligned communication; preliminary study reports reduced workload and high trust.
AI.motivation: Overcome operator burden and slow information flow by shifting VLMs from advisory tools to active coordination within the human-UAV loop, enabling scalable, safe disaster response.
AI.method: MBSE-based architecture with VLM Coordinator Agent, UAV Mission Control, and Task Allocator; software-in-the-loop integration; use-case and block definition diagrams; ICS-aligned communications; integrated simulation/control environment; preliminary human-factors evaluation with seven participants.
AI.result: Evidence of reduced perceived workload (mental demand, effort, frustration) and high ratings for AI trust and communication clarity; demonstrates feasibility of VLM-facilitated coordination in high-stakes disaster scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Advances scalable human-autonomy teaming in disaster response through MBSE, software-in-the-loop testing, and human-factors evaluation; has broader implications for aerospace autonomy and civil safety; requires further validation in larger, real-world drills.

title: RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation
summary: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

AI.tldr: Reinforcement learning from performance feedback (RLPF) trains code models to optimize runtime in addition to correctness; using staged rewards based on execution progress and improvement relative to a baseline/expert, improves correct-and-runnable rates and efficiency on PerfCodeBench; composite rewards outperform correctness-only or runtime-only baselines; training transfers modestly to other benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Code generation models rely on correctness signals, but runtime efficiency is under-optimized because runtime is fragile and uninformative when many programs fail. There is a need to align training signals with the objective of fast correct code.
AI.method: Propose RLPF: a reinforcement learning framework that converts execution outcomes into staged rewards. For failed programs, rank by execution progress; for correct programs, rank by improvement from baseline toward expert reference. Fine-tune Qwen3-32B on PerfCodeBench using RLPF. Compare composite reward against correctness-only and runtime-only baselines. Investigate model-generated references and transfer to EffiBench-X.
AI.result: Correct-and-runnable rate increases from 11.1% to 54.6%; relative efficiency improves from 8.1% to 38.6%. Model competitive with stronger open-weight systems; optimization transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision; composite reward more reliable than any single-signal baselines.
AI.conclusion: Code agents can be trained to optimize not only for passing tests but also for execution efficiency; performance-aware training yields substantial gains and transferability.

title: PanDent: Toward Comprehensive Tooth-Level Structure-Language Consistency in Dental Radiology
summary: Accurate evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in dental panoramic radiography (orthopantomogram, OPG) is limited by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation. This work introduces PanDent, a large-scale, clinically grounded OPG benchmark built upon fine-grained, expert-validated tooth-level annotations. The dataset comprises 9,524 high-quality OPGs, each associated with comprehensive structured annotations produced by experienced dentists and further validated by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist, providing clinically reliable supervision for tooth-level diagnosis and reasoning. Clinically consistent radiology reports are constructed from expert-validated findings using clinician-defined reporting logic, establishing explicit correspondence between structured clinical evidence and free-text descriptions. This design enables evaluation of whether MLLMs generate reports that are not only linguistically coherent but also clinically consistent with expert-validated tooth-level findings. Experiments are conducted on diverse MLLMs, including state-of-the-art (SOTA) proprietary models, general-domain open-source models, and medical-specific models. Results show that current MLLMs can generate fluent reports, yet fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, exhibiting substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis.
