Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, substantially enhancing visual localization accuracy and diagnostic correctness, and bringing model outputs closer to expert dental interpretation. These results establish PanDent as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI.

AI.tldr: PanDent is a large, expert-annotated OPG benchmark (9,524 images) with tooth-level labels and clinician-validated reports, enabling evaluation of MLLMs' clinical reasoning and alignment between findings and text; fine-tuning improves structure-language consistency and diagnostic localization.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks for multimodal LLMs in dental radiography. Tooth-level interpretation and clinically consistent reporting are needed to assess true clinical reasoning in MLLMs.
AI.method: Assemble PanDent with tooth-level annotations by dentists and an oral and maxillofacial radiologist, plus clinician-defined reporting logic to link structured findings to free-text. Generated reports are evaluated across SOTA proprietary models, general open-source models, and medical-specific models. Demonstrated that fine-tuning on PanDent improves structure-language alignment, localization accuracy, and diagnostic correctness.
AI.result: Models produce fluent reports but show substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis; fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency and clinical accuracy, bringing outputs closer to expert interpretation.
AI.conclusion: PanDent provides a rigorous benchmark for tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI, enabling more trustworthy multimodal diagnostics.

title: PIE-APT: A Unified Framework for Temporal Planning and Contradiction Hunting via Incremental Direct-Derivation Abduction
summary: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) present significant challenges, especially in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms often face decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while managing incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires expansive combinatorial search. This paper introduces a unified framework with two integrated modules---\textbf{PIE-Abducer} (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and \textbf{PIE-APT} (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)---operating natively on the highly expressive Description Logic. We model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Treating the incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions natively in OWL without external modal operators preserves logical decidability. To address incomplete knowledge, \textbf{PIE-Abducer} circumvents traditional Minimal Hitting Set (MHS) enumeration. Instead of combinatorial syntactic search, it injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences. \textbf{PIE-APT} then employs a recursive \textit{Generate-and-Test} architecture, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with \textbf{PIE-Abducer} up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict validation via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. We evaluate four OWL benchmarks stressing semantic abilities absent in classical planning: parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners and prove our direct-derivation approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

AI.tldr: A unified abductive planning framework for dynamic knowledge graphs using PIE-Abducer and PIE-APT, enabling non-monotonic DL updates with direct-derivation abduction and Generate-and-Test planning, achieving strong performance on OWL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Open-world dynamic knowledge graphs with incomplete information face decidability, ramification, and search challenges; existing abduction (via MHS) is costly and limits scalability. A framework that preserves DL decidability while addressing incompleteness and planning under dynamics is needed.
AI.method: PIE-Abducer performs incremental direct-derivation abduction by injecting the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch to extract missing premises, avoiding traditional MHS enumeration. PIE-APT uses a recursive Generate-and-Test loop that interleaves backward-chaining A* search with PIE-Abducer up to a bounded causal depth, followed by forward-chaining Temporal Projection for validation. Actions are modeled natively in OWL without modal operators; state transitions are non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories on a linear timeline; the incremental reasoner is treated as a black-box. The approach is evaluated on four OWL benchmarks emphasizing parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting.
AI.result: Empirical results show qualitative superiority over classical planners. PIE-Abducer yields substantial gains over MHS-faithful baselines in abductive enrichment, demonstrating robustness to incomplete knowledge and inconsistencies.
AI.conclusion: A decidable, integrated framework for reasoning and planning over dynamic DL-based knowledge graphs is achieved, combining direct-derivation abduction with abductive planning to address incomplete information and ramification while delivering practical performance improvements on OWL benchmarks.

title: Arm2Air: Cross-Embodiment Skeleton Transfer for 3D Relay Formation
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) relay networks can restore connectivity after communication infrastructure is damaged. Urban relay placement is difficult because line-of-sight blockage, communication range, altitude, and three-dimensional obstacles must be considered jointly. Arm2Air transfers obstacle-avoidance skeletons from robot arms to UAV relay placement through cross-embodiment transfer. Source-domain robot-arm motions from a pretrained Neural MP model are converted into ordered skeletons that pretrain a transformer-based transfer platform, which is then adapted to the UAV domain using limited target data and Low-Rank Adaptation. The transferred skeleton initializes a relay chain that is refined for connectivity, bottleneck capacity, delay, and movement cost. On nine held-out high-clutter 3D urban maps, Arm2Air reduced median end-to-end planning runtime by 64.9 percent relative to the fastest conventional planner. On the high-obstruction group of a separate 30-map dense urban holdout, it increased bottleneck capacity by 32.6 percent, reduced capacity variance by 74.7 percent, reduced maximum hop distance by 13.2 percent, reduced hop-distance variance by 75.2 percent, and reduced relay displacement by 16.9 percent relative to IMPC-MD. With only three target-domain training maps, Arm2Air reduced relay-position root mean square error by 53.6 percent relative to training from scratch while updating 0.134 million parameters, compared with 1.383 million for Scratch and Full Fine-tuning. These results demonstrate computationally and data-efficient UAV relay placement and suggest a broader principle for transferring ordered structural priors across heterogeneous embodied tasks.

AI.tldr: Cross-embodiment transfer of obstacle-avoidance priors from robot arms to UAV relay placement using a transformer-based platform and Low-Rank Adaptation, enabling data- and computation-efficient planning in dense urban environments.
AI.motivation: Urban UAV relay placement is challenged by 3D obstacles, LOS constraints, and mobility costs. Transferring structured priors from embodied robots can improve planning efficiency and robustness with limited target-domain data.
AI.method: Convert source-domain robot-arm motions from a pretrained Neural Motion Planner into ordered skeletons. Train a transformer-based transfer platform on skeletons, then adapt to UAV domain with limited target data using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Initialize a relay chain from transferred skeletons and refine for connectivity, bottleneck capacity, delay, and movement cost. Evaluate on nine high-clutter 3D urban maps and a separate 30-map dense urban holdout, comparing to baselines including IMPC-MD.
AI.result: Arm2Air achieves substantial gains: 64.9% median end-to-end planning runtime reduction vs fastest conventional planner on nine maps; on high-obstruction maps, +32.6% bottleneck capacity, -74.7% capacity variance, -13.2% max hop distance, -75.2% hop-distance variance, -16.9% relay displacement vs IMPC-MD. With only three target-domain training maps, reduced relay-position RMSE by 53.6% while updating 0.134M parameters (vs 1.383M for Scratch and Full Fine-tuning).
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates data- and computation-efficient UAV relay placement and introduces a broader principle: transferring ordered structural priors across heterogeneous embodied tasks.

title: SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training
summary: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

AI.tldr: SDO introduces a structure-aware data organization that dynamically tunes mini-batch composition and sample exposure based on representation-space locality and per-sample exposure, improving data efficiency for LLM fine-tuning and instruction-following tasks.
AI.motivation: Data organization during training is static and ignores evolving exposure; over-/under- optimized samples lead to inefficiencies. Aim: make data sampling adaptive to optimization state to balance coverage and gradient quality.
AI.method: Epoch-level use of frozen external embeddings to form KNN-based locality batching within an epoch; across epochs, track per-sample exposure and adjust sampling probabilities to downweight over-exposed samples, achieving exposure-balanced scheduling; applies to SFT, DPO, GRPO; plug-and-play.
AI.result: SDO accelerates convergence, especially early to mid training; yields more coherent gradients and balanced accuracy across question types; avoids permanently excluding samples.
AI.conclusion: Exposure-driven, structure-aware data organization can substantially improve data efficiency in LLM fine-tuning and policy optimization with modest overhead by avoiding warm-up and using external embeddings; potential generalizable approach to data sampling strategies.

title: VideoCoCo: Code-as-CoT for Physically-Consistent Video Generation via an Agentic Dual-Engine System
summary: Text-to-video models have achieved remarkable visual quality, yet they still struggle to generate physically consistent dynamics because the temporal evolution of a scene must be inferred implicitly from a highly compressed text prompt. Existing chain-of-thought approaches introduce intermediate plans or visual states, but these representations are typically non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control the complete spatiotemporal process. To address this limitation, we introduce VideoCoCo, an agentic dual-engine framework in which executable Blender code serves as a process-level chain of thought. Given a text prompt, a coding agent synthesizes a Blender program that explicitly specifies the scene and its temporal evolution. The executable simulation engine runs the program to produce a deterministic spatiotemporal draft, which is subsequently transformed into a photorealistic video by a generative video engine through draft-conditioned editing. This decomposition separates process-level reasoning from high-fidelity visual realization. To adapt the video editor to simulated drafts, we construct VideoCoCo-3K, a curated dataset of draft-instruction-target triplets. VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks. These results demonstrate that executable code provides an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation.

AI.tldr: VideoCoCo introduces an executable code-based process-level chain of thought (Blender programs) to drive text-to-video generation, with a two-stage pipeline: executable draft simulation and draft-conditioned editing for photorealistic output; VideoCoCo-3K dataset enables adaptation; reported SOTA gains on PhyGenBench and VBench-2.0.
AI.motivation: Current text-to-video systems struggle with physically consistent dynamics due to implicit, compressed prompts. Existing chain-of-thought methods produce non-executable or sparse intermediate representations, hindering controllability and fidelity.
AI.method: A dual-engine framework where a coding agent writes a Blender program that defines scene dynamics; the Blender engine deterministically simulates a draft; a separate generative video editor then refines the draft into photorealistic video, guided by the draft. A VideoCoCo-3K dataset of draft-instruction-target triplets supports adapting the editor to drafts.
AI.result: OmniWeaving baseline improves from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving best average scores on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Executable code can serve as an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation by separating process-level reasoning from high-fidelity rendering.

title: PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments
summary: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. PAUSE captures core challenges of real-world assistant deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state, authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. The benchmark incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, enabling evaluation beyond static tool execution. To support principled and reproducible evaluation, PAUSE adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework aligned with task characteristics. Open-ended service management tasks are assessed using semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics, while constraint-intensive tasks admit deterministic, state-based verification. Benchmark results show that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns. Finally, we present a user-centric synthesis pipeline that enables scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks, supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

AI.tldr: A stateful, user-centric benchmark (PAUSE) for evaluating personal AI assistants in service-integrated environments with realistic user simulations and multi-regime evaluation.
AI.motivation: Addresses limitations of existing benchmarks that fragment service contexts and ignore persistent user state, enabling evaluation of user-centric, long-horizon reasoning under permissions and configurations.
AI.method: Introduce PAUSE with: (1) stateful, multi-resource coordination under authorization constraints; (2) explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation; (3) a multi-regime evaluation framework combining semantic/trajectory metrics for open tasks and deterministic state verification for constraint-heavy tasks; (4) a user-centric synthesis pipeline to generate coherent environments, user configurations, and annotated tasks.
AI.result: State-of-the-art models fail to reach 70% task completion on stateful, configuration-aware scenarios, with clear, interpretable failure patterns; provides baseline benchmarks and diverse evaluation regimes.
AI.conclusion: PAUSE offers principled, reproducible, and extensible evaluation for personal AI assistants in realistic service settings, enabling scalable generation of tasks and environments to drive future research.

title: LabEvolver: Training-Free Experience Evolution for Safe and Grounded Wet-Lab Agents
summary: We introduce LabEvolver, a training-free framework that equips safe and grounded wet-lab agents with episodic memory from execution experience. LabEvolver couples a state-grounded inner trial loop for adaptive perception, online planning, and safety validation with an outer evolution loop that distills completed trajectories into reusable skill, strategy, and safety experience. On robotic solution-preparation tasks, LabEvolver demonstrates real-world feasibility, reducing pH-regulation completion time and safety-gate intercepts by 48.2% and 60.0%, respectively. On ALFWorld, it further improves cumulative success rate within 20 steps from 76.2% with ReAct to 91.4% over 500 continual tasks, showing generality beyond wet-lab settings. These results support learn-by-doing experience evolution as a feasible path toward closed-loop automated scientific discovery. The project page is available at https://github.com/AndyGao6186/LabEvolver.

AI.tldr: LabEvolver introduces a training-free, two-loop framework that uses episodic memory from execution to create reusable skills and safety policies, enabling safe, adaptive, and generalizable autonomous experimentation across wet-lab tasks and simulated environments.
AI.motivation: Address the demand for safe, data-efficient, and generalizable autonomous agents in experimental contexts by leveraging learn-by-doing experience evolution to reduce human intervention and accelerate discovery.
AI.method: A two-loop architecture: an inner state-grounded trial loop for adaptive perception, online planning, and safety validation; an outer evolution loop that distills completed trajectories into reusable skills, strategies, and safety experiences, enabling training-free operation.
AI.result: In robotic solution-preparation tasks, it shortened pH-regulation completion time by 48.2% and decreased safety-gate intercepts by 60.0%. In ALFWorld, cumulative success within 20 steps rose from 76.2% (ReAct baseline) to 91.4% across 500 tasks, demonstrating cross-domain generality.
AI.conclusion: Learn-by-doing experience evolution is a feasible path toward closed-loop automated scientific discovery, with a public project page for implementation available.

title: Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision
summary: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

AI.tldr: BridgeMIL is a two-stage MIL framework for EEG disease diagnosis that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains an encoder without instance labels by aligning nearby windows and within-subject sub-bags with variance/covariance regularization. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, supervising only subject-level predictions and retaining features to limit drift. It achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy across datasets/backbones and reveals that subject scarcity impacts performance more than instance scarcity, with more structured subject-wise representations.
AI.motivation: Traditional EEG disease diagnosis often labels individual short windows, assuming equal diagnostic value, which is fragile due to noisy/inconsistent instance evidence. MIL can handle subject-level labels, but EEG datasets have many more instances than subjects, hurting end-to-end representation learning. A decoupled, two-stage approach aims to learn robust instance representations from unlabeled or weakly labeled data and then align them with the subject-level objective.
AI.method: Stage 1: Pretrain encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags; apply variance and covariance regularization to avoid collapse and reduce redundancy, no negative pairs needed. Stage 2: Transfer encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator; apply supervision only to subject predictions; employ feature retention to limit representation drift across stages.
AI.result: BridgeMIL achieves the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings across three EEG disease datasets and five backbones, with an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling instance representation learning from subject-level supervision improves MIL performance for EEG diagnosis. The approach yields structured, subject-wise representations, highlights variability in inherited-label reliability across instances, and emphasizes subject scarcity as a larger performance bottleneck than instance scarcity.

title: IGME: Efficient Chained Method Ensemble for Transferable Semantic Segmentation Attacks
summary: Semantic segmentation models are vulnerable to transferable adversarial perturbations, yet evaluating transfer attacks on dense prediction models can be computationally expensive. Existing ensemble attacks often rely on multiple surrogate models, increasing the computation cost, even harder for segmentation. This paper studies an efficient single-source alternative for transferable attacks on semantic segmentation. We formulate transferable attack composition as a chained computation over differentiable attack components, allowing the expensive source-model gradient computation to be shared. To reduce the update instability introduced by chained composition, we further use an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction as an empirical stabilization heuristic. Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes evaluate the resulting transferability efficiency trade-off across CNN- and transformer-based segmentation models. IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model.

AI.tldr: IGME provides an efficient single-source transferable adversarial attack for semantic segmentation by chaining differentiable attack components and using a path-averaged gradient direction for stability. It reduces computational cost compared to ensembles while maintaining competitive transferability across CNN and transformer models on PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational burden of evaluating transferability in dense prediction models by avoiding multiple surrogate models, addressing high cost of ensemble attacks while preserving transfer effectiveness.
AI.method: Formulate transfer attack as a chained sequence of differentiable attack components, sharing the source-model gradient across the chain. Introduce an integrated-gradient–style path-averaged direction to stabilize updates in the chained composition.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes shows IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime versus model-ensemble attacks, for both CNN- and transformer-based segmentation models.
AI.conclusion: A single-source, chained-attack framework with path-averaged direction offers efficient, effective transferable adversarial attacks for semantic segmentation, reducing computation while maintaining performance across model types.

title: SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis
summary: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

AI.tldr: SkillMentor learns blind-spot diagnosis as a standalone capability via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failures, and curate reusable corrective skills, enabling self-evolution without executor updates or human supervision; yields ~44.2% average performance gains on AppWorld and BFCLv3.
AI.motivation: Agents typically focus on learning how to act; diagnosing what they do not know (blind spots) is underexplored and should be learnable without human annotations or executor adaptations.
AI.method: Train a Mentor policy with RL to autonomously generate diagnostic tasks, discover recurrent failure modes, and curate a library of corrective skills for future use.
AI.result: Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%, demonstrating effective learned blind-spot diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability that can drive self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

title: Write-Safe Flow Field Mapping under Ambiguous Onboard Sensing and Localization Drift
summary: Mobile robots can infer local flow structure from onboard sensing, but a locally plausible estimate is not always safe to write into a global map. Similar flow structures may produce ambiguous observations, while localization drift causes predicted patches to be written at incorrect locations. Repeated misregistered updates then accumulate into persistent ghost structures. We address this failure mode with a map-reference-aware conservative fusion framework. The model predicts a local velocity patch and a learned write-safety score that continuously attenuates uncertain map updates while permitting initialization when no reliable map reference is available. Across synthetic jet and crossflow environments, the proposed method reduces average ghost contamination by 42% relative to ungated fusion. A zero-shot hardware replay using real pressure and optical-flow measurements from a thruster wake further reduces ghost contamination by 39% while retaining 81% map coverage. These results show that safe map writing is critical for flow mapping under ambiguous sensing and localization drift.

AI.tldr: A map-reference-aware conservative fusion method with a learned write-safety score suppresses uncertain map updates during flow mapping to combat ghost structures caused by ambiguous sensing and localization drift; achieves significant ghost reduction in simulations and hardware replay.
AI.motivation: Locally inferred flow fields can be misregistered into a global map due to observation ambiguity and localization drift, leading to ghost patches. There is a need for a write-safe integration mechanism that prevents erroneous map updates while allowing initialization when references are unreliable.
AI.method: The approach predicts a local velocity patch and learns a write-safety score that attenuates uncertain map updates in a conservative fusion framework, while permitting initialization in absence of reliable references. Evaluations include synthetic jet and crossflow environments, plus zero-shot hardware replay using real pressure and optical-flow measurements from a thruster wake.
AI.result: Compared to ungated fusion, ghost contamination is reduced by 42% on synthetic scenarios. Zero-shot hardware replay reduces ghost contamination by 39% while preserving 81% of map coverage.
AI.conclusion: Safe map writing is essential for robust flow mapping under sensing ambiguity and localization drift; the proposed framework provides a practical mechanism to suppress ghost updates while maintaining map utility.

title: Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents
summary: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

AI.tldr: Post-training 4-bit quantization of weights in tool-using agents is largely lossless for standard task scores but amplifies existing failure modes (e.g., tool-name hallucination) at the process level; the apparent safety on standard metrics is masked by evaluation budgets; targeted repair prompts can fully mitigate damage.
AI.motivation: Assess whether aggressive weight quantization (4-bit) preserves task performance for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, across model families and domains, and to understand its effect on failure modes beyond standard scores.
AI.method: Evaluate two open-weight model families (dense and MoE) across τ^2-bench in two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes per cell) at 16-, 8-, 4-bit weights. Use two metrics: standard task score with multiple-comparison correction, and process-level diagnostics (per-cell error rate, failure set consistency, rank correlations, novel events). Test across multiple architectures, quantify equivalence bounds (±7.5 points in most damaged cell), analyze failure budget effects using a ten-error budget and a two-error budget, and attempt a targeted error-repair prompt (five telecom models) to assess repair potential. Include cross-precision comparison of failures (tool-name hallucination, telecom; retail entity errors) and report diagnostics alongside task reward.
AI.result: Quantization appears free on standard metrics: no per-cell score changes survive multiple-comparison correction; equivalence bounds keep changes within ±7.5 points. However process-level degradation is pronounced: quantization amplifies existing failures by up to 2.5× in error volume and up to +17.6 points per task; the same failure set persists across precisions (rank correlation ≥0.94; 0.18% novel events). The overall score remains flat due to the benchmark’s ten-error budget absorbing the extra failures; shrinking the budget to two errors reveals a 17-point gap, localized to the cell where quantization added error volume, consistent with masking hypothesis. A targeted 5-model repair prompt eliminates the damage specifically where it exists. Diagnostics from logs benchmarks (per-channel error rate, success under shrinking budget) are valuable and should be reported alongside task reward.
AI.conclusion: 4-bit weight quantization for tool-calling agents can preserve standard task performance but introduces nontrivial process-level risks by magnifying preexisting failure modes. Evaluation should extend beyond standard scores to include per-channel error metrics and budget-based success criteria. Where feasible, targeted repair prompts can remediate quantization-induced damage. Practitioners should report both reward and process diagnostics to avoid overestimating robustness.

title: ProgFormer: Hierarchical Voxel Diffusion Transformer for Longitudinal Brain MRI Prediction
summary: Predicting future structural MRI of a brain is challenging because longitudinal changes are often subtle and confined to specific anatomical regions, while most subject-specific brain structure remains stable over time. An effective model should therefore preserve global brain structural consistency while remaining sensitive to fine-grained disease progression. Existing latent-space-based methods improve computational efficiency, but suffer from information loss during their compression-reconstruction procedure. In contrast, direct voxel-space methods avoid latent reconstruction but commonly use a unified prediction pathway to model brain structure and progression-related changes. Subtle local changes may therefore be overshadowed by the dominant stable brain structure. To address these challenges, we propose ProgFormer, a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction. ProgFormer uses a coarse pathway to perform the primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens. This pathway models overall brain structure and longitudinal context. The fine pathway then uses the coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within individual patches. The two pathways jointly estimate a velocity field directly in voxel space through conditional flow matching, enabling end-to-end prediction without a separately learned image autoencoder. The predicted future scan is then generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the estimated velocity field over a sequence of Euler steps. Extensive experimental results on three widely used benchmarks, ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS, under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favourable performance compared against several state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: ProgFormer is a hierarchical voxel-space diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction, combining a coarse 3D patch-based pathway with a fine voxel-level refinement, and estimating a velocity field via conditional flow matching to generate future scans end-to-end without an autoencoder; it achieves favorable results on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS.
AI.motivation: Longitudinal brain MRI changes are subtle and localized; preserving global structure while detecting fine-grained progression is challenging. Latent-space methods risk information loss; pure voxel-space methods risk overshadowing subtle changes with stable anatomy. A method that integrates global and local modeling in voxel space is needed.
AI.method: Two-pathway architecture: a coarse pathway predicts the main brain structure from 3D patch tokens to capture global structure and longitudinal context; a fine pathway refines voxel-level details within patches using coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding. Jointly estimate a velocity field directly in voxel space via conditional flow matching, enabling end-to-end prediction without a separate autoencoder. Future scan is generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the velocity field over Euler steps.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation on ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS under pairwise and trajectory settings shows favorable performance compared with several state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: ProgFormer successfully combines global structural consistency with local progression sensitivity in a voxel-space diffusion framework, providing an end-to-end, autoencoder-free approach to longitudinal brain MRI forecasting with strong empirical performance.

title: Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

AI.tldr: A paired, weight-matched study shows diffusion language model robustness is weight-dependent and not architecture-intrinsic; decoding routing is the fragility point, with overconfidence and ineffective prompt-patching.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate the robustness and calibration of diffusion language models (DLMs) under natural input noise and adversarial perturbations, isolating architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent effects using carefully matched model pairs.
AI.method: A controlled comparison using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B; Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbations, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses, examining both input corruption handling and decoder routing behavior; also tests surface prompt patches.
AI.result: DLMs exhibit highly stochastic loss landscapes that resist gradient-based suffix attacks but offer no guaranteed defense against natural noise; robustness is weight-dependent rather than architectural; models show systematic overconfidence; mechanistic probing reveals input corruption is perfectly encoded and fragility lies in decoder routing; surface prompt patches do not outperform noisy baselines; robustness cannot be patched and must be inherent in the iterative decoding loop.
AI.conclusion: Effective robustness requires integrating noise-handling and calibration into the iterative decoding process of DLMs rather than relying on architectural changes or surface prompt fixes.

title: RedFlow: Redirect Failure into Action-Level Corrections for Flow-matching VLA Policy
summary: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies have shown strong potential for robotic manipulation but often suffer from compounding errors caused by distribution shifts during deployment. While offline reinforcement learning (RL) provides a practical way to improve deployed policies using rollout data, existing methods either ignore failure data or exploit it only at the trajectory level, resulting in low learning efficiency and persistent errors. We propose **RedFlow**, a fine-grained offline RL framework that redirects failure experiences into action-level corrective supervision for flow-matching VLA policies. RedFlow consists of two key components: (1) a **Context-Aware Corrective Matching** mechanism that identifies failure-inducing actions and retrieves successful alternatives from similar contexts as corrective targets, and (2) an **Adaptive Redirection Objective** that jointly reinforces successful actions, suppresses undesirable ones, and redirects recoverable failures toward corrective targets. By converting both successful and failed experiences into dense supervision, RedFlow enables robust recovery learning from mixed-quality data. Experiments on the LIBERO benchmark and three real-world manipulation tasks show that RedFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art offline RL baselines, improving the real-world success rate from 56.7% to 74.7%. It also matches strong on-policy methods (PPO, GRPO, and DDPO) while requiring roughly an order of magnitude fewer training samples.

AI.tldr: RedFlow is a fine-grained offline RL framework for flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that converts both success and failure experiences into dense, action-level corrective supervision. It uses Context-Aware Corrective Matching to identify failure-inducing actions and retrieve alternatives from similar contexts, plus an Adaptive Redirection Objective to reinforce good actions, suppress bad ones, and redirect recoverable failures towards corrective targets. It achieves higher real-world success in LIBERO and real-world tasks, surpassing offline RL baselines and approaching on-policy methods with far fewer samples.
AI.motivation: Deploying flow-matching VLA policies in robotics leads to compounding errors due to distribution shifts; offline RL can leverage rollout data, but existing methods either ignore failure data or use coarse trajectory-level signals, reducing learning efficiency. There is a need for fine-grained, action-level guidance that leverages mixed-quality data.
AI.method: Proposes RedFlow with two components: (1) Context-Aware Corrective Matching to detect failure-inducing actions and retrieve successful alternatives from similar contexts as corrective targets; (2) Adaptive Redirection Objective that jointly reinforces successful actions, suppresses undesirable ones, and redirects recoverable failures toward corrective targets. Converts successes and failures into dense supervision to enable robust recovery learning from mixed-quality data. Experimental validation on LIBERO benchmark and three real-world manipulation tasks, comparing to state-of-the-art offline RL baselines and on-policy methods.
AI.result: Empirical results show consistent outperformance of offline RL baselines, increasing real-world success rate from 56.7% to 74.7%. It matches strong on-policy methods (PPO, GRPO, DDPO) while requiring roughly an order of magnitude fewer training samples.
AI.conclusion: RedFlow offers a fine-grained, data-efficient offline RL approach for flow-matching VLA policies by turning both success and failure experiences into action-level corrective supervision; its components enable targeted learning from mixed-quality data and yield robust real-world performance improvements.

title: The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models
summary:
A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

AI.tldr: Full, all-or-nothing alignment of the last circuit parts is the rate-limiting step for capability formation in transformers; partial credit is ineffective, with ignition behaving like a threshold process. The authors derive a rate equation and validate it empirically and in a controlled model, identifying targeted interventions (e.g., reinitializing query-key slices) that restore learnability.
AI.motivation: Explain how capabilities emerge in language models, quantify why partial credit fails, and formalize the dynamics and interventions governing capability formation in circuit-level terms.
AI.method: Empirical ablation and diagnostic analysis on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales; compare five-part vs three-part circuits; measure wait times and integrity of capability after ablation; derive a rate equation with sites × attempts × drive × exp(-β·K) minus destruction; forward/backward/complete analyses; controlled gated-attention model to validate mechanism; interventions including reinitializing query-key slices and manipulating SGD noise (annealing/pinning).
AI.result: A no-partial-credit regime is the rate-limiting step; removing three parts in a five-part circuit yields similar waits to removing three in a three-part circuit, implying wait counts reflect missing parts, not size. Ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in most discriminating cells, while partial-credit predictions would yield 50–83%. A rare-event ignition barrier grows with missing parts, enabling a rate equation. Forward ignition occurs once a concentration floor is exceeded and can be dated from the precursor. Backward analysis shows delayed learning for withheld capabilities, even as validation loss declines. Reinitializing only query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) whereas reinitializing value slices does not (0/6). The mechanism is proven in a gated-attention model where occupation enforces a deadline. SGD noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test; introducing noise and schedule-based annealing pins circuits and enables learning. Scope covers conjunction circuits up to 1.4B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Capability formation is governed by an all-or-nothing alignment of circuit components, with a threshold ignition dynamic and a rate-limited progression. Targeted interventions at specific circuit slices can restore Learnability, suggesting training-time strategies and architectural considerations to manage or prevent abrupt loss of learnability. The results are demonstrated on conjunction circuits up to 1.4B and validated in a controlled model.

title: Drawing-Recode: Annotation Grounding for Parametric CAD Code Generation from Raster 2D CAD Drawings
summary: Recovering Parametric CAD sequences from raster-format 2D Computer-Aided Design (CAD) drawings accumulated prior to digital transformation is important for part reproduction and manufacturing process automation. However, existing studies either process only vector drawings or are limited to specific domains, and fail to explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information, limiting their use of dimensional information for 3D Parametric CAD sequences recovery. We propose Drawing-Recode, a framework that generates Parametric CAD sequences as CAD code from raster 2D CAD drawings. Drawing-Recode extracts geometric features via an image encoder and recognizes annotations through a separate text recognition module, then explicitly grounds annotations to geometric information using cross-attention and our proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL). The resulting features are fed into a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format. Experiments show that Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions. We expect Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings and to part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

AI.tldr: A framework (Drawing-Recode) converts raster 2D CAD drawings into Parametric CAD sequences by extracting geometry, recognizing annotations, grounding them via cross-attention and Annotation Grounding Loss, and generating SPCC code via an LLM; it outperforms baselines and handles industrial-like scanned drawings.
AI.motivation: Raster 2D CAD drawings from pre-digital archives lack explicit dimensional-geometry linkage, hindering part reproduction and automation. Existing methods handle only vector data or domain-specific tasks and fail to connect annotations to geometry.
AI.method: An image encoder extracts geometric features; a separate text recognition module reads annotations. Cross-attention grounds annotations to geometry and uses an Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL) to align them. Features feed into a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate CAD code in Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format.
AI.result: Experiments show the approach outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings that resemble industrial conditions.
AI.conclusion: Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings for industrial settings, enabling improved part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

title: Bridging Inference-Time Scaling and Episodic Memory with Action-Centric Graphs
summary: Recent advancements in inference-time scaling have significantly unlocked the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, for agents, these approaches suffer from a critical inefficiency, operating in a stateless manner and engaging in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms largely rely on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, leading to prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, \textit{GAMER}~(Graph-based Action-centric Memory with Episodic Reasoning), that bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory. Our approach models historical reasoning as a dynamic \textit{Action-Centric Graph}. By decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, our method can save token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines. To extract knowledge from the graph effectively, we use a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate the positive~(suggestion) and negative~(avoidance) value of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During the inference phase, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally, so that positive values provide action suggestions, while negative values indicate high-risk actions. By performing efficient searches on the graph, our method significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that \textit{GAMER} achieves superior performance by \textbf{20.81\%/6.17\%} for success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

AI.tldr: GAMER is a graph-based, action-centric memory for agents that decouples memory from LLMs and uses TD-learning to value action nodes for efficient, guided inference.
AI.motivation: To overcome inefficiencies of stateless inference and memory-dependent baselines that rely on LLMs, by providing a lightweight, episodic memory mechanism that reduces token costs while preserving reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: Construct an Action-Centric Graph as dynamic memory; decouple memory from the LLM; apply dual-stream Temporal Difference learning to assign positive (suggestions) and negative (avoidance) values to action nodes based on past successes/failures; during inference, perform bidirectional optimization with the learned value function and conduct efficient graph searches to guide decision-making.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on multiple benchmarks shows GAMER achieves 20.81% improvement in success rate and 6.17% improvement in progress rate over vanilla baselines; also claims reduced token/money usage via smaller memory context.
AI.conclusion: GAMER successfully bridges inference scaling and episodic memory, enabling more efficient, knowledge-guided action selection in LLM-based agents through a decoupled, graph-based memory with episodic reasoning.

title: DexDirect: Direct Kinesthetic Arm Guidance for Efficient Dexterous Demonstration Collection
summary: Scalable collection of dexterous manipulation demonstrations remains a major bottleneck for robot learning. High-fidelity interfaces often require costly hardware and extensive setup, while low-setup, low cost alternatives tend to provide less precise control and impose greater cognitive workload on operators. We present DexDirect, a direct kinesthetic arm guidance for efficient dexterous demonstration collection. The operator drags a 6-DoF gravity-compensated robot arm directly by a handle, while a single webcam retargets operator's other hand onto a 16 joints 13-DoF dexterous robot hand. User studies suggest DexDirect collects 17.2x and 3.2x more successful demonstrations compared to purely vision (AnyTeleop) and pose-tracking (TeleDex) baselines. An adapted NASA-TLX shows DexDirect greatly reduces mental demand, effort, and frustration, despite raising physical demand. A diffusion policy trained on DexDirect demonstrations reaches a 90% success rate on a cube pick-and-place task. These results suggest that direct kinesthetic arm guidance combined with vision-based hand retargeting provides an efficient low-setup and scalable interface for collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations

AI.tldr: DexDirect enables scalable dexterous manipulation demonstration collection via direct kinesthetic arm guidance with vision-based hand retargeting, improving demo success and reducing mental workload; diffusion-policy achieves 90% cube pick-and-place; suggests efficient low-setup interface for dexterous learning.
AI.motivation: The collection of dexterous manipulation demonstrations is bottlenecked by costly high-fidelity interfaces and ambiguous low-setup methods that increase cognitive load. A scalable, low-setup interface is needed to accelerate robot learning.
AI.method: Operate a 6-DoF gravity-compensated robot arm via kinesthetic guidance using a handle; retarget the operator's other hand with a webcam to a 16-joint, 13-DoF dexterous hand. Compare with vision-based baselines (AnyTeleop/TeleDex) in user studies; assess mental workload with an adapted NASA-TLX; train a diffusion policy on gathered demonstrations and evaluate on cube pick-and-place.
AI.result: DexDirect yields 17.2x more successful demonstrations than AnyTeleop and 3.2x more than TeleDex. NASA-TLX indicates reduced mental demand, effort, and frustration, though physical demand increases. A diffusion policy trained on DexDirect demos achieves 90% success on a cube pick-and-place task.
AI.conclusion: Direct kinesthetic arm guidance coupled with vision-based hand retargeting provides an efficient, low-setup, scalable interface for collecting dexterous demonstrations, enabling effective robot learning in dexterous tasks.

title: Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance
summary: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

AI.tldr: Proposes a framework to diagnose long-horizon failures by comparing actual full-task success with a baseline prediction derived from short, individual stages, using the horizon residual (log-ratio of actual to baseline).
AI.motivation: Long-horizon benchmarks show failures grow with task length, but this does not reveal causes; a baseline built from short stages is needed to separate trajectory-induced degradation from inherently hard decisions or state changes (e.g., context rot).
AI.method: Define horizon residual as the log-ratio between actual full-task success and a baseline predicted from short stages. Require controlled experiments with identical agent configurations and pre-specified stage definitions, checkpoints, information access, and budgets to ensure fair comparison; use trajectory-induced degradation as the explanatory focus.
AI.result: This is a position paper that formalizes how to assess long-horizon failures; the horizon residual reveals differences between the full rollout and the chosen baseline, guiding targeted experiments to uncover causes.
AI.conclusion: To diagnose long-horizon failures, compare full-rollout results with a baseline built from short-stage performance via horizon residual; context rot is a common mechanism; further empirical work is needed to apply this approach.

title: Inference-Time Agentic Decision Rules Beat Longer Evolving Search for Multi-Image Medical Reasoning
comment: Presented at the CVPR 2026 Workshop on Multi-Modal Reasoning for Agentic Intelligence
summary: Multi-image medical VQA is not merely a prompt-length problem; it is a fundamental challenge of agentic decision-making. Medical vision-language agents must aggregate evidence across ordered images, remain robust to answer-order perturbations, and avoid overfitting to noisy search-time feedback. We study MedFrameQA through a controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies, optimized using the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration and evaluated on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test). Across five independent repeated runs, the strongest method emerges as the simplest robust aggregator: the \textbf{order-vote} policy achieves $57.89 \pm 0.65\%$ final-test accuracy, significantly outperforming the fixed baseline ($52.73 \pm 0.42\%$) and the more complex, albeit brittle, order-rerank variant ($55.79 \pm 0.43\%$). Paired bootstrap analysis confirms these significant gains. Extending the evolutionary search budget from 50 to 100 generations yields no generalization benefit: while holdout performance marginally increases, final-test accuracy drops from $57.89\%$ to $56.02\%$. Our findings suggest that for multi-image medical reasoning, defining the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget.

AI.tldr: A simple, robust order-vote aggregator outperforms baselines for multi-image medical VQA; increasing the evolutionary search budget yields little to no generalization benefit; choosing the agentic decision rule is more impactful than search budget.
AI.motivation: Address the fundamental challenge of agentic decision-making in multi-image medical VQA, requiring evidence aggregation across ordered images, robustness to answer-order perturbations, and resistance to noisy feedback.
AI.method: Controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies evaluated on MedFrameQA using a shared high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration, across a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test) with five independent repeated runs. Performance assessed via final-test accuracy, fixed baselines, and order-rerank variants; significance via paired bootstrap. Extended search budget from 50 to 100 generations tested.
AI.result: The order-vote policy achieves 57.89 ± 0.65% final-test accuracy, significantly higher than the fixed baseline 52.73 ± 0.42% and order-rerank 55.79 ± 0.43%. Paired bootstrap confirms significance. Extending to 100 generations yields no generalization benefit: holdout slightly up but final-test drops to 56.02%.
AI.conclusion: Defining the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than increasing the optimization search budget for multi-image medical reasoning; simple robust aggregators can outperform more complex, brittle strategies.

title: Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset
summary: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

AI.tldr: HLE appears unidimensional, measuring a general reasoning factor; domain subscores have little empirical validity; measurement precision is centered at moderate ability and poorly discriminates top frontier models.
AI.motivation: Assess whether HLE's eight domain labels reflect separable latent skills and whether the benchmark differentiates among high-ability LLMs.
AI.method: Apply a 2PL IRT model to 428-item, text-only MC subset with 29 LLMs; compute McDonald's ω_h, domain variance explained, domain residual correlations, domain-total score correlations; analyze test information function.
AI.result: Evidence for a single general factor (ω_h ≈ 1.0); domain labels explain ~3.5% of item variance; domain residuals nearly identical (d ≈ 0.016); domain-ability estimates highly correlated with total score (r ≥ 0.81); measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability (θ < 0) and drops above θ = 0, where frontier models sit.
AI.conclusion: HLE domain subscores do not justify distinct capability interpretations; the benchmark has limited ability to discriminate among strongest models; interpret results with emphasis on total score and reconsider domain labeling and item design for high-ability discrimination.

title: RoboBRIDGE: A Modular Framework for Bridging Policies to Robust Real-World Robotic Agents
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have attracted growing interest as a scalable approach to robotic manipulation. While these models are effective action predictors, deploying them as robotic agents exposes critical gaps: no mechanism for failure recovery, inconsistent execution over long horizons, and limited robustness to shifts in observations, tasks, or embodiments. Existing solutions address these limitations individually through model retraining or environment-specific modules, yet what is needed is a general framework that systematically transforms a pretrained VLA into a robotic agent. We present RoboBRIDGE, a modular framework that provides an orchestration layer over five coordinated modules, namely Monitor, Perceptor, Planner, Controller, and Robot Interface, to compose robust robotic agents from off-the-shelf components, including pretrained VLAs. The Monitor pairs rapid failure detection with hierarchical recovery to correct errors before they cascade. When the environment diverges from the current plan, the Planner triggers replanning while the Perceptor updates scene understanding asynchronously, avoiding execution stalls. Within the Controller, primitive skill fine-tuning factors manipulation into domain-invariant primitives with dedicated LoRA adapters, reducing sensitivity to domain shifts when a VLA is used. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world case studies spanning multiple robot platforms and VLA backbones, RoboBRIDGE consistently outperforms both standalone policies and prior augmented VLA deployments. These results suggest that reliable robotic agency does not arise from scaling action predictors alone, but from structured orchestration around them.

AI.tldr: A modular framework, RoboBRIDGE, orchestrates pretrained vision-language-action models forRobotics through five coordinated modules (Monitor, Perceptor, Planner, Controller, Robot Interface) to enable failure recovery, robust replanning, asynchronous perception, and domain-robust control using LoRA adapters; validated across multiple platforms and VLA backbones with superior performance to baselines.
AI.motivation: Address critical gaps in VLA-based robotic agents: no failure/recovery mechanism, poor long-horizon consistency, and limited robustness to observation/task/embodiment shifts; a general framework is needed to turn pretrained VLAs into reliable robotic agents.
AI.method: Introduce RoboBRIDGE with five modules (Monitor, Perceptor, Planner, Controller, Robot Interface) that orchestrate failure detection/recovery, replanning, asynchronous scene understanding, and domain-invariant control via LoRA adapters; leverage pretrained VLAs and evaluate across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world setups on multiple robots.
AI.result: RoboBRIDGE consistently outperforms standalone policies and prior augmented VLA deployments across diverse benchmarks and platforms, demonstrating robust, scalable robotic agency through structured orchestration rather than mere scaling of action predictors.
AI.conclusion: Effective robotic agency emerges from systematic orchestration of pretrained VLA components into a modular pipeline with failure handling, replanning, and domain-robust control, as demonstrated by RoboBRIDGE across multiple datasets and real-world scenarios.

title: TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification
summary: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

AI.tldr: Introduces TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts for sample-specific modality reliability in multimodal fusion, using out-of-fold unimodal-predictor losses to estimate risk; combines risk with expert subspace compatibility for sparse routing plus an always-active shared path; outperforms state-of-the-art on four biomedical datasets in predictive performance, calibration, Macro-F1, Brier score, and zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal fusion methods rely on cross-modal interactions but do not quantify modality reliability for a given sample, making it hard to detect unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched modalities; need risk-aware, interpretable routing in fusion.
AI.method: Proposes TIER-MoE: a risk-guided mixture-of-experts with subspace routing. Risk defined as the expected unimodal predictor loss for the sample, learned from out-of-fold predictions from models not trained on that sample. Combines risk with expert-subspace compatibility to achieve sparse modality-expert routing; includes an always-active shared path to preserve multimodal complementarity.
AI.result: Evaluated on four public multimodal biomedical datasets (Alzheimer's status, skin-lesion malignancy, retinal classification). Demonstrates improved predictive performance and probability calibration, with gains in Macro-F1 and Brier score, and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.
AI.conclusion: Risk-guided, subspace Mixture-of-Experts effectively identifies modality reliability and leverages it for selective routing, yielding robust multimodal fusion with better accuracy, calibration, and generalization.

title: Objective-Aligned Direct Answer SFT for Robust Multi-Frame Medical VQA
comment: Presented at the CVPR 2026 Workshop on Multimodal Foundation Models for Biomedicine: Challenges and Opportunities
summary: Multi-frame medical VQA appears to reward increasingly complex adaptation: controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, static hard-negative mixing, and staged continuation all appear plausible from first principles. We test a simpler competing hypothesis on MedFrameQA: methods that remain tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective should be the strongest \emph{robust} adaptation family once evaluation is controlled across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration. We compare controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The strongest robust family is direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B. Empirically, this family yields substantial improvements in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines while remaining remarkably stable across repeated seeds and matched controls, ensuring our claims reflect true family-level robustness rather than an isolated hyperparameter peak. Furthermore, post-hoc calibration effectively repairs confidence estimation without compromising accuracy, and the core approach transfers consistently to secondary backbones like Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The main result is therefore not that a complex auxiliary mechanism wins, but that objective-aligned direct answer SFT is the strongest robust adaptation family we found for MedFrameQA. By establishing this strong, minimalist baseline, we hope to redirect community focus toward fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity.

AI.tldr: Direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B is the strongest robust adaptation for MedFrameQA, outperforming complex controller-based and mixed-supervision methods; post-hoc calibration improves confidence estimates without hurting accuracy, and the approach generalizes to backbones like Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
AI.motivation: To identify whether robust performance in multi-frame medical VQA arises from simple objective-aligned training or from more elaborate architectural strategies, under controlled experimental conditions.
AI.method: Systematically compare multiple adaptation families—controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT)—across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration, using MedFrameQA benchmarks and MedGemma-1.5-4B, with transfer to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
AI.result: The strongest robust family is direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B, yielding substantial improvements in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines and demonstrating high stability across seeds and controls. Post-hoc calibration improves confidence estimation without compromising accuracy and the method transfers to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
AI.conclusion: Objective-aligned direct answer SFT provides the strongest robust adaptation for MedFrameQA; this minimalist baseline should redirect research focus toward robust optimization rather than architectural complexity, with demonstrated cross-backbone transfer.

title: Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure.
