Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

AI.tldr: Explorative Modeling (XMs) introduces training with multiple candidate generations and training on the best match, enabling end-to-end generative modeling and yielding major efficiency gains and strong results across domains.
AI.motivation: Generative modeling faces multi-modal distributions and is typically trained with factorized generation to scale, hindering end-to-end learning. A training paradigm that supports end-to-end generation and mode-aware optimization is desirable.
AI.method: Propose Explorative Modeling (XMs): during training, consider K candidate generations, compare to data, and train on the best match; demonstrates across continuous/discrete domains (images, video, language) and enables a new pretraining axis as well as end-to-end reconstructive modeling.
AI.result: Exploration scaling improves performance with data/model scale; FLOP efficiency up to 4.1x, sample efficiency 6.2x, parameter efficiency 47%; ImageNet FID improves to 1.43 without guidance; end-to-end reconstructive modeling matches diffusion with 16-256x fewer inference steps.
AI.conclusion: XMs establish a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and provide a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm, enabling end-to-end training and improved efficiency across modalities.

title: MMOOC: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Out-of-Context Evaluation in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks, but often fail under imperfect or shifted contexts. A reliable MLLM should refuse truly out-of-context (OOC) questions with subject-level context shifts while still answering shifted in-context (Shifted IC) questions with non-subject context shifts. Existing benchmarks mainly target OOC or visually unanswerable questions, but overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and cover limited OOC shifts. To fill this gap, we present MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating refusal and robust answering abilities of MLLMs. MMOOC contains over 41K image-question pairs, including answerable Shifted IC cases and unanswerable OOC cases, spanning three question formats, eight shift types and six visual scenarios, with data quality ensured through MLLM-based filtering and human verification. We evaluate model responses using Accuracy and Refusal Rate, and further introduce an LLM-as-a-Judge metric to assess the correctness of model reasoning. Experiments on diverse MLLMs show that current models still struggle to balance answer-ability and refusal under shifted contexts. We further analyze key failure patterns and show that post-training can improve robustness. MMOOC will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: MMOOC is a large-scale benchmark (41K image-question pairs) for evaluating MLLMs' ability to refuse OOC questions and robustly answer Shifted IC questions; includes three formats, eight shift types, six visual scenarios; uses MLLM-based filtering and human verification; introduces Accuracy, Refusal Rate, and LLM-as-a-Judge; shows models struggle; post-training improves robustness; public release.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks mostly cover either out-of-context (OOC) refusals or visually unanswerable cases, with limited coverage of answerable Shifted IC cases and narrow OOC shifts. There is a need for a dataset that jointly probes refusal under OOC and robust answering under Shifted IC to assess and improve MLLMs' reliability.
AI.method: Construct MMOOC with 41K image-question pairs across three question formats, eight shift types, and six visual scenarios. Data quality is achieved via MLLM-based filtering followed by human verification. Evaluation uses Accuracy, Refusal Rate, and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric to assess the correctness of model reasoning. Extensive experiments on diverse MLLMs analyze failure patterns and the impact of post-training on robustness.
AI.result: Current MLLMs still struggle to balance answer-ability and refusal under shifted contexts. Identified key failure patterns. Post-training can improve robustness. MMOOC will be publicly available.
AI.conclusion: MMOOC fills a gap in evaluating both refusal to OOC and robust answering to Shifted IC in multimodal LLMs, offering a large, diverse, quality-filtered dataset and new evaluation metrics to drive future research; intended for public release.

title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
summary: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

AI.tldr: Proposes a shift from consumer-centric AI literacy to a critical, empowerment-focused framework.
AI.motivation: Existing AI literacy models emphasize technical skills and responsible use, which may reproduce epistemic passivity and unequal access; a critical literacy approach seeks epistemic agency and governance participation.
AI.method: Theoretical synthesis drawing on Foucault's power-knowledge, Freire's critical pedagogy, and digital literacy to conceive AI literacy as three-part: contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance.
AI.result: A three-part framework that treats AI literacy as cultivating epistemic agents who can use, critique, and govern AI, with attention to structural inequities and epistemic injustices.
AI.conclusion: AI literacy should empower individuals to evaluate, resist assumptions in AI, and engage in governance, moving beyond training consumers to fostering active, participatory epistemic agents.

title: FasTac: A Curved Multispectral Vision-Based Tactile Sensor for High-Speed High-Precision 3D Shape and Force Perception
comment: 13 pages, 11 figures, including 2 pages of supplementary material. Submitted to IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics
summary: Curved tactile fingertips for dexterous manipulation must resolve fine contact geometry, distinguish normal and tangential loads, and capture transient signals. Existing curved vision-based tactile sensors struggle to combine accurate 3D reconstruction, three-axis force estimation, and high-speed processing in a compact form. This article presents FasTac, a curved vision-based tactile sensor integrating multispectral photometric stereo, dynamic-convolution force estimation, and hardware acceleration on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). Single-image-sensor simultaneous multispectral imaging provides spatially aligned observations for robust surface normal estimation, followed by boundary-prior fast Poisson depth reconstruction. HyperForce uses position-aware dynamic convolution to model the spatially nonuniform mechanical response of curved elastomers and estimate three-axis forces. The complete image-to-normal-force pipeline is deployed on an FPGA. Experiments show that near-infrared (NIR) illumination and the boundary prior decrease depth mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.2730 mm to 0.0415 mm; HyperForce achieves normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) values of 2.74% and 2.39% for normal and shear forces, respectively; and FPGA deployment shortens processing latency from 3.26 ms on the GPU to 1.09 ms. Multi-object reconstruction, feedback grasping, and vibration measurement validate fine geometric perception, stable force feedback, and dynamic contact sensing.

AI.tldr: A curved vision-based tactile sensor (FasTac) integrates multispectral photometric stereo and boundary-prior Poisson depth reconstruction with FPGA-accelerated HyperForce dynamic-convolution for fast 3D surface normals and 3-axis force estimation on curved elastomers.
AI.motivation: To achieve high-resolution 3D contact geometry, robust normal/tangential force estimation, and real-time processing in a compact curved tactile sensor for dexterous manipulation—overcoming the limitations of existing curved vision-based tactile sensors that struggle to fuse 3D reconstruction, multi-axis force sensing, and speed.
AI.method: Single-image multispectral photometric stereo for robust surface normal estimation; boundary-prior fast Poisson-based depth reconstruction; HyperForce with position-aware dynamic convolution to model nonuniform elastomer response for 3-axis force estimation; full image-to-normal-force pipeline implemented on an FPGA; near-infrared illumination used for improved depth accuracy.
AI.result: Depth MAE reduced from 0.2730 mm to 0.0415 mm with NIR and boundary prior; Normal and shear force NMAE of 2.74% and 2.39%; FPGA latency decreased from 3.26 ms (GPU) to 1.09 ms; successful multi-object reconstruction, feedback grasping, and vibration sensing validating fine geometric perception and dynamic contact sensing.
AI.conclusion: The FasTac–HyperForce framework delivers accurate 3D surface normals and fast 3-axis force estimation for curved tactile sensing, with FPGA acceleration enabling real-time performance in dexterous manipulation tasks.

title: The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
summary: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

AI.tldr: First convergence guarantees for plain Adam under heavy-tailed noise (p in (1,2]); suboptimal iteration complexity; known-domain-radius case achieves optimal rate.
AI.motivation: Deep learning gradients often exhibit heavy-tailed noise; understanding Adam's behavior under minimal moment assumptions is crucial.
AI.method: Extend online-to-nonconvex conversion to heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise; develop discounted regret analysis without restrictive parameter coupling; analyze convergence to (ρ, ε)-stationary points; study impact of known-domain radius.
AI.result: Adam converges to (ρ, ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise but with suboptimal iteration complexity and p-dependent convergence; with known-domain radius, convergence rate matches optimal complexity in the standard setup.
AI.conclusion: Provides theoretical insight into robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes; indicates need for further improvement to attain optimal rates without domain knowledge or changes to the algorithm.

title: Learning Color Grading, No Photo Sharing: Federated Aesthetic Preference Learning for Personalized Image Enhancement
summary: Personalized image enhancement should reflect individual aesthetic taste, yet learning such preferences commonly depends on private photos and ratings that are unsuitable for centralized collection. The task must infer preference from sparse, heterogeneous feedback and translate it into natural-looking color transformations on resource-constrained user devices. We introduce FedPAIE, a federated personalized aesthetic image enhancement framework for user-adaptive color grading without centralizing raw photos or ratings. FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to limit proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance. Training remains lightweight throughout the pipeline: scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer. Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity. FedPAIE thus connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches.

AI.tldr: Privacy-preserving federated framework for personalized image color grading with lightweight components and regularization to prevent overfitting to proxy scores.
AI.motivation: Infer individual aesthetic preferences from sparse, heterogeneous feedback without centralizing raw photos or ratings, and deliver natural color transformations on resource-constrained devices.
AI.method: FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer in a federated setting, calibrates it to a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer trained on unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to limit proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance. Training remains lightweight: scorer updates ≤0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation ≤0.265M, inference uses a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer.
AI.result: Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES show effective open-world personalization with a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity, validating decentralized preference learning for personalized image transformations without requiring paired user retouches.
AI.conclusion: FedPAIE demonstrates the feasibility of decentralized, privacy-preserving personalized image enhancement by combining a lightweight federated scorer with a local, regularized CLUT enhancer and minimal on-device training.

title: Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation
summary: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

AI.tldr: LLMs (GPT-4) can generate higher-quality ideas for college-student products, outperforming human ideation on average purchase intent and top-tier quality, but produce less novelty and more similarity; few-shot prompts yield the best average intent; overall significant potential with caveats on diversity.
AI.motivation: Assess whether AI-based ideation can outperform human ideation for new product ideas and understand trade-offs in quality, novelty, and diversity.
AI.method: Compare three idea pools: human (pre-LLM), GPT-4 zero-shot, GPT-4 few-shot; evaluate using market-research-predicted purchase intent (average), text mining for similarity, and human novelty ratings; analyze top 10% performance; price point ≤$50; target college students.
AI.result: AI-generated ideas show higher average purchase intent than human-generated; few-shot > zero-shot for avg intent. AI ideas shown to be less novel and more similar, especially with few-shot. AI seven times more likely to be in top 10% ideas; seven-to-one conservative estimate due to not counting productivity. Overall AI creativity offers substantial benefit for high-quality ideation, with diversity trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted ideation substantially enhances high-quality product ideas for new product development targeting students under $50, though designers should mitigate reduced novelty by incorporating diversity strategies and human-AI collaboration.

title: One Future, Every Robot: Label-Efficient Collective-State Prediction with Decentralized JEPA
summary: Can every robot in a swarm predict the same future collective state from only local observations and bandwidth-limited messages? We formulate this as decentralized shared-state prediction and introduce Collective-State JEPA (CS-JEPA), a recurrent joint-embedding predictive architecture whose output at every robot represents one common future token field. At deployment, each robot uses a 16-frame local history and one 64-float recurrent message per directed edge; there is no global pooling, target encoder, episode clock, or recorded future action. After pretraining without downstream collective labels, frozen representations are evaluated with ridge probes fitted on 6, 12, or 24 globally labeled episodes. Against raw-future reconstruction with the same receiver anchor and deployment capacity but 9,607 additional training-only parameters, a prospectively registered five-seed follow-up improves prediction-error and inter-robot-agreement label-budget AUC on in-distribution, ring, mutual-kNN, and unseen-size families up to 108 robots. Every effect favors CS-JEPA in 5/5 outer seeds. In a separate sealed eight-seed follow-up, matched action-conditioned predictors receive each candidate four-step plan before producing receiver-local predictive representations. CS-JEPA reduces branch-value MSE by 45.5% and improves within-context candidate-score Pearson correlation by 0.1291, with both effects favorable in 8/8 seeds, including at unseen N=32. These results support common-future JEPA targets as a label-efficient primitive for decentralized swarm prediction under topology and size shift, with additional evidence of planning-relevant value estimation.

AI.tldr: CS-JEPA enables decentralized swarm prediction by having each robot output a common future token field using a recurrent joint-embedding predictive architecture, trained without downstream labels and evaluated with label-efficient probes across varying topologies and sizes, showing robust improvements over raw-future reconstruction and evidence of planning-relevant value estimation.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a swarm of robots can converge on a shared prediction of future collective states using only local observations and bandwidth-limited messages, enabling scalable, label-efficient, decentralized coordination under topology and size variations.
AI.method: Introduce CS-JEPA: a recurrent joint-embedding predictive architecture where each node outputs a common future token field. Deployment uses 16-frame local history and 64-float recurrent messages per directed edge; no global pooling, target encoder, episode clock, or recorded future action. Pretrain without downstream collective labels. Evaluate frozen representations with ridge probes on 6, 12, or 24 globally labeled episodes. Compare to raw-future reconstruction with the same receiver anchor and deployment capacity, plus 9,607 extra training-only parameters. Conduct multiple follow-ups: five seeds showing improvements in in-distribution, ring, mutual-kNN, and unseen-size families up to 108 robots; eight-seed follow-up with action-conditioned predictors using four-step plans before producing receiver-local predictive representations. Metrics include prediction-error, inter-robot-agreement label-budget AUC, branch-value MSE, and Pearson correlation for candidate scores."
AI.result: CS-JEPA consistently outperforms raw-future reconstruction across multiple seeds and settings. Five-seed follow-ups report improvements in prediction quality and inter-robot agreement across in-distribution and diverse topologies, including unseen sizes up to 108 robots. Eight-seed follow-ups show reductions in branch-value MSE by 45.5% and increases in within-context candidate-score correlation by 0.1291, indicating planning-relevant value estimation. Across ring, mutual-kNN, and unseen-size families, CS-JEPA achieves 5/5 outer seeds favorable results. Overall, label-efficient common-future JEPA demonstrates robust predictive alignment in decentralized swarm contexts with topology/size shifts."
AI.conclusion: Common-future JEPA (CS-JEPA) is a viable, label-efficient primitive for decentralized swarm prediction, yielding robust predictive alignment and evidence of planning-relevant value estimation under topology and size variability. This supports scalable coordination in swarms where local observations and bandwidth-limited messages must suffice to forecast a shared future state.

title: FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize
summary: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

AI.tldr: FunL2O automates feature design for learning-to-optimize by using LLM-driven program evolution in a FunSearch loop, outperforming hand-crafted features across both continuous and discrete optimization tasks and multiple LLMs.
AI.motivation: Hand-crafted feature mappings are a major bottleneck in L2O, often fixed across domains. Automated, flexible feature design is needed to improve generalization and ease deployment.
AI.method: In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions; a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. Evaluation spans linear/quadratic programming (solution prediction, warm-start) and mixed-integer optimization (GNN-guided backdoor branching, Predict-and-Search) across four LLMs.
AI.result: Evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations across continuous and discrete tasks and across multiple LLMs.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution is a general, effective approach to automate representation design in L2O, enabling better performance without manual feature engineering.

title: Witness Evidence Portfolios: Single-Prefill Risk Detection for Closed Multimodal Answers
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures; includes supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/SouthWinter/WEP
summary: Reliable deployment of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) requires deciding whether a confident visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system. Confidence scores capture candidate margins, but not where the estimated signed visual readouts associated with those margins come from or how they are distributed. We study inference-time risk detection for closed visual answers using the same white-box prefill path that produces the answer. Witness Evidence Portfolios (WEP) first estimates, layer by layer, which visual contributions support or contradict the predicted candidate. It summarizes these contributions through two interpretable route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration. Nested grouped validation chooses the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, which is fused with candidate confidence. WEP needs no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier. Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model--dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs. WEP targets white-box closed-answer systems and uses a labeled calibration slice.

AI.tldr: A white-box, inference-time risk-detection method for closed visual answers in multimodal LLMs that decomposes evidence via per-layer witness contributions and two interpretable route families, selecting a sparse portfolio and fusing with confidence to improve error detection without perturbations.
AI.motivation: Trusted decision-making in MLLMs when visual answers must be trusted or escalated; confidence scores alone don't reveal the source of risk; need interpretable, layerwise evidence to detect risks at inference time.
AI.method: White-box prefill path; per-layer witness evidence; two route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration; nested grouped validation to select the more reliable family and sparse top-k route portfolio; fuse with candidate confidence; no image perturbations, decoding changes, backprop, or external verifier; uses a labeled calibration slice.
AI.result: Across three MLLMs and four binary benchmarks, mean error AP improves by 0.134; all 12 model-dataset gains positive; image-cluster bootstrap intervals positive on 10 of 12; demonstrates effectiveness of WEP for inference-time risk detection in white-box closed-answer systems.
AI.conclusion: WEP offers a practical, interpretable, perturbation-free risk-detection framework for closed MLLMs, leveraging layerwise evidence and calibrated routing to improve decision reliability without additional verification.

title: Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation
summary: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework to audit and compare agentic bioinformatics workflows by focusing on workflow trajectory (Function), traceable Support (Evidence), and context-specific Validation.
AI.motivation: Current reviews emphasize system type or final outputs but fail to ensure accountability of workflows; there is a need for auditable, transparent evaluation of agentic bioscience workflows.
AI.method: Define the Function--Evidence--Validation components; map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark resources (128 publications) across genomics, single-cell/spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation; analyze gaps in replayability, provenance, validation, and prospective testing; advocate workflow-correctness as the assessment metric.
AI.result: FEV framework defined and demonstrated via extensive mapping of systems and resources; highlights that planning/execution progress outpaces replayability and validation; provides a practical basis for auditing and comparing agentic bioinformatics workflows.
AI.conclusion: FEV offers a transparent, auditable basis for evaluating agentic bioinformatics; enables cross-domain comparison and guides design toward robust validation, traceability, and workflow-level accountability.

title: Machines that know they are aging: a framework for hardware-aware autonomous intelligence
summary: Autonomous systems inevitably age, yet their artificial intelligence typically assumes hardware remains in its original condition. Batteries degrade, sensors drift, processors accumulate timing errors, and memory reliability declines, creating a growing mismatch between assumed and actual capability. This can lead to agnostic collapse, where mission failure arises from accumulated hardware degradation rather than a single component fault. We propose Aging-Aware Autonomous Intelligence (AAAI), a framework that integrates hardware health directly into reasoning, planning, and mission execution. AAAI is built on three pillars: hardware self-awareness, which continuously estimates the health of power, sensing, memory, and computation subsystems using physics-of-failure models; self-adaptive reasoning, which adjusts inference complexity, planning horizon, and task priorities according to remaining hardware capability; and survival-centric intelligence, which allocates remaining operational life across mission objectives through performance optimization, resource conservation, and graceful degradation. Rather than introducing new hardware, AAAI unifies prognostics, lifecycle management, and hardware-aware computing into a closed-loop cognitive architecture. We argue that such integration is essential for autonomous systems operating in inaccessible or safety-critical environments, including space missions, marine robotics, and implantable medical devices. By enabling machines to recognize and respond to their own aging, AAAI improves resilience, extends operational lifetime, and supports safer, more graceful mission completion.

AI.tldr: A framework called AAAI that integrates hardware aging into autonomous AI, using hardware self-awareness, self-adaptive reasoning, and survival-centric intelligence to optimize performance and prolong operation in aging systems.
AI.motivation: Autonomous systems degrade over time (batteries, sensors, processors, memory) leading to degraded performance or mission failure. A unified framework aims to prevent agnostic collapse by accounting for aging in decision-making.
AI.method: Three pillars: (1) hardware self-awareness using physics-of-failure models to estimate health; (2) self-adaptive reasoning that adjusts inference complexity, planning horizon, and task priorities; (3) survival-centric intelligence that allocates remaining life across objectives via optimization of performance, conservation, and graceful degradation. Closed-loop integration of prognostics, lifecycle management, and hardware-aware computing.
AI.result: Conceptual framework with architectural blueprint and qualitative benefits; no empirical evaluation reported.
AI.conclusion: Integrating prognostics and hardware-aware computing into a closed-loop cognitive architecture is essential for resilient, long-lived autonomous systems operating in inaccessible or safety-critical environments.

title: ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders
comment: Research paper. Includes supplementary material and publicly available source code
summary: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

AI.tldr: ECG-InterpBench offers a capacity-controlled, reproducible benchmark for interpreting ECG foundation-model representations using sparse autoencoders as standardized probes, evaluating multiple models, depths, widths, and seeds to map interpretability dimensions and reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Current ECG foundation-model benchmarks emphasize predictive performance but provide limited insight into interpretability,faithful decomposition, or cross-analysis reproducibility of representations. A standardized, capacity-matched benchmark is needed to compare interpretability profiles across models.
AI.method: Use sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and match their capacity across models. Evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds to build a 450-cell interpretability atlas across 75 six-model comparison blocks. Metrics include sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements coverage, and cross-seed reproducibility. Also quantify patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to sparsity. Replicate on MIMIC-IV-ECG for validation.
AI.result: The study reveals that ECG foundation models have distinct interpretability profiles. Matched replication indicates reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility can identify different leading models. Provides executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits.
AI.conclusion: ECG-InterpBench complements performance benchmarks by offering a capacity-controlled, reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across multiple dimensions of representation interpretability.

title: JigShape: Evaluating Visual-Geometric Reasoning in VLMs through Jigsaw Puzzles
summary: Jigsaw puzzle solving requires jointly reasoning about visual content and geometric constraints, yet existing benchmarks use rectangular cuts that create ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions. We introduce \textit{\ours{}}, a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking pieces where geometric constraints provide strong local compatibility requirements that, combined with visual content, yield unambiguous ground truth. Across 95K instances at four grid densities (4$\times$4 to 16$\times$16), we find that \textbf{zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning}: only one of five frontier models (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4$\times$4 puzzles, while all others perform at chance level. While supervised fine-tuning achieves $>$97\% on 4$\times$4, \textbf{all models collapse on larger grids}: GPT-5.5 drops from 70\% to near-random on 8$\times$8, and even fine-tuned models fall below 5\% on 12$\times$12. This ``scaling cliff'' suggests current architectures cannot maintain consistent constraint satisfaction as the number of pieces increases. \ours{} establishes scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

AI.tldr: Introduces a tab-and-blank interlocking jigsaw benchmark (ours) with strong local geometric constraints to address ground-truth ambiguity in texture-repeated regions, evaluating 95k instances across 4x4 to 16x16 grids and revealing a scaling cliff where zero-shot and finetuned models fail to maintain geometric reasoning as puzzle size grows.
AI.motivation: Rectangular-cut jigsaws cause ambiguity in ground truth due to texture repetition, hindering evaluation of geometric reasoning. A benchmark with explicit geometric interlocking pieces is proposed to enforce local compatibility and enable unambiguous ground truth, enabling robust evaluation of VLMs' geometric reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: Construct a dataset of 95k puzzle instances using tab-and-blank interlocking pieces across four grid densities (4x4 to 16x16). Evaluate zero-shot and supervised models, including GPT-5.5 among frontier models, on puzzle-solving tasks to assess their geometric reasoning and scaling behavior.
AI.result: Zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning: only one of five frontier models (GPT-5.5) surpasses random baseline on 4x4 puzzles; others are at chance. Supervised fine-tuning yields >97% accuracy on 4x4, but performance collapses on larger grids: GPT-5.5 drops from ~70% to near random on 8x8; fine-tuned models fall below 5% on 12x12. Indicates a scaling cliff where constraint satisfaction cannot be maintained as piece count grows.
AI.conclusion: The ours benchmark establishes scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models, highlighting current architectural limitations in maintaining local constraint satisfaction across increasing puzzle size.

title: DeepResearch Agent System
summary: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

AI.tldr: A sparse-activation 30B-parameter LLM-based agent system for deep information retrieval and autonomous research, featuring a 128K context window, dual-mode reasoning (ReAct and IterResearch), multi-tool coordination, GRPO-based RL, automated data synthesis, and open-source release, achieving notable speedups and accuracy gains across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Enable efficient, scalable, multi-step autonomous research with long-context understanding and integrated tool use, addressing limitations of dense models in speed, context length, and modularity.
AI.method: Sparse activation architecture with 30B total parameters (3B active per token); 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention; dual-mode reasoning (ReAct for baseline tasks and IterResearch for iterative deep research with up to 20 steps); multi-tool coordination including retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing; reinforcement learning optimization using the GRPO algorithm with token-level policy gradients; automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion; fully open-sourced data synthesis, training, and inference pipelines.
AI.result: Claims include 3.2× faster inference than dense siblings of equal scale; 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context baselines; 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines; 92.1% tool-use accuracy; GRPO-based training stability improved by 35% and convergence by 42%; 92.5% usability rate for automated data synthesis; benchmarks: 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, 91.2% on WebWalkerQA; system is fully open-sourced and applicable to academia, business analysis, R&D, and education.
AI.conclusion: The system presents a strong, end-to-end research agent combining long-context capabilities, modular tooling, and reinforcement learning to boost efficiency and performance. While promising, the abstract omits experimental details (baselines, data, ablations) and reproducibility considerations; independent verification is needed for the reported gains.

title: TEA-AgriVLN: Traversability Estimation Alarm for Agricultural Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an agent to follow a natural language instruction, predicting a sequence of low-level actions to navigate a robot from a starting point to a target location. The A2A benchmark and the AgriVLN method pioneeringly extended VLN-CE from indoor scenes to agricultural scenes, while we observed a challenging distinction: In indoor scenes, whether a zone is traversable tends to be clear to classify, such as wood floors are traversable but concrete walls are not. In agricultural scenes, however, this issue tends to be ambiguous, such as an unripe cornfield might be traversable for a robotic dog but might be non-traversable for a human. To address this issue, we propose the TEA module, which estimates the traversability of the camera image, then alarm the decision-maker for rethinking when the predicted action does not align with the traversability map. We integrate it into the AgriVLN backbone to build our TEA-AgriVLN method. When evaluated on A2A, it improves Success Rate (SR) from 0.47 to 0.54 and Navigation Error (NE) from 2.91 m to 2.70 m, showing the state-of-the-art performance in the agricultural VLN-CE domain. We further implement the ablation studies and the case study, discussing the effectiveness and limitations of TEA on different ground categories and scene classes. Code: https://github.com/AlexTraveling/TEA-AgriVLN.

AI.tldr: TEA-AgriVLN introduces a traversability-aware module (TEA) for Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) in agriculture. TEA estimates camera-based traversability, alarms the agent when an action conflicts with the traversability map, and is integrated into the AgriVLN backbone. It achieves state-of-the-art results on A2A (SR: 0.54, NE: 2.70 m) with ablations and case studies highlighting effectiveness and limitations. Code is released.
AI.motivation: In agricultural VLN-CE, traversability can be ambiguous (unripe fields may be traversable for robots but not for humans). Indoor VLN-CE assumptions about clear traversability do not transfer well, leading to suboptimal actions. A traversability-aware mechanism is needed to align actions with environmental feasibility and improve navigation performance.
AI.method: Propose TEA module that estimates per-image traversability from the camera feed. TEA prompts the decision-maker to rethink action when predicted action conflicts with the traversability map. Integrate TEA into the AgriVLN backbone to form TEA-AgriVLN. Evaluate on A2A with ablations and case studies to analyze effectiveness across ground categories and scene classes. Code provided.
AI.result: On A2A, TEA-AgriVLN raises SR from 0.47 to 0.54 and reduces NE from 2.91 m to 2.70 m, achieving state-of-the-art performance in agricultural VLN-CE. Ablation studies and case analyses discuss strengths and limitations across ground categories and scene classes.
AI.conclusion: TEA effectively mitigates traversability ambiguity in agricultural VLN-CE, yielding significant navigation improvements. While promising, limitations exist across certain ground types and scene classes; further refinements could broaden generalization. Code is publicly available.

title: Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 29th International Conference on Information Fusion (IEEE FUSION)
summary:
Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

AI.tldr: Conditional generation framework for long-term ship trajectory prediction that emphasizes physics-informed conditioning on environmental context via cross-attention, with a Modality Masking strategy to handle sensor outages; achieves superior accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Addresses limitations of kinematic-only and multimodal baselines that treat environmental factors as mere features and fail to encode the directional physical influence of weather on vessel dynamics; also tackles data intermittency from sensor fallback.
AI.method: Proposes the Conditional Informer encoder-decoder. Introduces a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates—but is not generated by—vessel dynamics. Employs Modality Masking during training to mitigate catastrophic degradation when modalities are missing. Evaluated on AIS and ERA5 datasets.
AI.result: Outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Modality Masking reduces fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models and prevents shortcut learning.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that conditioning trajectory generation on environmental context with a physics-informed attention mechanism improves long-horizon predictions and robustness under sensor dropout; Modality Masking is an effective strategy to prevent degradation due to missing modalities.

title: RefineSVG: Visual Feedback-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Image-to-SVG Generation
comment: 17 pages, 5 main-paper figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). Includes the complete supplementary material
summary: We propose RefineSVG, a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework that enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation through self-correction. Existing MLLM-based approaches rely on single-pass open-loop inference, where the model receives visual input only once and must generate thousands of SVG code tokens without intermediate verification. This paradigm inevitably leads to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images. RefineSVG overcomes this limitation by invoking an external rendering engine after an initial SVG generation pass to compare the rendered output against the target image. The comparison yields a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) that is fed back to the model as a ReAct-style correction signal, driving a targeted correction step. To support this render-observe-correct interaction, we further introduce an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary that compresses token sequences by over 52%. A progressive training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning aligns the model with closed-loop visual correction. Extensive experiments show that RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.Code is available at https://github.com/liuxiaobo66/RefineSVG.

AI.tldr: RefineSVG enables high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation via a single-step closed-loop feedback agent that renders, compares, and corrects SVG outputs using a Diff-Map, aided by an SVG-focused vocabulary and RL-based training.
AI.motivation: Conventional MLLM approaches are open-loop and prone to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination when generating lengthy SVG code from images.
AI.method: Generate initial SVG with an MLLM; render it; compute Diff-Map residuals against the target image; feed residuals as a ReAct-style correction signal to drive targeted refinement; employ an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary to compress token sequences (>52%); training pipeline: supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning; evaluation on fidelity, structure, and code efficiency; open-source code release.
AI.result: RefineSVG consistently outperforms baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency, including reduced token usage via the compact vocabulary; extensive experiments validate effectiveness on complex images.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop render–observe–correct interaction with a compact SVG vocabulary and agentic RL aligns MLLMs with high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation, mitigating drift and hallucinations; code is publicly available.

title: What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering
summary: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

AI.tldr: Proposes an operational definition of prompt graph engineering as an explicit, executable prompt graph, validated across six systems, with a four-condition test and a four-axis research agenda.
AI.motivation: To formalize a practice already used in industry, aligning vocabulary, governance, and reproducibility of prompt-driven workflows.
AI.method: Conducts conceptual analysis of sources with persistent identifiers, traces the genealogy from dataflow/build systems to prompt-topologies, defines four constitutive conditions, and tests inclusion/exclusion via a four-part test across six systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, Claude Code subagents). Compares against six neighboring concepts.
AI.result: Provides a constitutive definition and a four-condition test for prompt graph engineering; demonstrates consistent inclusion/exclusion across real systems; clarifies boundaries with related concepts; delivers a shared vocabulary and an agenda for future research along four design tensions.
AI.conclusion: Delivers an operational definition and naming framework for a practice already in use, enabling formal study, interoperability, and governance, plus a structured research program.

title: X-NavDP: Generalizing Navigation Diffusion Policy to Novel Behavior and Embodiments with Group Q-score Reweighted Matching
summary: Pretraining navigation diffusion policies rely on large-scale expert demonstrations. These data are typically generated by a fully-informed oracle planner suited to a single nominal robot. This limits the policy's generalization to diverse embodiments and challenging scenarios (e.g., escaping dead ends or detouring long obstacles) that demand diverse local reactive behaviors with only onboard local observations. Post-training the policy with reinforcement learning (RL) offers a principled remedy. However, previous RL for diffusion approaches lead to only marginal improvements. This is because the intractable likelihood of diffusion policies renders policy gradients unstable in addition to inefficient policy exploration. To address these challenges, we propose a data-efficient diffusion RL post-training framework - GQRM (Group Q-score Reweighted Matching). Our framework introduces two complementary designs: (i) a self-bootstrapped exploration strategy with behavior perturbation that preserves the pretrained policy prior, and (ii) a group Q-score normalization mechanism that computes per-trajectory values on each state for efficient reweighted score matching. By conducting distributed online RL training across heterogeneous embodiments, the resulting fine-tuned policy, X-NavDP, achieves state-of-the-art cross-embodiment visual navigation performance, improving the overall success rate from 61.20% to 84.28% in simulation and 10% to 65% in real-world hard cases. The code and model are publicly available at https://yty-sky.github.io/x-navdp-project-page.

AI.tldr: A data-efficient diffusion RL post-training framework (GQRM) for cross-embodiment visual navigation that preserves pretrained priors while enabling exploration, using group Q-score normalization for reweighted score matching; achieves substantial gains across simulation and real-world tests; code released.
AI.motivation: Pretraining on single-embodiment, fully-informed planners limits generalization to diverse robots and hard scenarios. RL post-training is needed but diffusion policies pose unstable gradients and exploration challenges.
AI.method: Two design pillars: (i) self-bootstrapped exploration with behavior perturbation that preserves the pretrained policy prior; (ii) group Q-score normalization computing per-trajectory state-values for efficient reweighted score matching. Training is distributed online across heterogeneous embodiments to fine-tune a policy (X-NavDP).
AI.result: Significant gains in cross-embodiment visual navigation: simulation success rate 61.20% -> 84.28%; real-world hard-case success rate 10% -> 65%. Code and model released at project page.
AI.conclusion: GQRM enables effective, data-efficient RL post-training for diffusion-based navigation, yielding robust cross-embodiment performance and practical deployment potential; demonstrates that combining prior-preserving exploration with group-wise value reweighting can overcome diffusion-policy training challenges.

title: Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search
summary: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

AI.tldr: Contrastive critics are not reliably safe for max-based action selection; off-support values inflate due to norm drift and score saturation; cosine bounding does not fix this; TD-Q with value calibration improves ordering; contrastive scores can aid compatibility ranking but require calibrated scalar for selection.
AI.motivation: Assess whether contrastive critics can serve as effective value-like objectives for best-of-K selection, planning, and critic-guided generation, and identify failure modes and remedies across tasks.
AI.method: The study analyzes unbounded bilinear scores vs cosine-bounded scores, introduces a controlled support decomposition to attribute bilinear regret to norm drift, and conducts experiments with contrastive, cosine, and hybrid critics across OGBench navigation tasks (PointMaze, AntMaze, HumanoidMaze) and a toy exact-Q* setting. It compares against Bellman-trained TD-Q, evaluates costs via simulator rollouts, and uses training/readout decomposition to locate the source of misranking and off-support selection.
AI.result: Unbounded bilinear scores inflate off-support values; cosine bounding does not eliminate this issue. Norm drift accounts for most raw bilinear regret, but both cosine and hybrid critics still select off-support actions and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top decile and fail to rank fixed-query actions by value. TD-Q succeeds under a parameter-matched function class control. Costs vary by task: PointMaze and exact-Q* show single-step costs, while AntMaze and HumanoidMaze exhibit well-powered nulls where the controller can self-correct. Training/readout decomposition links misranking to the cosine objective; raw-trained embeddings preserve weak ordering after inference normalization. Candidate maximization can exploit false positives from norm drift, saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful as compatibility rankers for navigation/manipulation, but action selection requires a calibrated scalar.
AI.conclusion: For robust action selection, use a value-calibrated scalar (e.g., TD-Q) or calibrate contrastive scores appropriately. Contrastive critics are valuable for compatibility ranking, but direct max-based action selection should rely on calibrated value estimates rather than uncalibrated contrastive scores.

title: Calibrate Before Reason: Robust Visual Token Reduction against Semantic Drift in VLMs
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from prohibitive inference overhead due to long sequences of visual tokens. However, existing visual token reduction methods mainly improve efficiency by pruning or compressing redundant tokens without examining whether the resulting representation remains semantically consistent with the original representation. Mapping the original N-token visual sequence to K tokens may discard, dilute, or misassign critical visual cues, triggering severe semantic drift that deviates the VLM's understanding. In this paper, we first introduce the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' to visual token reduction and propose CaRe, a training-free robust framework that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning to preserve semantic fidelity in VLMs. CaRe consists of two mutually complementary modules: 1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which identifies calibration anchors with stable model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; 2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable calibration signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors. Extensive evaluations across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks verify that CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines. While pruning 94.4% of visual tokens, our method retains 96.4% of the original full-token performance, delivering up to 2.30 times faster end-to-end inference speed relative to unpruned vanilla models.

AI.tldr: CaRe (Calibrate Before Reason) is a training-free framework for visual token reduction in vision-language models that preserves semantic fidelity. It uses two modules: Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring to find stable anchors under perturbations, and Confidence-Gated Token Calibration to inject signals from unselected tokens into anchors. It achieves strong token pruning (up to 94.4% tokens) with minimal accuracy loss (96.4% preserved) and up to 2.30x faster inference across architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing token reduction methods prune or compress tokens but risk semantic drift, altering the original representation and hurting VLM understanding. A calibration approach is needed to maintain semantic fidelity without retraining.
AI.method: CaRe comprises two mutually complementary modules: (1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring identifies calibration anchors by evaluating model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; (2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration extracts reliable signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors. The framework is training-free and focuses on calibrating before reasoning.
AI.result: CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks. It prunes 94.4% of visual tokens while retaining 96.4% of full-token performance, achieving up to 2.30x faster end-to-end inference speed compared to unpruned vanilla models.
AI.conclusion: CaRe provides a training-free, robust approach to visual token reduction that preserves semantic fidelity in VLMs while enabling substantial speedups, generalizing across architectures and benchmarks.

title: From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

AI.tldr: Prompt-based Implicit Association Test applied to ChatGPT variants yields weak, analysis-dependent evidence of racial sentiment differences; no robust model bias detected.
AI.motivation: Assess whether LLMs exhibit sentiment bias across racial prompts by adapting psychological methods (IAT) to large language models, informing bias evaluation in critical domains like government and healthcare.
AI.method: Crossed 14 base questions with 8 racial categories plus a race-agnostic control (126 prompts); each prompted to GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4T (378 responses). Sentiment scoring: positive labels retain source score, negative labels invert, neutral=0. Analyzed with two-way ANOVA and rank-transformed sensitivity analysis; post hoc Tukey tests; notes on post hoc hypothesis generation.
AI.result: Small main effect of racial condition (F(8,351)=2.04, p=.042, ηp^2=.044); no main effect of model (F(2,351)=0.07, p=.933) or interaction (F(16,351)=0.23, p=.999); rank-transformed analysis non-significant (F(8,351)=1.53, p=.145); Tukey-corrected pairwise differences non-significant; one uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian difference reported as hypothesis-generating; overall weak, analysis-dependent evidence. Sentiment scoring cannot disentangle evaluative bias from content valence.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights limitations of sentiment-based bias measures in LLMs and calls for design improvements and interdisciplinary development of behavioral bias metrics for models.

title: FA-RDP: A Frequency-Adaptive Reactive Diffusion Policy for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: In contact-rich manipulation, action multimodality and reactivity dominate different stages of a single episode. Before contact, multiple trajectories might be equally valid, making it important to preserve diverse action modes. After contact, geometric constraints and force limits narrow the solution space, while successful execution demands rapid responses to force feedback. However, standard diffusion policies use a fixed inference frequency and sampling steps throughout the episode, forcing a fundamental compromise: low-frequency, multi-step sampling better preserves pre-contact multimodality but responds slowly to force feedback, whereas high-frequency sampling improves reactivity but tends to collapse distinct pre-contact modes. To resolve this tradeoff, we present FA-RDP, a frequency-adaptive reactive diffusion policy. A shared multi-frequency visual-force Transformer predicts action chunks at both low and high frequencies, while a learned multimodality indicator dynamically selects multi-step low-frequency sampling before contact and one-step high-frequency sampling as action ambiguity decreases. We further introduce Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD), which reparameterizes the diffusion network to predict actions on the robot action manifold while retaining DDPM-based residual supervision. Experiments on three contact-rich manipulation tasks show that FA-RDP achieves the highest success rate while preserving diverse pre-contact trajectory modes. Code and videos are available at https://fa-rdp.github.io.

AI.tldr: Frequency-adaptive diffusion policy for contact-rich manipulation (FA-RDP) with manifold-consistent distillation (MCD) to preserve pre-contact multimodality and ensure post-contact reactivity.
AI.motivation: Diffusion policies with fixed inference frequency force a trade-off: low-frequency sampling preserves diverse pre-contact modes but is slow to respond; high-frequency sampling improves reactivity but collapses multimodal pre-contact trajectories.
AI.method: FA-RDP uses a shared multi-frequency visual-force Transformer to predict action chunks at both low and high frequencies. A learned multimodality indicator dynamically selects multi-step low-frequency sampling before contact and one-step high-frequency sampling as action ambiguity decreases. Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD) reparameterizes the diffusion network to predict actions on the robot action manifold while retaining DDPM-based residual supervision.
AI.result: Experiments on three contact-rich manipulation tasks show FA-RDP achieves the highest success rate while preserving diverse pre-contact trajectory modes. Code and videos are available at the authors' site.
AI.conclusion: The approach resolves the fixed-frequency trade-off in diffusion-based policies for contact-rich manipulation by enabling frequency-adaptive sampling and manifold-aware action prediction, leading to improved success and maintained multimodality.

title: SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups
summary: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

AI.tldr: SE(3)-MeanFlow enables few-step, simulation-free diffusion-style backbone generation by operating in the Lie algebra and deriving closed-form velocity targets, outperforming flow-matching baselines with fewer sampling steps.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational bottleneck of SE(3)-based generative models for protein backbones by avoiding ODE integration and Jacobian-vector products, enabling faster, high-throughput design.
AI.method: Extend MeanFlow to SE(3) by working in so(3) and R^3; derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations; introduce SE(3) alpha-Flow to remove JVP in the rotation branch; use a warm-up stage followed by a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss; apply rectification-based post-training.
AI.result: Matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that require multiple times more sampling steps; the advantage increases in the few-step regime, with rectification enabling leading performance at matched budgets, with a modest diversity trade-off.
AI.conclusion: SE(3)-MeanFlow provides a fast, principled, few-step generative framework on Lie group geometry for protein backbone design, offering simulation-free training targets and competitive or superior performance compared with heavier baselines.

title: PrintAnything: Learning an Intermediate Representation for 3D printing G-code Generation
summary: Point clouds are one of the most fundamental and widely used 3D representations, serving as the most basic geometric representation of 3D shapes. Nevertheless, most existing 3D printing pipelines require a watertight mesh as input, preventing the direct use of point clouds for fabrication. A common workaround is to reconstruct meshes from point clouds; however, the resulting meshes often contain geometric artifacts, such as incorrect faces or topological inconsistencies, that are difficult to repair and may lead to printing failures. To overcome these limitations, we propose PrintAnything, a novel framework that learns to produce executable 3D printing G-code directly from 3D point clouds without requiring mesh reconstruction. To enable point clouds to serve as direct input for slice-wise toolpath generation, we introduce a slice-wise point projection strategy that transforms unstructured 3D point clouds into slice-aligned 2D representations consistent with layer-by-layer nature of fused deposition modeling in 3D printing.
