AI.method: Decompose state into a learnable anchor and an initial deviation; allow nonzero deviations to drive recurrence while mapping zero deviation to zero; enforce exact anchor invariance with a zero-deviation mask; set zero-deviation forcing bias to zero as a design choice; the anchor serves as a one-step fixed point.
AI.result: Empirical gains in controlled recurrent quality across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA; ablations identify the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the main contributors; a trained-model case study links anchor-response dynamics to observed recurrent motion.
AI.conclusion: SCSE provides a principled mechanism to reconcile input conditioning with shared recurrence, guaranteeing exact anchor invariance and reducing the previously ambiguous role of zero-deviation bias, yielding robust improvements in looped Transformer performance across diverse benchmarks.

title: Now You Have My Healthy Attention: A U-DiT for Brain-MRI Inpainting
summary: The ASNR-MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis (Inpainting) task asks for the anatomically plausible completion of healthy brain tissue within a masked region of a T1-weighted MRI, providing a tumor-free anatomical reference for downstream analysis. As the task is scored by distortion metrics (SSIM, PSNR, MSE), we build a deterministic regression model and focus on giving it inductive biases tailored to inpainting. Our network follows the U-DiT principle of performing self-attention on a downsampled token grid: a volumetric encoder-decoder imports long-range context through a downsampled global self-attention block with three-dimensional rotary position embeddings, while convolutions and skip connections preserve high-frequency detail. Two ideas drive our results. First, we constrain the attention so that occluded ("void") tokens attend only to known-healthy tokens of the same volume, with a learned bias toward each query's contralateral homologue, forcing the completion to be inferred from observed anatomy rather than from other unknown regions. Second, we add a contralateral-symmetry input that supplies the mirrored healthy hemisphere as a patient-specific prior; since the brain is approximately bilaterally symmetric and lesions are typically unilateral, this prior improves the distortion metrics at matched structural similarity. On the official BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard our submission reaches a mean healthy-region SSIM of $0.864$, PSNR of $24.7$\,dB and MSE of $4.6{\times}10^{-3}$ over $219$ cases. We further analyse the residual smoothness inherent to distortion-optimal regression and discuss its implications for anatomical realism.

AI.tldr: Deterministic 3D inpainting model using U-DiT with occlusion-aware attention and contralateral symmetry prior; achieves strong distortion metrics on BraTS-2026.
AI.motivation: Provide anatomically plausible completion of healthy tissue inside masked region to support downstream analyses; leverage global context while preserving fine details; enforce inference from observed healthy anatomy and symmetry.
AI.method: Volumetric encoder-decoder with downsampled token grid; global self-attention on coarse grid; 3D rotary position embeddings; skip connections; occluded tokens restricted to known-healthy same-volume tokens with learned bias toward contralateral homologues; additional patient-specific contralateral symmetry input as a prior.
AI.result: Validation metrics: mean healthy-region SSIM 0.864, PSNR 24.7 dB, MSE 4.6e-3 over 219 cases; analysis of residual smoothness and implications for realism.
AI.conclusion: Inductive biases tailored to inpainting yield strong distortion metrics and highlight the role of symmetry priors and constrained attention; potential limitations include reliance on bilateral symmetry and the need to evaluate realism beyond distortion metrics.

title: Simplifying Neural Networks During Training
summary: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

AI.tldr: NC-inspired training framework identifies when to simplify networks by monitoring representation collapse with Inverse Fisher Criterion, then replaces trailing layers with a lightweight head; achieves major parameter reduction with little accuracy loss across MLP, VGG, and ResNet.
AI.motivation: Exploit overparameterized networks by simplifying during training, leveraging Neural Collapse (structured class representations) and the Tunnel Effect (essential layers for feature extraction) to reduce computation without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: Monitor representation dynamics using the Inverse Fisher Criterion as a stable proxy for variability collapse to locate the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable; replace trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model; validate on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures.
AI.result: Shows substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to the full model across multiple architectures; code available at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: ND-based, NC-inspired dynamic network simplification during training is viable; Inverse Fisher Criterion effectively signals when to prune, enabling efficient compression with minimal performance loss and broad applicability across architectures.

title: Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective
summary:
Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

AI.tldr: Unified theoretical framework for Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) linking TI/MI objectives to intra-class and inter-class geometric/statistical structure; theoretical mappings for Graph Cut / LogDet / Facility Location variants; synthetic validation showing alignment with theory; guidance for designing SIM-based objectives in representation learning.
AI.motivation: Understand the geometric and statistical implications of SIMs and connect them to classical representation learning concepts (variance, covariance, centroid separation, Mahalanobis distance, etc.).
AI.method: Develop a unified framework that maps Total Information (TI) and Mutual Information (MI) objectives—across Graph Cut, LogDet, and Facility Location variants—to intra-class (within-class variance, generalized variance, imbalance-aware separation) and inter-class (centroid/Fisher-like separation, Mahalanobis-distance separation, nearest-mode overlap) structure. Validate with controlled synthetic experiments varying variance, covariance, class imbalance, separation, and multimodal overlap.
AI.result: TI objectives characterize intra-class structure (VAR, generalized variance, covariance volume, imbalance-aware separation); MI objectives characterize inter-class structure (centroid separation, Fisher-type discrimination, Mahalanobis-distance separation, nearest-mode overlap). Empirical results from synthetic experiments align with the theoretical mappings, supporting a unified geometric/statistical view of SIMs.
AI.conclusion: First unified geometric and statistical understanding of SIMs, enabling principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

title: ViP-Rig: Visual-Prompted Controllable Rigging
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Zihan Qin and Mingze Sun contributed equally. Xianming Liu is the corresponding author
summary: Rigging is inherently task-dependent because the same mesh may require different skeletons and deformation behaviors across animation tasks. In practice, artists often inspect an initial rig and repeatedly edit its skeletal structure and deformation behavior to meet specific animation requirements. Existing automatic methods primarily generate a plausible rig from geometry, offering limited explicit control over the resulting skeleton and deformation behavior. In this work, we present ViP-Rig, a visual-prompted framework that supports both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing by injecting features extracted from user-drawn or edited 2D skeletal and rigidity prompts into frozen pretrained backbones. Specifically, ViP-Rig consists of two stages, Skeleton Generation and Skinning Prediction. In the first stage, the skeletal sketch is processed by the Dense-to-Compact Visual Prompt Encoding to produce compact, fixed-length conditioning tokens. The resulting tokens are injected into a frozen pretrained autoregressive generator through gated adapters to control joint placement and branching structure while preserving the generator's geometric prior. In the second stage, the rigidity map is processed using the same visual encoding design, while the pretrained skinning backbone remains frozen. The resulting tokens are symmetrically injected into the point and joint streams to modulate point-joint compatibility and the resulting skinning weights. Experiments on Articulation-XL2.0 and zero-shot evaluation on ModelsResource show that ViP-Rig more accurately recovers target skeletons and skinning weights than geometry-conditioned baselines under prompt-guided evaluation. Qualitative results further demonstrate explicit and localized control in both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing.

AI.tldr: ViP-Rig introduces a visual-prompted rigging framework that enables prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing by injecting 2D-skeletal and rigidity prompts into frozen backbones, using a two-stage pipeline (Skeleton Generation and Skinning Prediction) to achieve explicit control over skeletons and deformation weights with improved accuracy over geometry-conditioned baselines.
AI.motivation: Rigging is inherently task-dependent and current automatic methods offer only geometry-based, weakly controllable rigs. There is a need for controllable rigging that can adapt to different animation tasks through user prompts.
AI.method: Proposes Dense-to-Compact Visual Prompt Encoding to produce fixed-length conditioning tokens from user prompts. These tokens are injected into frozen pretrained autoregressive generators via gated adapters to control joint placement and branching for skeletons, and similarly into skinning backbones to modulate point-joint compatibility and skinning weights. Two-stage pipeline: Skeleton Generation and Skinning Prediction; both backbones remain frozen.
AI.result: ViP-Rig achieves more accurate recovery of target skeletons and skinning weights than geometry-conditioned baselines, demonstrated on Articulation-XL2.0 with prompt-guided evaluation and zero-shot evaluation on ModelsResource. Qualitative results show explicit, localized control in both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing.
AI.conclusion: ViP-Rig enables explicit, user-guided rigging while preserving geometric priors, improving control over skeleton topology and skinning, and supporting both prompt-driven and result-driven editing through a frozen-backbone, prompting framework.

title: Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs
summary:
Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

AI.tldr: CTDG next-destination prediction benchmarks are highly sensitive to negative sampling and candidate-set configuration, which can flip model rankings and inflate/deflate scores. The authors show that even uniform, finite candidate sets propagate sampler bias into evaluation and propose all-entity ranking as the primary, unbiased evaluation method for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Evaluation of CTDG models using sampled negatives is unstable and potentially misleading due to the sampler's influence on scores. There is a need for evaluation designs that separate model quality from sampling choices.
AI.method: Factorial evaluation across repeated/new positives and seen/unseen negatives; minimal scorer based on pair-history membership; controlled representation interventions; experiments on six models/datasets (LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, Wikipedia) comparing Uniform-20 metric to full catalog.
AI.result: Model rankings can change between the expected Uniform-20 metric and full catalog; the effect of modules varies with candidate-set size and training objective; negative sampling and time-varying history leakage influence evaluation; all-entity ranking eliminates negative-selection and sampling variation, offering a clearer basis for architecture comparisons.
AI.conclusion: All-entity ranking should be the primary evidence for CTDG architectural comparisons when a full catalog is enumerable; report sampling-based metrics as supplementary and explicitly analyze the influence of candidate set size and negatives to avoid misleading conclusions.

title: FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning
summary: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: FedOGL mitigates catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graph learning by preserving semantic-structural memory, with client-side replay/distillation and global structure projection, and server-side compact prototypes for privacy-preserving cross-client knowledge sharing; achieves a 42.67% reduction in forgetting relative to strong baselines.
AI.motivation: In federated graph learning with private multimodal streams, models must continually learn emerging classes while preserving historical categories and rejecting unknown samples. Catastrophic forgetting arises from modality-semantic overwriting, topology erosion, and federated memory fragmentation, especially when sharing updates across clients without central data access.
AI.method: FedOGL introduces a dual-level memory preservation framework. On the client side, historical decision behavior is preserved via replay and task-start distillation, and graph-propagation memory is protected by projection onto a globally shared structural basis. On the server side, compact category prototypes are maintained and transferred to enable cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows FedOGL reduces forgetting-induced performance degradation by 42.67% compared to the best-performing baselines, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: FedOGL effectively preserves semantic-structural knowledge in federated multimodal graph learning, enabling robust continual learning across clients with data privacy, and enabling efficient cross-client knowledge sharing through prototypes.

title: Deep learning-based hierarchical insect classification using camera trap imagery
summary: Declining insect populations make reliable biodiversity monitoring increasingly urgent, yet monitoring of insect biodiversity is hampered by a lack of standardised data and by costly and time-consuming manual identification by expert entomologists. Deep learning-based image classifiers, processing data from automated non-lethal camera traps, have the potential to transform and scale insect biodiversity monitoring. However, challenges remain in acquiring expert-annotated datasets, developing model architectures that generalise well across diverse taxonomic levels and training models on highly imbalanced data. Hierarchical data also benefits from designing models that default to higher-confidence, coarser-level predictions, when uncertain about finer taxonomic levels. In this paper we address these challenges with a deep learning-based hierarchical classification model. First, we present a manually curated, long-tailed dataset of around one million images of insects, extracted from 1,801 camera-trap video recordings and annotated with a five-level, 34-class hierarchy. Further, we adapt a hierarchical classification model architecture to a five-level variable-depth hierarchy, with class-balanced weighting. Our model improves on non-hierarchical classifiers by leveraging biological taxonomy to extract granularity-specific visual features and makes hierarchy-consistent predictions to the deepest taxonomic level that meets a confidence threshold (T = 0.6). Our model achieved a per-level accuracy of 80-99% on test data, across five levels of hierarchy. Furthermore ...

AI.tldr: A deep learning hierarchical classifier for insect biodiversity using a long-tailed, curated dataset; achieves hierarchy-aware, coarse-to-fine predictions with high per-level accuracy (80-99%), addressing data imbalance and taxonomic generalization.
AI.motivation: Reverse the bottlenecks in insect monitoring caused by lack of standardized data, costly expert annotation, and imbalanced datasets; leverage taxonomy to improve model generalization and provide reliable predictions at multiple taxonomic levels.
AI.method: Adapt a hierarchical classification model to a five-level, variable-depth taxonomy with class-balanced weighting; train on a curated ~1M-image, 34-class dataset from 1,801 camera-trap videos; enforce hierarchy-consistent predictions that default to coarser levels when finer levels lack confidence (threshold T = 0.6).
AI.result: Model outperforms non-hierarchical classifiers by exploiting taxonomy-derived features; achieves 80–99% per-level accuracy across five taxonomic levels and produces predictions consistent with the hierarchical structure.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the feasibility and benefits of taxonomy-guided hierarchical deep learning for scalable, non-lethal insect biodiversity monitoring, with robust confidence-aware predictions and improved handling of long-tailed data.

title: Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time
summary: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

AI.tldr: Orca combines neural operators with structural causal models to model continuous-time causal dynamics, enabling counterfactuals with irregular observations and feedback loops.
AI.motivation: Standard SCMs are static and acyclic, unsuitable for dynamic systems that evolve in time, are irregularly observed, or involve feedback. A functional, time-aware framework is needed for causal reasoning in such settings.
AI.method: Extend neural operator architectures to functional mechanisms: each node is a time-dependent function; each mechanism maps parent functions to the child function, respecting the arrow of time; latent exogenous noise is treated as a reusable input function; formalize the model class and inference for counterfactuals.
AI.result: Formal model class is proposed; counterfactual reasoning demonstrated on synthetic continuous-time examples; code available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Neural-operator-based SCMs provide a natural foundation for causal reasoning in continuous-time domains with feedback and irregular observations, enabling counterfactuals; potential for broader impact.

title: Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

AI.tldr: LoRA fine-tuning exhibits matching statistical bounds: upper and lower bounds scale as rd/n for rank-r adaptation; a rank-selection dichotomy exists between constrained ERM and adaptive nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators, with over-ranking penalties arising from unregularized ERM rather than LoRA itself.
AI.motivation: Address missing matching lower bounds and formal guidance on choosing LoRA rank r in rank-constrained fine-tuning; understand why over-parameterization penalties appear in practice.
AI.method: 1) Local Rademacher analysis yields an O~(rd/n) excess risk bound for rank-r LoRA when target rank ≤ r; 2) Fano-type packing gives minimax lower bound Omega(rd/n) for any estimator within the rank-r LoRA class; 3) Compare constrained ERM vs adaptive nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators; 4) Empirical validation on synthetic trace-regression and real LoRA fine-tuning across DistilBERT/RoBERTa on SST-2/MRPC.
AI.result: Resulting bounds tightly match up to log factors; rank selection: constrained ERM optimality at intrinsic rank r*, over-ranking harmful; adaptive estimators mitigate over-ranking with rate saturating at Theta~(r* d / n); collectively clarifies that over-parameterization penalties stem from unregularized ERM rather than LoRA class; empirical validation shows the predicted U-shaped validation loss and significant loss inflation at large ranks in some configurations.
AI.conclusion: The study completes the statistical characterization of LoRA fine-tuning in the locally quadratic regime, providing formal guidance on rank choice and highlighting the role of regularization; it reconciles empirical over-parameterization effects with optimization rather than model class, and supports predictions with both synthetic and real-data experiments.

title: Beyond Classification: Pathology Foundation Models as Detection Encoders for Mitotic Figures
summary: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are models trained on vast amounts of typically unlabeled data and have been shown to yield regularized latent spaces that can be used effectively in downstream classification tasks. This is also true for the classification of mitotic figures vs. other cells. However, it is so far unclear if the latent space of current FMs provides features that are discriminant and spatially suitably resolved to also serve as a backbone for dense object detection paradigms. In this work, we investigate this question for common current pathology FMs (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) and compare their performance against a fully end-to-end trained baseline based on a ResNet50 architecture. We combine FM backbones with representatives of single stage, dual stage and self-attention-based detectors (RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR respectively) on the multi-domain MIDOG++ dataset, and on the TUPAC16 dataset as an out-of-domain case. We show that the H-optimus-0 and Virchow models yielded competitive performance, indicating that the latent spaces of current FMs, all trained on image-level self-supervision, are suitable for direct mitotic figure detection and may be slightly more robust on our out-of-domain test case. All code is made available publicly at https://github.com/DeepMicroscopy/FM4MFdet.

AI.tldr: FM backbones can serve as effective dense detectors for mitotic figure detection; H-optimus-0 and Virchow show competitive performance to ResNet50 baselines; potential out-of-domain robustness; code released.
AI.motivation: Assess whether latent spaces of current pathology FMs trained with self-supervision yield discriminant, spatially resolved features suitable for dense object detection and not just image-level classification.
AI.method: Evaluate multiple FM backbones (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) integrated with RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR detectors on MIDOG++ and TUPAC16, compared to end-to-end ResNet50 baseline.
AI.result: H-optimus-0 and Virchow yielded competitive performance; FM latent spaces are suitable for direct mitotic figure detection and may be more robust on out-of-domain data (TUPAC16). All code publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Current image-level self-supervised pathology FMs can serve as effective backbones for dense object detection in pathology; some models may offer robustness advantages; supports broader adoption and further exploration of FM backbones for detection tasks.

title: Search as Computation Allocation
summary: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

AI.tldr: Formalizes terminal computation-allocation problems and links computation under budget to terminal decision loss; shows VOC relates to information measures (mutual information, knowledge-gradient) and recovers A*-like search as an approximation.
AI.motivation: Provide a unified decision-theoretic framework for computations spent before a decision, connecting information-theoretic quantities to decision performance and showing implications for search algorithms.
AI.method: Define terminal computation-allocation problems; derive Bellman equations for budgeted and priced computation; relate VOC to information measures; analyze computation topologies (bandits, trees, expansions); propose frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model; show approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy as limits.
AI.result: Characterizes when information gain aligns with or diverges from value of computation; establishes conditions under which mutual information equals myopic VOC and knowledge-gradient equals VOC under simple regret; demonstrates that optimizing approximate VOC yields known search algorithms; clarifies no single universally optimal acquisition rule.
AI.conclusion: Unifies disparate computation strategies under a common VOC-information framework; highlights trade-offs between information gain and practical decision efficiency; shows how classic search algorithms emerge as special cases of approximate VOC optimization.

title: Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries
summary: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: Introduces an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) for transient-stability assessment and critical clearing time (CCT) estimation, aligning the model with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing dynamics and enforcing exact state chaining across events to enable differentiable CCT boundary estimation and direct CCT readout.
AI.motivation: Reliable, data-efficient CCT estimation is challenging due to complex fault-clearing dynamics requiring many simulations; existing surrogates struggle with boundary accuracy and event transitions.
AI.method: An ES-PINN that encodes pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics with explicit state chaining at event interfaces; introduces a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin as a differentiable proxy for the CCT boundary; allows boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and an optional distilled readout for direct CCT prediction; provides a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error bound with exact event chaining.
AI.result: Empirically improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems across mechanical and electrical contingencies and multiple clearing configurations, outperforming matched neural-surrogate baselines; full-network DAE validation, multi-fault tests, and runtime analyses support robustness and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: ES-PINN offers accurate, differentiable CCT boundaries with improved trajectory fidelity and sensitivity analysis, leveraging exact event chaining to reduce interface defects; suitable for scalable, efficient transient-stability assessment in realistic power systems.

title: ENCORE: Event-Assisted Complementary Motion Refinement for Learned Video Compression
summary: Learned video compression relies on accurate temporal modeling to remove redundancy between adjacent frames. However, most existing codecs infer motion solely from discretely sampled RGB frames, making their estimates vulnerable to fast motion, blur, occlusion, weak texture, low illumination, and abrupt brightness changes. Event cameras asynchronously capture fine-grained intensity changes between RGB timestamps and therefore provide complementary evidence about inter-frame dynamics. We propose ENCORE, an Event-Assisted Complementary Motion Refinement framework for learned video compression. ENCORE first employs Complementary Motion Representation (CMR) to decompose aligned RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion representations. Spatial Energy and Redundancy-Informed Calibration (SERIC) then identifies event-specific responses that are active and novel relative to RGB, suppresses weak or redundant evidence, and predicts a candidate flow correction. Finally, Energy-Aware Routing (EAR) determines where and how strongly the correction should refine the RGB flow. Events serve solely as an auxiliary modality for motion modeling, while RGB remains the only coding and reconstruction target. Experiments on BS-ERGB, HQ-EVFI, and CED demonstrate consistent gains across datasets and GOP lengths. On BS-ERGB, ENCORE achieves up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings, while retaining clear improvements on the other two datasets.

AI.tldr: Proposes ENCORE, an event-assisted motion refinement framework for learned video compression that uses event cameras to refine RGB-based motion estimation, achieving notable BD-rate savings across datasets.
AI.motivation: RGB-only motion estimation struggles under fast motion, blur, occlusion, and other challenging conditions; event cameras offer fine-grained, asynchronous changes to complement inter-frame dynamics.
AI.method: Introduce Complementary Motion Representation to split RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion; use SERIC to identify event-specific responses relative to RGB, suppress weak/redundant evidence, and predict a flow correction; employ EAR to decide where/how strongly to apply the correction; RGB remains the coding target; events are auxiliary.
AI.result: Experiments on BS-ERGB, HQ-EVFI, CED show consistent gains; up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings on BS-ERGB; improvements on other datasets and GOP lengths.
AI.conclusion: Events can serve as an auxiliary modality for motion modeling; ENCORE improves learned video compression by refining RGB motion estimates with event information while keeping RGB as sole reconstruction target.

title: An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding
summary:
Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

AI.tldr: MSEval is a real-world, multi-agent coding benchmark that evaluates how team topology affects speed, cost, and quality across 10 authentic, full-stack tasks using an automated execution and grading system.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that fail to capture practical time and monetary costs and conflate reasoning with communication; a real-world, reproducible standard is needed to evaluate multi-agent software construction
AI.method: Develop MSEval with 10 authentic projects across 10 domains, hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics; use LegoGent to test 10 collaboration topologies with periodic syncs and native CI/CD pipelines; employ automated grader TAgent to measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost over 100 runs
AI.result: Topology choice significantly impacts performance, with >30-point score differences and roughly double wall-clock time for identical tasks/models; structured pipelines achieve fastest convergence and highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degrades performance
AI.conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible benchmark for measuring how multi-agent teams build software, with a GitHub release at the provided URL.

title: NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation
summary:
Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

AI.tldr: A neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables combines a MINE-based MI estimator with neural marginal entropy estimators inspired by MI-NEE, using Donsker–Varadhan representation for MI and divergence-to-uniform for entropy; shows improved accuracy over a KSG-based baseline on Gaussian data (1–8 dimensions), suggesting neural approaches for normalized dependency in continuous multidimensional settings.
AI.motivation: Need to estimate mutual information for continuous, high-dimensional data and normalize it to enable comparability across datasets; existing estimators suffer from dimensionality sensitivity and numerical instability.
AI.method: Use a neural framework: estimate MI via MINE (Donsker–Varadhan) and estimate marginal entropies by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference, then combine to form a normalized MI estimator; provides a neural alternative to KSG-based normalization.
AI.result: Experimental validation on Gaussian data from 1–8 dimensions shows improved accuracy versus a KSG-based normalized MI baseline.
AI.conclusion: Neural normalization of mutual information is a promising direction for measuring dependency in continuous multidimensional settings, addressing normalization and stability challenges of traditional estimators.

title: Split and Drive: Dual-Axis Disentanglement for Real-Time Gaussian Head Avatars
summary: Creating photorealistic animatable head avatars from a single image remains a fundamental challenge in digital human synthesis. While recent 3D Gaussian Splatting methods have achieved promising results, they rely on external tracking pipelines whose latency is excluded from inference measurements. Furthermore, they adopt unified representations that entangle geometrically distinct facial regions, limiting both expressiveness and rendering fidelity. We propose SpiD (Split and Drive), a single-image Gaussian head avatar framework built on two disentanglement axes. The compute axis internalizes per-frame driving, eliminating external tracking dependency at inference. The feature axis decomposes the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches, each modeling a geometrically distinct facial domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistently strong performance against state-of-the-art methods while achieving the fastest inference speed among all compared methods on a single GPU with the complete driving pipeline included.

AI.tldr: SpiD splits driving and geometry into two axes: a compute axis for per-frame driving, and a feature axis with three specialized Gaussian branches for distinct facial regions, delivering fast, high-fidelity single-image head avatars without external trackers.
AI.motivation: Address latency and entanglement in existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods: external tracking pipelines add inference latency and unified representations limit expressiveness; a single-image, fast, and expressive head avatar framework is desired.
AI.method: Introduce SpiD with two disentanglement axes: compute axis for per-frame driving (self-contained inference) and feature axis dividing the avatar into three geometrically distinct Gaussian branches for facial regions.
AI.result: Achieves strong performance vs state-of-the-art methods and records the fastest inference speed among compared methods on a single GPU when the complete driving pipeline is included.
AI.conclusion: SpiD offers a compact, disentangled Gaussian head avatar framework that is fast and expressive for single-image inputs, addressing external-tracking latency and geometry entanglement issues.

title: Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

AI.tldr: CSCR extends critic-free GRPO by downweighting tokens with high counterfactual sensitivity and renormalizing token-level advantages, improving long-CoT reasoning performance over GRPO with the same update budget; ablations validate the diagnosis and optimal modulation level.
AI.motivation: Address unreliability of privileged (self-teaching) shifts in on-policy self-distillation for verifiable rewards, which tend to concentrate on surface-form tokens and counterfactual sensitivity rather than content-relevant learning signals.
AI.method: Compute token-level sensitivity via counterfactual re-scoring of trajectories under opposing outcomes, observe that many tokens shift similarly and that high-sensitivity tokens dominate updates; introduce CSCR to downweight these tokens and renormalize the remaining token advantages while preserving total credit budget; integrate as an extension to GRPO.
AI.result: CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO on long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks using the same number of policy updates; targeted ablations show moderate downweighting is most effective and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization; privilege-induced directions are unreliable.
AI.conclusion: Privileged shifts do not reliably encode answer-aligned learning signals; downweighting by counterfactual sensitivity and preserving credit budget yield more robust, reliable supervision and improved reasoning performance.

title: VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction
summary: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

AI.tldr: VESTIGE is a parameter-free, domain-agnostic masking strategy that aligns MLM masking with an empirical per-position degradation profile, improving reconstruction and detection on degraded sequences (e.g., ancient DNA) and generalizing to other corruption profiles.
AI.motivation: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning assumes a position-agnostic reconstruction difficulty. When degradation is concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption breaks and models can underperform relative to simple baselines. A masking distribution that mirrors the empirical corruption profile is needed to improve learning and downstream reconstruction.
AI.method: Introduce VESTIGE, a drop-in, parameter-free collator that uses an empirically measured per-position corruption profile to shape the MLM masking distribution. Rescale so the mean masking rate matches standard MLM (15%). Apply to ancient DNA reconstruction (cytosine deamination) using mapDamage2 profiles, across DNABERT-2 on mammoth CDS data (two specimens, seven genes). Evaluate across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, comparing against standard MLM. Assess via validation cross-entropy, ESMFold TM-scores, and a 1D CNN biosecurity classifier (AUC). Demonstrate domain-agnostic applicability to other corruption types (FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, nanopore).
AI.result: VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 percentage points, p < 1e-8). Cross-entropy reduced by 13% (3.274 vs 3.757). ESMFold reconstructions achieve TM-score > 0.95 across six reconstructions (three genes). A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier attains AUC = 0.935, with 98.2% of reconstructions correctly cleared (1.76% residual due to reference-genome features, not artefacts). The approach remains domain-agnostic, serving as a knowledge-guided training routine for degraded inputs by substituting any position-/context-specific corruption profile for the PMD array.
AI.conclusion: VESTIGE provides a domain-agnostic, knowledge-guided masking framework that improves MLM-based learning on degraded data and generalizes to diverse corruption profiles (FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, nanopore). It is a drop-in replacement for the standard collator and can enhance intelligent systems operating on degraded sequences.

title: TongueReenact: Geometry-Anchored Tongue Synthesis for Face Reenactment
summary: Modern face reenactment systems achieve impressive pose and expression transfer using geometry-driven representations. However, they largely ignore tongue dynamics, leading to anatomically inconsistent mouth interiors during speech and expressive motions. We introduce the first framework for cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment. We propose a foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline that produces a dedicated tongue segmentation model for in-the-wild reenactment without curated annotations. We further introduce a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis, with adaptive mask dilation for seamless mouth boundary transitions. Extensive experiments demonstrate improvements of more than two times over all baselines on every tongue-specific metric. We additionally propose a VLM-based evaluation protocol that replicates expert annotation at scale, confirming perceptual superiority across all ablation variants.

AI.tldr: Tongue-aware face reenactment enabling cross-identity tongue transfer via self-supervised segmentation and diffusion-based synthesis, achieving >2x gains and scalable evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing face reenactment methods largely ignore tongue dynamics, producing anatomically inconsistent mouth interiors during speech/expressions. There is a need for cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer and data-efficient segmentation without curated annotations.
AI.method: Foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping to create a dedicated tongue segmentation model without curated labels; a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis with adaptive mask dilation to ensure seamless mouth boundary transitions.
AI.result: More than twofold improvements over all baselines on tongue-specific metrics; a VLM-based evaluation protocol matches expert annotations at scale, validating perceptual superiority across ablations.
AI.conclusion: First framework enabling cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment; introduces scalable evaluation and state-of-the-art tongue realism, advancing the fidelity of talking avatars.

title: Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators
summary: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

AI.tldr: DSF introduces a time-evolving spectral propagation operator for dynamic graphs using vector-valued, time-dependent Chebyshev coefficients treated as recurrent states; it delivers competitive accuracy with far lower parameters and memory.
AI.motivation: To explore whether the graph propagation operator should itself evolve over time, not just node states/history, enabling a compact, efficient temporal inductive bias.
AI.method: Dynamic Spectral Filtering: at each snapshot t, propagate with a Chebyshev polynomial filter whose coefficients are vector-valued and time-dependent. Treat coefficients as recurrent temporal states updated by a recurrent branch with global and order-specific gates; the temporal state is node-count agnostic.
AI.result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link prediction, DSF achieves AP of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860 with 93k–133k parameters, 68–182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6–2.1s per epoch. Relative to DEFT, DSF uses far fewer parameters and memory and is competitive in accuracy (better on MOOC, near on Reddit, slightly worse on Wikipedia). Relative to other baselines, DSF uses 3.3–38.6x less memory.
AI.conclusion: A direct spectral-response evolution in the propagation operator is an effective temporal inductive bias for efficient temporal graph learning, achieving strong accuracy with substantially reduced resource usage.

title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules
summary: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

AI.tldr: A convex-optimization framework jointly modeling learning rate and batch size yields a closed-form optimal batch-size schedule for any LR schedule and joint scaling laws that outperform fixed-batch baselines, highlighting the value of dynamic batch sizing in large language model training.
AI.motivation: Static batch sizes ignore the interaction with learning rate, potentially limiting training efficiency and generalization. A principled analysis can reveal optimal batch-size dynamics conditioned on the LR schedule.
AI.method: Formulate loss dynamics via convex optimization to derive a joint characterization of the training trajectory in terms of LR and batch-size schedules, yielding a closed-form optimal batch size for any prescribed LR schedule and resulting joint scaling laws applicable to general optimizers and architectures.
AI.result: Derives an explicit batch-size schedule as a function of the LR schedule; proposes joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static-batch baselines; demonstrates improved training dynamics/efficiency in large language model settings.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, schedule-aware batch sizing is significant for efficient, scalable training and should be incorporated alongside LR schedules, especially in large-scale models.

title: Temporal Concentration from Rollout Errors: Implicit Preference Optimization for Text-to-Video Diffusion
summary: Recent advances in preference alignment for diffusion-based video generation, particularly via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have significantly improved visual quality. However, temporally sparse artifacts such as motion collapse, object flickering, and color oversaturation remain a major barrier to perceptual realism. Existing methods struggle with these issues due to two key limitations: (1) the preference attribution bottleneck, where offline human annotations are costly and fail to accurately capture learning dynamics, while online reward signals are rollout-aware but often unstable and biased; and (2) temporal credit misallocation, where uniformly applied supervision cannot effectively target the brief segments in which artifacts occur. To address these challenges, we propose concentrated Implicit Preference Optimization (cIPO), a post-training framework for video diffusion models. cIPO derives implicit preference signals directly from the denoising process: given a real video, the model adds forward noise and reconstructs it via iterative denoising, treating the original as the preferred sample and the reconstruction as the dispreferred one. This formulation captures inference-time errors without requiring human annotations or external reward models. Moreover, frame-level discrepancies between original and reconstructed videos reveal when failures occur. cIPO leverages this by computing temporal reconstruction errors and concentrating optimization on high-error segments, enabling more precise correction of failure-prone regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that cIPO consistently enhances video authenticity and temporal coherence across multiple datasets, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of implicit preference with temporally concentrated optimization.

AI.tldr: Proposes cIPO, a post-training framework for diffusion-based video generation that uses implicit preferences derived from the denoising process and concentrates learning on high-error temporal segments to improve authenticity and temporal coherence.
AI.motivation: To overcome two main issues in DPO-based video generation: (1) the preference attribution bottleneck due to costly offline annotations and unstable online rewards, and (2) temporal credit misallocation where uniform supervision fails to target failure-prone moments.
AI.method: During post-training, add forward noise to real video and reconstruct via iterative denoising; treat the original video as the preferred sample and the reconstruction as the dispreferred one to derive implicit preferences without annotations. Compute frame-level reconstruction errors to identify high-error segments and concentrate optimization on those segments during fine-tuning.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows consistent improvements in video authenticity and temporal coherence across multiple datasets, demonstrating effective and efficient implicit preference optimization with temporally concentrated updates.
AI.conclusion: Implicit preferences derived from the denoising process, when concentrated on high-error temporal segments, provide a robust and data-efficient pathway to enhance video diffusion models without external rewards or annotations.

title: MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos
summary: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

AI.tldr: Introduces MMHBench, a multimodal benchmark for long-form video mental health understanding with 268 videos and 2,184 questions; evaluates 22 multimodal LLMs; proposes MAQG to generate multi-perspective questions; finds long-form mental health understanding remains challenging.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of existing benchmarks that reduce mental health understanding to coarse-grained classification and poorly reveal whether models capture genuine psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations.
AI.method: Construct MMHBench with two complementary evaluation settings: (1) third-person interpretation focusing on observable behaviors and multimodal evidence; (2) first-person perspective-taking requiring perspective-conditioned reasoning. Introduce Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) to synthesize questions from diverse social roles, refined via multi-role feedback and expert-guided verification.
AI.result: Benchmark comprises 268 long-form videos and 2,184 questions; 605 third-person and 1,579 first-person questions; evaluated 22 representative multimodal LLMs (open-source and closed-source). Demonstrates current models struggle with long-form video mental health understanding.
AI.conclusion: Long-form video mental health understanding is still highly challenging for contemporary multimodal LLMs; the benchmark and MAQG framework provide a rigorous platform for future research and model development.

title: Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

AI.tldr: Extends Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) by adding a clean teacher trained on clean data, using cross-layer attention to fuse knowledge from clean and robust teachers into a student, improving clean accuracy while preserving robustness; competitive with state-of-the-art (e.g., B-MTARD) on CIFAR-10/100.
AI.motivation: IBD degrades clean accuracy while improving robustness; need to preserve clean performance while maintaining adversarial robustness; leverage both clean and robust teachers via attention-based distillation.
AI.method: Introduce an extra clean teacher (trained on clean data) into the distillation from a robust teacher; use cross-layer attention to transfer features from both teachers to the student; experiments on CIFAR-10/100; compare with original IBD and B-MTARD; analyze attention module training settings.
AI.result: Improved clean accuracy over original IBD with similar adversarial accuracy; competitive harmonic mean of clean/robust accuracy versus state-of-the-art; detailed analysis of attention module settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-teacher cross-layer attention distillation effectively preserves clean accuracy while maintaining robustness, and is competitive with current methods; attention module settings influence outcomes.

title: Landmark shape spaces with induced metrics
summary: We present a unification of Kendall's landmark shape spaces, where rigid motions are factored out and scale fixed on landmark configurations equipped with Euclidean geometry, with landmark configuration spaces carrying Riemannian metrics descending from right-invariant Sobolev metrics on the diffeomorphism group. The resulting new landmark shape spaces achieve the defining properties of both approaches: The regularity of the descending metric prevents landmarks from colliding, the metric is defined in the ambient space independent of the number of landmarks, local rigid transformations are preserved, global rigid motions are removed, and scale fixed. To achieve this, we define a particular Sobolev-type operator, the screened elasticity operator, whose null-space consists exactly of the rigid motions, we show how this operator descends to achieve the desired geometry, and we present approaches to solving matching problems and computing geodesics numerically. The resulting construction allows the use of landmark configuration spaces with sufficiently regular metrics in applications while retaining the shape invariances that are a hallmark of Kendall's shape spaces.

AI.tldr: Unifies Kendall's landmark shape spaces with diffeomorphism-based Riemannian metrics via a Sobolev-type operator (screened elasticity) whose null-space matches rigid motions, yielding regular, ambient-space metrics independent of landmark count with both local and global rigid-motion handling and fixed scale, plus numerical methods for matching and geodesics.
AI.motivation: To combine the favorable features of Kendall's landmark shape spaces (rigid-motion invariance, scale handling) with those of configuration spaces endowed with right-invariant Sobolev metrics derived from the diffeomorphism group, overcoming issues like landmark collisions and dependence on the number of landmarks.
AI.method: Introduce a Sobolev-type operator called the screened elasticity operator whose null-space consists precisely of rigid motions. This operator descends to the landmark configuration space to induce a geometry with desired invariances: global rigid motions removed, local rigid transformations preserved, scale fixed, and metric regularity preventing collisions. Develop matching and geodesic computation algorithms in this framework.
AI.result: A new class of landmark shape spaces inheriting both Kendall-type invariances and diffeomorphism-based Sobolev-regular metrics. The metric is ambient-space defined and independent of the number of landmarks; collisions are mitigated; local/global rigid motions are handled as intended; scale is fixed; and practical procedures for matching and geodesic computation are proposed.
AI.conclusion: The construction enables applying landmark configuration spaces with sufficiently regular metrics while preserving Kendall’s shape invariances, combining robustness against collisions, scale handling, and overall geometric invariances in a unified framework.

title: A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models
summary: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

AI.tldr: A benchmark compares five direction-based defenses against VLM jailbreaks across 15 model/layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude-controlled protocol, plus a random control. No single defense dominates both refusal recovery and utility preservation. Image conditioning shift often preserves utility (low loss) in LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B, while other defenses succeed on different models. The image-conditioning direction is largely architecture-specific and poorly transferable, and CMRM shows positive alignment with it. The results imply partial geometry overlap between defenses and require calibration per language-decoder family.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate multiple direction-based defenses against vision-language model jailbreaks in a controlled, cross-architecture setting, quantify trade-offs between refusal recovery and utility preservation, and assess geometry and transferability of defense directions across model families.
AI.method: Five candidate directions (mean image conditioning shift, CMRM-style refusal direction, ShiftDC-like attack-specific residual, prompt instruction to ignore the image) plus a random control were tested under a magnitude-controlled protocol. The evaluation spans 15 model/layer cells across four architectural families. For each prompt-direction pair, the intervention norm is matched with a random vector of identical norm. Metrics include refusal recovery and utility preservation; cosine alignment with the CMRM direction was analyzed; cross-architecture transferability was examined.
AI.result: No single candidate dominates both objectives.
