Image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at measurement-noise floor across all families. Prompt instruction dominates on Qwen2.5 VL; attack-specific residual dominates on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image-conditioning direction is largely direction-specific (13/15 cells) and strongly architecture-specific, with no transferability across at least the LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B pairing. CMRM direction shows positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells (mean ≈0.35; range 0.17–0.65; 15–25× the random-null; p ≈ 3e-5). These findings suggest partial overlap in the recovered geometry and that defense directions should be calibrated per language-decoder family.
AI.conclusion: Direction-based defenses against VLM jailbreaks exhibit model- and language-specific behavior. Practically, one should calibrate the defense direction to each language-decoder family to balance refusal quality and utility, recognizing limited cross-model transferability and partial geometric overlap among defense recipes.

title: ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation
summary:
Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

AI.tldr: ROCS proposes a request-oriented compute sharing paradigm for recommendation inference that delays candidate interactions, isolates candidate-specific representations, and shares request-side features across candidates. It introduces Generalized Layer Masking (GLM), Deep Cross Attention (DCA), and In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) to enable efficient, per-request computation with minimal quality loss, achieving substantial inference-accuracy and efficiency gains across backbones and production workloads.
AI.motivation: Production inference costs constrain scaling of feature-interaction and sequence modules in modern recommender systems. RO CS targets this bottleneck by reusing request-side features across candidates and postponing candidate-dependent computations to the latest possible stage, thereby increasing throughput without sacrificing prediction quality.
AI.method: ROCS framework with three core components: Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation within feature-interaction architectures, Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures, and In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) for fast GPU execution. The paradigm reduces per-candidate computation by sharing substantial work across candidates per request.
AI.result: Empirical results on public benchmarks show ROCS improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across various backbones. In production-scale workloads, ROCS yields up to 3x QPS improvements on retrieval models with no quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking, and some systems exhibit more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity reduction, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.
AI.conclusion: ROCS is an effective and deployable paradigm for increasing inference efficiency in recommendation systems, enabling substantial quality-preserving throughput gains across diverse architectures and production workloads.

title: BladeYOLO: Wind Turbine Blade Defect Detection with Limited Annotations and Weak-Saliency Awareness
comment: Accepted to IEEE TGRS, Code: https://github.com/zhangfangtao/BladeYOLO
summary: Wind turbine blade defect detection remains highly challenging in real-world inspection scenarios due to limited on-site data and the subtle visual characteristics of defects. In practice, blade defects are often small-scale, low-contrast, and difficult to distinguish from complex backgrounds, which significantly limits the robustness of existing detectors. To address these challenges, we propose BladeYOLO, a defect detection framework for wind turbine blades. Specifically, we integrate a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone initialized with DINOv3 self-supervised pre-trained weights into YOLOv12-L, enabling the transfer of large-scale generic visual priors to blade defect detection and improving feature representation under limited training annotations. To enhance the perception of subtle defects, we further develop a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module, which consists of a Detail-Enhanced Multi-scale Branch for preserving high-frequency structural cues and a Cross-Mamba module for progressively propagating high-level semantic guidance to shallow features. In addition, we introduce a lightweight Style-Injector module that captures environment-related style information via Fourier decomposition and injects it into selected ViT self-attention layers, thereby improving robustness against environment-induced appearance variations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BladeYOLO achieves superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset, with additional annotation-budget experiments showing its favorable performance under reduced training annotations. Evaluation on the public Wind Surface Defect dataset further provides supportive evidence for the cross-dataset robustness of BladeYOLO. In particular, on this public dataset, BladeYOLO outperforms the best competing method by 3.5\% in mAP$_{50}$ and 2.5\% in mAP$_{50-95}$.

AI.tldr: BladeYOLO integrates a DINOv3-pretrained Vision Transformer backbone into YOLOv12-L, with a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module and a Fourier-based Style-Injector, delivering robust blade defect detection under limited data and showing cross-dataset improvements (mAP50 +3.5%, mAP50-95 +2.5%).
AI.motivation: Wind turbine blade defect detection is hindered by small-scale, low-contrast defects and limited on-site labeled data amid complex backgrounds; improving feature representation and robustness to appearance variations is needed.
AI.method: Backbone: ViT initialized with DINOv3 self-supervised weights integrated into YOLOv12-L. Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement with Detail-Enhanced Multi-scale Branch and Cross-Mamba to propagate high-level guidance to shallow features. Style-Injector module uses Fourier decomposition to inject environment-related style into selected ViT self-attention layers.
AI.result: BladeYOLO achieves superior performance on WTBlade-Defect with favorable annotation-budget performance under reduced training data. On the public Wind Surface Defect dataset, BladeYOLO outperforms the best competing method by 3.5% in mAP50 and 2.5% in mAP50-95, indicating strong cross-dataset robustness.
AI.conclusion: The approach effectively leverages large-scale priors, high-frequency detail cues, and style-aware robustness to detect blade defects under limited data, with notable cross-dataset generalization.

title: IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models
summary: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

AI.tldr: IFHierBench introduces a hierarchical, constraint-aware instruction-following benchmark with 600 prompts across four depth levels and 35 constraints, each paired with per-scope checkers; results show current LLMs struggle with nested constraints, ~50% accuracy, worsening with depth.
AI.motivation: To address the limitation of flat constraint evaluations in instruction-following benchmarks, which fail to target specific sections of structured outputs, and to push models toward reliable multi-level adherence in single-pass LLM calls used in real-world deployments.
AI.method: Create IFHierBench dataset: 600 prompts stratified by constraint-tree depth (4 levels) and 35 constraints. Each prompt includes a deterministic checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every scope (artifact, structure, nested fields). Evaluate seven models (proprietary and open-weight).
AI.result: Strongest model barely exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy; accuracy degrades sharply with increasing constraint depth; nested constraints remain a major gap across models.
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial gap in reliably following hierarchical constraints; future work should develop training methods and evaluation that account for constraint adherence at finer granularity to improve instruction-following in hierarchical outputs.

title: DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

AI.tldr: DAS-PMVC is a partial multi-view clustering framework that integrates anchor-graph alignment, structure-enhanced feature learning, and a dual alignment strategy (pretraining with anchor graphs; training with contrastive loss and Hungarian matching) to mitigate view misalignment and select relevant samples, achieving superior clustering performance.
AI.motivation: Multi-view data often suffer from misalignment and irrelevant samples due to data collection limitations. PVAP (partial view alignment problem) arises from view asymmetry; there is a need for robust alignment and discriminative representation learning that leverages structural information across views.
AI.method: 1) Anchor graph structure alignment to derive consistent latent-space embeddings from anchor-point relationships for initial view alignment. 2) Structure-enhanced feature learning via pretraining and multi-view graph convolutional networks to extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure. 3) A dual alignment strategy: pretraining-based initial alignment followed by training-time contrastive loss and Hungarian algorithm to further align latent features.
AI.result: Experimental results on various datasets show that DAS-PMVC outperforms state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority.
AI.conclusion: DAS-PMVC effectively mitigates PVAP by combining anchor-based alignment, graph-structured feature learning, and a dual alignment strategy, enabling more accurate and robust partial multi-view clustering.

title: mmRadarTwin: A Measurement-Calibrated Signal-Level Digital Twin Platform for Indoor mmWave Radar
summary: Indoor mmWave radar perception is difficult to reproduce because measured range-angle responses depend on scene geometry, material response, multipath, hardware conventions, and signal processing. Existing ray-tracing and digital-twin tools often expose rendering, channel, or path-level quantities, while radar sensing requires complex signal products that can be processed and compared in the same domain as real FMCW measurements. We present mmRadarTwin, a signal-level and path-attributed digital-twin platform for indoor mmWave radar. mmRadarTwin links a real radar measurement branch with an Unreal Engine scene-simulation branch through a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. The simulator writes complex multi-channel receive grids and exports per-path contribution records that identify the actor, material tag, propagation event, and output-bin support of each simulated return. We evaluate mmRadarTwin in an office deployment using a commodity monostatic mmWave radar and mobile scene-capture hardware. Across 154 measured poses spanning 22 radar locations, the current physics-only path-basis simulator recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions in the central usable field of view while exposing residuals caused by weak or missing path support, shifted responses, unsupported anchors, and missing physical mechanisms. Rather than claiming complete radar-map reconstruction or cross-room generalization, mmRadarTwin establishes a practical systems workflow for constructing, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins.

AI.tldr: mmRadarTwin is a signal-level digital twin for indoor mmWave radar that couples a real measurement chain with Unreal Engine scene simulation to produce per-path contributions and a shared receive-channel interface; in office tests it recalls ~70.8% of geometry-supported regions in the central view, enabling a practical workflow for diagnosing and constructing radar twins rather than full reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Indoor mmWave radar perception is highly sensitive to scene geometry, materials, multipath, hardware conventions, and DSP; existing tools mainly provide high-level rendering or channel data, making direct comparison to FMCW measurements difficult. A signal-level, path-attributed twin is needed to reproduce, analyze, and diagnose radar responses in a way aligned with real measurements.
AI.method: mmRadarTwin links a real radar measurement branch with an Unreal Engine scene-simulation branch via a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. The simulator outputs complex multi-channel receive grids and per-path contribution records detailing actor, material tag, propagation event, and output-bin support for each simulated return, enabling a path-basis, signal-level reconstruction.
AI.result: Evaluated in an office deployment with a commodity monostatic mmWave radar and mobile scene-capture hardware across 154 poses and 22 radar locations. The physics-only path-basis simulator recalled 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions within the central usable field of view, with residuals attributed to weak/missing path support, shifted responses, unsupported anchors, and missing physical mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: mmRadarTwin provides a practical systems workflow for constructing, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins, rather than claiming complete reconstruction or cross-room generalization; it highlights both the potential and current limitations of path-based, signal-level radar simulation in real indoor environments.

title: One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs
summary: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

AI.tldr: Neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment (MLS-Neurons) identifies modality- and language-shared safety neurons to defend LVLMs against compound multilingual multimodal attacks by updating ~0.03% of parameters, achieving strong safety with preserved utility.
AI.motivation: Multilingual, multimodal safety for large vision-language models (LVLMs) is difficult due to isolated language and modality defenses, scarcity of safety data, and high fine-tuning costs; a transferable, parameter-efficient defense against compound attacks is needed.
AI.method: Identify unimodal safety neurons by contrasting responses to harmful vs benign samples and measuring functional saliency via activation strength and downstream impact. Intersect unimodal neurons within each language to obtain modality-shared neurons (MS-Neurons). Cross-language intersection of MS-Neurons using English as an anchor yields modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). Update only this minimal shared subset (~0.03% of parameters) with English supervision transferred to multilingual/multimodal settings.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show significant improvements over state-of-the-art safety benchmarks across diverse multilingual and multimodal tasks while preserving general utility.
AI.conclusion: MLS-Neurons enable effective cross-dimensional safety defense with minimal parameter updates, providing robust protection against compound attacks in LVLMs.

title: Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot transfer of GNNs trained on geometrically renormalized (GR) coarse graphs to the full-resolution graph preserves much of the original predictive performance while reducing training cost; representations and predictive trajectories align across scales, suggesting structural similarity can trump size in GNN transferability and enabling scale-equivariant designs.
AI.motivation: GNNs scale poorly on graphs with millions of nodes; it is valuable to know whether a model trained on a smaller, coarse-grained replica can be deployed on the full graph without retraining.
AI.method: Train GNNs on graphs coarse-grained via geometric renormalization (GR). Transfer the learned weights directly to the original, full-resolution network. Evaluate on synthetic and real-world networks, comparing performance, and analyze representation and trajectory alignment across scales.
AI.result: Training on GR-scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. Structural similarity may be more important than graph size for transferability.
AI.conclusion: Structural similarity across graph scales is a key determinant of GNN transferability. This finding motivates scale-equivariant graph architectures and practical zero-shot transfer pipelines that leverage coarse-grained training to deploy on full graphs without retraining.

title: Towards Practical Algorithm Selection for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in Medical Imaging
summary: Numerous unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) algori-thms exist, but for clinical practice, selecting the best-suited one along with proper hyperparameters often remains unclear, as the unlabeled deployment (target) domain prevents direct evaluation. We propose a label-free criterion that jointly selects the algorithm and hyperparameters for UDA. Given a pool of candidate models from multiple algorithms trained with different hyperparameters, our approach scores each candidate against an agreement reference, and selects the one with the highest score. The agreement reference is constructed in two levels without using target labels. First, we leverage multiple label-free selection signals, using each to nominate a model within every algorithm. Second, the nominated models are aggregated across algorithms to form a reference prediction for each unlabeled target sample. The candidate whose predictions agree most with this reference is then selected for deployment. Experimental results on four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios show that our method achieves better selection performance than other methods and remains effective across different algorithm pools. Our approach takes a step towards practical, label-free algorithm selection for clinical deployment of UDA.

AI.tldr: A label-free criterion to select UDA algorithms and hyperparameters for clinical deployment by scoring candidates against an agreement reference built without target labels.
AI.motivation: In clinical practice, unlabeled target domain prevents direct evaluation of candidate UDA models, necessitating a label-free selection mechanism to choose the best-performing algorithm and hyperparameters.
AI.method: From a pool of candidate models (across algorithms and hyperparameters), score each candidate against an agreement reference built without target labels. Two-level reference: first, use multiple label-free signals to nominate a model within every algorithm; second, aggregate nominated models across algorithms to form a reference prediction for each unlabeled target sample. The candidate whose predictions most closely agree with this reference is selected for deployment.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios shows the proposed method achieves better selection performance than competing methods and remains effective across different algorithm pools.
AI.conclusion: The work advances practical, label-free algorithm selection for clinical deployment of unsupervised domain adaptation, enabling better-informed deployment decisions without access to target labels.

title: Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training
summary: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

AI.tldr: Meta-Task reframes terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format, in-loop generation/verification within a real container to improve reliability and diversity. It decouples task requirements along multiple dimensions, uses a multi-phase design for novel specs, optionally leverages external materials, and applies LLM-as-Judge filtering. Demonstrates strong data efficiency on Terminal-Bench 2.0, with 3,221 synthesized trajectories yielding 22.5% Avg Pass@1 on Qwen3-14B and 31.8% on Qwen3-32B, outperforming peers with less data.
AI.motivation: Existing synthesis methods suffer from (1) weak reliability due to a disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity/scalability due to reliance on existing repositories. There is a need for synthesis that is verifiable within the generation loop and capable of expanding task diversity.
AI.method: Define Terminal-Bench-format tasks that an agent can operate in a real container to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks. Decouple target task requirements across multiple dimensions. Introduce a multi-phase mechanism to dynamically design novel task specifications before producing tasks. Optionally incorporate external material support to enhance diversity/realism. Apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure final training data quality.
AI.result: Empirical results on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and 31.8% for Qwen3-32B, outperforming concurrent approaches while using substantially less training data.
AI.conclusion: Meta-Task improves reliability, diversity, and scalability of terminal task synthesis by embedding the generation loop in the target environment, decomposing specifications, and leveraging judging. It demonstrates superior data efficiency for terminal-agent training on large LLMs.

title: Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold
summary: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

AI.tldr: An expand-then-compress framework builds a complementary union of teachers via multi-round expansion (RGRPO) and reliability-gated compression (TU-OPD with Consensus-Residual Decomposition), yielding a single Qwen3-1.7B student that outperforms the best individual teacher across math reasoning, code generation, and instruction following.
AI.motivation: RL policies often overfit to particular solution modes, acting as local probes rather than globally reliable supervisors. A multi-basin solution manifold motivates constructing and distilling a union of diverse teachers to cover more modes.
AI.method: Expansion: train a sequence of teachers from a common init using Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization, guiding later rounds toward uncovered examples. Compression: reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation where only reliable teachers contribute, with per-example quality weights; Consense-Residual Decomposition preserves winner teacher token preferences to avoid suppressing specialists.
AI.result: Empirical gains: the Qwen3-1.7B student surpasses the strongest single teacher on mathematical reasoning (2.0% relative), code generation (8.3%), and instruction following (6.9%), while retaining a single-model inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Stronger students arise from constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union rather than selecting a single superior teacher; multi-teacher distillation is an effective, simple principle for improving performance across domains.

title: Face and Voice Cross-modal Association with Learning Convex Feature Embedding
summary: Face-and-voice association learning is one of the most challenging tasks in deep learning. In this paper, we propose a simple but powerful cross-modal feature embedding method for the association of faces and voices. Previous work has studied cross-modal association tasks to establish the correlation between voice clips and facial images. These works have addressed cross-modal discrimination but underestimate the importance of handling heterogeneity in inter-modal features between audio and video, resulting in a lot of false positives and false negatives. To tackle the problem, the proposed method learns the embeddings of cross-modal features by making another feature exist between cross-modal features, facilitating the voice and face features of the same person to be embedded in a convex hull. Moreover, the incorporation of cross-modal attention mechanisms with convex embedding techniques represents a highly effective strategy for the attenuation of false positives and false negatives, accomplished via the minimization of inter-class discrepancies. We exhaustively evaluated our method for cross-modal verification, matching, and retrieval tasks on the large-scale VoxCeleb dataset. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves notable improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: A cross-modal face-voice embedding method using convex hull embedding and cross-modal attention to align face and voice features, reducing heterogeneity-induced errors; evaluated on VoxCeleb with improved state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal face-voice association is hampered by inter-modal feature heterogeneity; existing methods emphasize discrimination but fail to handle cross-modal discrepancy, leading to many false positives/negatives.
AI.method: Learn embeddings by introducing an intermediate cross-modal representation to form a convex hull for same-person features; incorporate cross-modal attention with convex embedding to minimize inter-class discrepancies; train to align audio and visual features into a common representation.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments on VoxCeleb for verification, matching, and retrieval show notable improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Convex cross-modal embedding with attention effectively reduces misclassifications in face-voice association and benefits cross-modal retrieval tasks.

title: The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty
summary: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

AI.tldr: Proposes accel, a geometry-based, cost-free uncertainty proxy for Flow Matching (FM) in embodied models, using the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass to detect uncertainty and enable online failure detection, with strong empirical performance under deployment budgets.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty estimation for FM action heads is needed for safe deployment, but existing methods incur extra training, high computation, and limited generalization. A cheap, generalizable online proxy is highly desirable.
AI.method: Present a geometric interpretation that FM uncertainty corresponds to deviation from an affine-isotropic contraction field. Introduce accel (denoising acceleration) as a proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, requiring no additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. Provide theoretical justification and empirical validation, and test its utility in online failure detection.
AI.result: Accel closely tracks FM uncertainty and identifies failing rollouts well before termination. It matches or outperforms costly resampling- and training-based baselines across deployment-budget scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Accel is a faithful, generalizable, and cost-free uncertainty proxy for FM, enabling safer deployment of conditional generative FM systems; code and demos are available at the provided repository.

title: RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It
summary: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

AI.tldr: RIPPLE reframes Griffin–Lim as an inter-channel phase prior and learns to generate phase to preserve cross-channel structure, outperforming per-channel recovery in multi-channel audio and seismic tasks.
AI.motivation: Phase relations carry inter-channel content (spatial audio, seismic polarization). Magnitude-focused generation with independent phase recovery discards this information and can mislead downstream analyses. A learned inter-channel phase model is needed to preserve physics-driven coherence.
AI.method: RIPPLE initializes phase from the source and treats Griffin–Lim as a phase prior; a rectified flow refines the phase under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. It is evaluated on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation.
AI.result: Outperforms recovery-based pipelines on inter-channel coherence metrics. In seismic results, S-wave polarization error declines from 57.3° (random) with per-channel recovery to 33.8° with learned phase; performance gains are observed across architecturally distinct generators.
AI.conclusion: Phase should be generated rather than recovered; learning inter-channel phase preserves physical inter-channel information and improves downstream analyses, with demonstrated cross-domain applicability.

title: Collaborative Feature Aggregation for Face Super-Resolution and Robust Re-Identification
summary: We propose a novel collaborative approach for face super-resolution (SR) and robust person re-identification from sequential or multi-view facial images. Traditional SR methods often suffer from blurring and distortion in faces recovered from poor-quality images due to low resolution. Image- and video-based facial SR methods using facial landmarks or segmentation also have similar challenges. To overcome these limitations, we leverage multiple correlated facial observations, across time or viewpoints, by introducing a transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation method that unifies identity features from multi-sequence or multi-view data. This allows faces in multiple sequences of an individual to contribute to accurately estimating common facial features. Furthermore, we propose a cascade SR network to progressively restore the high-resolution image of the target's face with gradual facial feature unification. The unified identity representation is further utilized in person re-identification scenarios, enabling accurate matching even under severe image degradation. The exhaustive experimental results and comparisons show that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating consistent improvements in both face super-resolution and re-identification performance. Our work highlights the effectiveness of joint identity reconstruction and progressive image restoration from multiple facial inputs in enhancing downstream visual recognition tasks.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based collaborative framework for face super-resolution (SR) and robust re-identification that leverages multi-view/multi-sequence facial observations, combined with a cascade SR network for progressive high-resolution restoration, achieving state-of-the-art results under degraded imagery.
AI.motivation: Traditional SR methods suffer from blurring/distortion on low-quality faces; landmark/segmentation-based SR methods face similar drawbacks. Leveraging multiple correlated observations across time or viewpoints can improve facial feature estimation and robustness in re-ID.
AI.method: A transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation that unifies identity features from multiple sequences/views; a cascade SR network progressively restores the target face with gradual feature unification; unified identity representations are used for robust person re-identification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show the approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both face SR and re-ID, with consistent improvements under severe image degradation.
AI.conclusion: Joint identity reconstruction across multiple facial inputs, coupled with progressive image restoration, enhances downstream recognition tasks and demonstrates the value of cross-view/time collaboration for face analysis.

title: Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL
comment: full version of a paper accepted at ISWC26
summary: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

AI.tldr: Exponential-time complexity for SHACL fitting under ELI; polynomial-time for special cases.
AI.motivation: Automatic learning of SHACL shapes for data graph validation; formal complexity analysis to guide algorithms.
AI.method: Formalization of SHACL core fragment (ELI) with well-founded, stable, and supported semantics; define fitting existence and most specific fitting; analyze complexity and bounds.
AI.result: Tight exponential-time upper bounds established for fitting existence and most specific fitting; polynomial bounds identified for relevant special cases.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates inherent hardness of SHACL shape learning under these semantics; informs practice and motivates heuristics or restrictions to achieve tractable learning.

title: LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

AI.tldr: LSPO recovers gradient on cliff prompts in RLVR via per-step supervised LoRA adapters, boosting math-reasoning performance; achieves gains up to +10.7 on AIME24/pass@4 and +3.8 average across 16 cells.
AI.motivation: In reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards for mathematical reasoning, group-normalized advantages are zero on cliff prompts where every rollout fails, creating a structural blind spot that prevents learning at the frontier of model capability.
AI.method: At each RL update: detect cliff prompts; fit a small, low-rank LoRA adapter through a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions; re-roll cliff prompts using base+adapter to generate successful completions; insert these back into the RL batch with importance-sampling correction; perform a GRPO step on the base model alone; the adapter's supervised gradient is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model at inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B using n=5 seeds and 1000-step horizon; LSPO’s 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 wins, 1 tie); gains include up to +10.7 on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 on MATH500/pass@1; average improvement +3.8 across cells.
AI.conclusion: LSPO provides an effective gradient-recovery mechanism for cliff prompts in RLVR, enabling the base model to surpass baselines while keeping the adapter transient (used only during sampling). Its practicality hinges on the overhead of per-step supervised LoRA fitting and cliff-detection accuracy.

title: Convolutional Neural Shading for High-Quality 3D Reconstruction from Multi-View Images
summary: We propose a convolutional neural shading (CNS), a novel pipeline to reconstruct high-quality 3D shapes from multi-view images. Several recent studies have used neural radiance fields and other neural differentiable rendering methods to understand 3D geometry. However, these approaches rely on single-point geometric information, such as positions and normals of the surface, leading to a lack of detailed local geometry. Our approach addresses the inherent limitations of single-point information by leveraging a neural shader to capture variations even in dark and textureless regions with a convolutional neural shader, resulting in far more accurate geometry predictions. Additionally, our method mitigates surface irregularities at image boundaries by introducing a fine-detail displacement network, which utilizes spatial information of surface geometry and learns fine displacement details by correlating neighboring values in the rendering coordinates. Through extensive experiments, our proposed method has demonstrated significant quality improvements in the reconstructed shapes and rendered images over current state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: A convolutional neural shading (CNS) pipeline for high-quality multi-view 3D reconstruction, using a neural shader to capture local geometry variations in challenging regions and a fine-detail displacement network to reduce surface boundary artifacts, achieving state-of-the-art improvements.
AI.motivation: Neural radiance fields and differentiable renderers often rely on single-point geometry (positions, normals), which limits recovery of detailed local geometry, particularly in dark/textureless regions and at image boundaries.
AI.method: Introduce a convolutional neural shading (CNS) pipeline. A neural shader captures local variations beyond single-point cues, and a fine-detail displacement network leverages spatial surface information to learn high-frequency displacements by correlating neighboring rendering coordinates, reducing boundary artifacts in multi-view reconstruction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate significant quality improvements in both reconstructed shapes and rendered images over current state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The CNS framework effectively mitigates single-point information limitations, delivering more accurate geometry and rendering through neural shading and fine-detail displacement.

title: From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

AI.tldr: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD) improves internalized LLM agent capabilities by using outcome-verified supervision and comparative learning. It builds a prefix-tree of failed student rollouts, selectively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations, applying localized learning at the first divergence and distilling the teacher's suffix.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of action-level supervision in self-distillation (lack of environment-outcome validation and underutilization of rollout information), by leveraging outcome-verified teacher guidance and comparative learning over entire trajectories.
AI.method: Construct a prefix tree from failed student rollouts. From student-reached states, adaptively invoke a skill-conditioned teacher. Keep only continuations that are outcome-verified as successful. At the first state-aligned divergence, apply localized comparative learning between student and teacher streams and distill the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior.
AI.result: Across ALFWorld and WebShop, evaluated on three model scales, OVCSD consistently surpasses skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 absolute success-rate gains on ALFWorld and 5.4 on WebShop, with less than 3% privileged interaction during training.
AI.conclusion: OVCSD provides a principled framework for outcome-validated, comparative self-distillation, enabling more reliable internalization of capabilities in LLM agents and demonstrating strong cross-domain improvements with modest training overhead.

title: Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches
summary: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

AI.tldr: Benchmark across three paradigms for predictive process monitoring (PPM): sequence models trained from scratch, LLM-based approaches, and tabular foundation models with in-context learning. Findings: sequence models excel at next-activity prediction, tabular foundation models are competitive for temporal tasks, and LLMs are generally slower and do not outperform the others.
AI.motivation: PPM uses event logs to predict ongoing process instances. With the rise of foundation models, including LLMs, it is unclear whether they outperform traditional sequence models for PPM, or whether tabular foundation models can match specialized sequence-based approaches. A systematic benchmark across paradigms is needed.
AI.method: A controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks comparing three modeling paradigms: (1) sequence models trained from scratch (e.g., LSTM/GRU), (2) foundation-model approaches based on large language models (LLMs) for PPM, and (3) tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities. Tasks include next activity and temporal predictions (e.g., remaining time).
AI.result: Sequence models consistently achieve the best performance for next activity prediction. Tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks. LLMs typically lag behind and incur higher costs.
AI.conclusion: Classical sequence-based models remain strong baselines for PPM, especially for next-activity prediction. Tabular foundation models show promise for temporal predictions, while LLMs do not consistently outperform traditional approaches and are costlier, indicating a need for further research into efficient adaptation of foundation models for PPM.

title: What Makes Deep Learning Work for Traditional Chinese Medicine Tongue Diagnosis? A Comprehensive Ablation Study
summary: Deep learning has shown promise for automated tongue diagnosis in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), yet the design space remains underexplored. We conducted a systematic ablation study spanning 20+ model versions under rigorous 5-fold cross-validation on TongueDx2 (5,109 images, 976 expert-annotated) and a merged dataset of 11,101 samples. We compared six backbone architectures, four loss functions, five augmentation strategies, and six training strategies. The best 976-sample model achieved weighted-F1 of 0.6625 using ConvNeXt-Tiny with restrained augmentation and weak-group ensemble, while the best 11,101-sample model reached weighted-F1 of 0.7761. Six key design principles emerged: (1) ConvNeXt-Tiny offers optimal parameter efficiency; (2) BCE substantially outperforms Asymmetric Loss (+2.7%); (3) restrained color augmentation is critical; (4) weak-group ensemble replacement (+2.1%) outperforms probability averaging; (5) data scaling yielded +20.6% improvement; (6) expanding from 13 to 45 label dimensions caused catastrophic collapse (0.78 to 0.22). These principles are generalizable to multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive ablation study across 20+ model variants on TongueDx2 and a merged dataset to identify practical design choices for multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance.
AI.motivation: Systematically explore design space in DL-based tongue diagnosis to improve performance, generalization, and guidelines for imbalanced, multi-label medical imaging.
AI.method: 5-fold cross-validation on two datasets (TongueDx2: 5,109 images with 976 expert labels; merged dataset: 11,101 samples). Compared six backbone architectures, four loss functions, five augmentation strategies, and six training strategies; evaluated with weighted-F1 and ablation effects.
AI.result: Best 976-sample model: ConvNeXt-Tiny with restrained augmentation and weak-group ensemble; weighted-F1 0.6625. Best 11,101-sample model: weighted-F1 0.7761. Six design principles: (1) ConvNeXt-Tiny offers parameter efficiency; (2) BCE outperforms Asymmetric Loss (+2.7%); (3) restrained color augmentation is critical; (4) weak-group ensemble (+2.1%) over probability averaging; (5) data scaling yields +20.6%; (6) expanding from 13 to 45 labels caused catastrophic collapse (0.78 to 0.22). These principles generalize to multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance.
AI.conclusion: The study yields generalizable guidelines for effective design of multi-label medical image classifiers under label imbalance, emphasizing architecture choice, loss, augmentation, ensembling, and label dimensionality considerations.

title: MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation
summary: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

AI.tldr: Reframe credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons from large multimodal models, enabling robust, dynamic-agent credit estimation and reward shaping; analyzed theoretically (convergence, robustness) with Shapley values for interpretability; empirically improves coordination across tasks.
AI.motivation: Credit assignment under partial/delayed feedback and dynamic agent participation is a core bottleneck in cooperative MARL, particularly in embodied AI contexts where agent counts and feedback quality vary.
AI.method: Replace absolute contribution estimation with relative, pairwise comparisons among agents via large multimodal models. Convert comparison outcomes into contribution scores used in a potential-based reward shaping framework. Provide theoretical analyses for convergence and robustness; use Shapley values as interpretive reference.
AI.result: The framework is claimed to converge robustly and to handle dynamic agent participation. Shapley values offer interpretability. Empirical results across challenging tasks show improved cooperative behavior guided by MARS-RA.
AI.conclusion: Rank-aggregation-based credit assignment using multimodal, pairwise comparisons is a robust, interpretable approach for embodied MARL with changing agent participation, enabling effective cooperation through reward shaping and Shapley-based interpretation.

title: Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays
summary: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

AI.tldr: Introduces a λ-parameterized deterministic learning-augmented Balance with (4/λ+1/λ^2)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency; a randomized algorithm for the adversarial model achieving (e+1)-competitiveness against oblivious adversaries; proves an e lower bound for randomized online algorithms; combines the two into a randomized learning-augmented algorithm with (e/λ+1/λ^2)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency; supports findings with numerical experiments and discusses empirical performance.
AI.motivation: Address online aggregation with delays on a line metric, leveraging advice (online suggested service lengths) while remaining robust to adversarial inputs. The work seeks to improve classical deterministic bounds by introducing learning-augmented and randomized strategies, quantify the trade-offs via λ, and validate both theory and experiments.
AI.method: - For each λ in (0,1], present a deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm achieving (4/λ+1/λ^2)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency. - Develop a randomized algorithm in the classical adversarial model that is (e+1)-competitive against an oblivious adversary, beating the prior deterministic Balance benchmark of 5-competitiveness. - Establish a lower bound of e on the competitive ratio for randomized online algorithms, improving previous bound e/(e-1). - Combine the two approaches to obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm with (e/λ+1/λ^2)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency. - Validate results with numerical experiments to assess practical performance.
AI.result: Main theoretical contributions include tight (or near-tight) competitive ratios for both deterministic and randomized online algorithms under delays on a line metric, including new lower bounds for randomized models and a λ-parametrized robustness/consistency framework. The empirical results corroborate the theoretical trade-offs and demonstrate improved performance over baselines.
AI.conclusion: The work advances learning-augmented and randomized online algorithm design for delay-tolerant line-metric aggregation by showing how advice and randomness can jointly yield stronger guarantees. It characterizes robust-consistent trade-offs via λ, provides improved competitive bounds (notably a randomized (e+1)-competitive algorithm and an e lower bound), and supports findings with experiments, suggesting practical applicability of the proposed algorithms.

title: OPLD: On-Policy Latent Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Interleaved multimodal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves visual reasoning by incorporating auxiliary visual evidence into intermediate reasoning. However, existing approaches remain constrained by externally defined reasoning traces and visual operations, limiting their ability to develop flexible and abstract visual thinking. Reasoning with latent has recently offered a promising direction by internalizing intermediate computation into continuous representations. Nevertheless, existing visual-latent methods mainly supervise latent states through alignment with compressed auxiliary visual features, treating them as proxies for visual observations rather than active reasoning states. Consequently, they capture the provided evidence but fail to fully internalize the abstract reasoning process induced by multimodal CoT. In this paper, we propose OPLD (On-Policy Latent Distillation), a simple framework that transfers the reasoning capability induced by privileged multimodal CoT into latent reasoning representations. Extensive experiments on diverse multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that OPLD consistently outperforms existing latent reasoning methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. The results suggest that supervising latent representations at the reasoning-process level provides a more effective paradigm for multimodal latent reasoning than conventional feature-level alignment.

AI.tldr: OPLD distills reasoning from privileged multimodal CoT into latent representations, achieving strong performance on multimodal tasks by supervising latent state trajectories rather than feature alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing latent reasoning approaches rely on aligning latent states to compressed visual features, which captures evidence but not abstract reasoning; externally defined reasoning traces and visual operations limit flexibility.
AI.method: On-Policy Latent Distillation (OPLD): distill CoT-level reasoning policy from privileged multimodal CoT into latent representations; supervise latent trajectories at the reasoning-process level; end-to-end training that aligns latent states with CoT steps using on-policy signals.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms existing latent reasoning methods on diverse multimodal benchmarks; achieves state-of-the-art on multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Supervising latent representations at the reasoning-process level provides a more effective paradigm for multimodal latent reasoning than feature-level alignment; OPLD offers a simple, strong approach.

title: Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation
summary: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them. This paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's weights, or into the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted? We study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples. Supplying the correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over a response-only control; replacing it with an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Dividing the same training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges, however, loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%. Matching the bank's stored capacity with one rank-64 adapter does not reproduce this loss. Nor is the result explained by learning rate or optimizer steps. Initializing the family adapters from a shared, trained judge recovers test accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch training at the same learning rate (95% interval 18.88-21.02). The result changes when specialization governs deferral rather than judgment. On RewardBench 2, learned correctness heads route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing any reward score. Across 20 locked repartitions, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy, compared with 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute. Every run passes an exact one-sided 95% risk audit; margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy while using at least 0.94 compute. These results suggest a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

AI.tldr: Shared judgment learning (a single, unified evaluator) generally outperforms training distinct criterion-specific judges when data are scarce, and domain adaptation should be applied at auditable release boundaries rather than inside judge weights; only with enough data should specialization be introduced to preserve both accuracy and auditability.
AI.motivation: Understand how to allocate domain specialization in agentic evaluators: should specialization live in the evaluator's weights or in the deferral/triggering rules? The goal is to maximize locked-test accuracy and robust auditing while minimizing compute and data fragmentation.
AI.method: Empirical study on 99,952 rubric-conditioned examples. Experiments include: (1) effect of supplying the correct vs unrelated rubric; (2) training eight criterion-family LoRA judges (distributed across criteria) and its impact on accuracy and audited coverage (5% target); (3) capacity matching with a single rank-64 adapter; (4) initialization of family adapters from a shared judge; (5) varying whether specialization governs deferral vs judgment; (6) RewardBench 2 cascade using learned correctness heads (0.6B-4B-8B) vs 8B baseline; (7) 20 locked repartitions with corresponding risk audits; (8) compute and margin-based rule comparisons.
AI.result: Key empirical findings: correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points; unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Splitting training across eight LoRA judges reduces accuracy by 10.05 points and audited coverage from 24.44% to 5.43%, not rescued by simply matching bank capacity or by learning-rate/optimizer changes. Initializing the family adapters from a shared trained judge recovers accuracy to 76.85% (≈20 points above scratch). Specialization that governs deferral rather than judgment shifts outcomes. On RewardBench 2, a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade of learned correctness heads yields 89.40% accuracy over 20 repartitions vs 84.75% for 8B alone, with 0.415 normalized parameter compute; all runs pass an exact one-sided 95% risk audit, and margin-based rules stay near 84.8% with ≥0.94 compute.
AI.conclusion: A qualified design rule emerges: defer domain specialization until there is sufficient data to justify splitting the evaluator's judgment, and constrain domain-specific adaptation to the auditable release boundary to maintain test accuracy and auditability without excessive compute.

title: Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations
summary:
Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

AI.tldr: Introduces contrastive concept importance (CCI) to explain model decisions by attributing the logit margin between a target class and a foil class to an automatic visual concept basis, yielding signed, decomposable explanations that reveal class-pair-specific behavior and align with semantic hierarchies.
AI.motivation: To address the non-contrastive nature of standard concept attributions and the needs arising from misclassification, confusion, and low-margin predictions by answering 'why P rather than Q?'.
AI.method: Define CCI, compute attribution of logit margin to a concept basis, produce signed scores indicating support for target vs foil, decompose into target-logit and foil-logit effects; use automatic concept extraction and CRAFT-style bases; evaluate with insertion/deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition, and semantic hierarchy.
AI.result: CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by non-contrastive attributions; highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to determine whether they support fine-grained distinctions; validated on ImageNet with concept bases and evaluation curves.
AI.conclusion: CCI provides interpretable contrastive explanations and helps distinguish globally important vs class-pair-specific concepts, including whether effects are shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive; useful for understanding misclassification and fine-grained distinctions.

title: S-Avatar: Diffusion-Guided Gaussian Head Avatars from a Single Image
summary: We propose S-Avatar, a novel method for generating photorealistic 3D head avatars from a single image using a diffusion-guided 3D model generation module and strategies for animating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). While single-image head avatar reconstruction is crucial for lifelike Virtual Reality (VR) applications, existing approaches often struggle to preserve 3D consistency under unseen viewpoints. S-Avatar addresses this limitation through a three-stage pipeline. First, a high-resolution 3DGS is synthesized directly from a single image using a diffusion-based Gaussian splat generation module. Next, the parametric head model FLAME is aligned with the generated 3DGS by optimizing its parameters and spatial transformations. Finally, to adapt the 3DGS to FLAME variations, we construct a binding template that encodes the spatial relationship between the initial splats and FLAME. The dynamic 3D head avatar can then be rendered in real time by deforming the 3DGS with the binding template. By combining diffusion-guided canonical 3DGS generation with FLAME-based control, our method achieves efficient and accurate reconstruction with enhanced 3D consistency. Evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that S-Avatar outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation, achieving superior realism and consistency. Consequently, our approach represents a significant advance in accessible avatar creation, applicable to a wide range of VR/AR applications. The project page is available at https://github.com/hailsong/savatar.

AI.tldr: Single-image photorealistic 3D head avatar (S-Avatar) using diffusion-guided 3D Gaussian splats and a FLAME-based binding for real-time, consistent novel-view animation; claims state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Address 3D inconsistency in single-image head avatar reconstruction, enabling lifelike VR/AR avatars with reliable novel-view and expression realism.
