Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets moves the other three frontier models by at most +/-3.4 pp but reduces GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. We release the code, prompts, and theories distilled.

AI.tldr: A neurosymbolic protocol prompts large models to distill complete ASP theories for VQA within 1 hour; frontier models achieve near-perfect CLEVR and high GQA accuracy; GPT-5 is strong on CLEVR but weak on GQA/CLEVRER; handwritten references provide modest gains for frontier models and harm GPT-5; code/prompts/theories are released.
AI.motivation: Writing ASP theories from scratch is hard; the study tests whether a fixed agent with a solver in the loop can distill complete and correct theories, in a dataset-agnostic, prompt-driven protocol.
AI.method: 1-hour prompt-based protocol starting from an empty file; nine models (four frontier: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro; two mid-tier; three open weights); benchmarks: CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER; evaluate with/without handwritten reference theories; measure accuracy across tasks.
AI.result: Frontier models: 100% CLEVR; 92.8–98.8% GQA; CLEVRER (Sonnet/Opus/DeepSeek V4 Pro): 92.7–95.3%. GPT-5: 98.7% CLEVR; 41.8% GQA; 86.7% CLEVRER. Adding handwritten references improves frontier models by up to ~3.4 pp, but reduces GPT-5 by 3–19 pp.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that the protocol can distill complete and correct ASP theories for non-trivial VQA benchmarks, with model scale being a key factor; resources (code/prompts/theories) are released to the community.

title: TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents
summary: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

AI.tldr: TAPO introduces Transition-Aware Policy Optimization, a lightweight plug-in that jointly optimizes LLM agents via standard RL and an action-conditioned next-observation prediction task using rollout data, improving performance without extra data or cost.
AI.motivation: Generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks benefits from predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Dense supervisory signals (environmental transitions) are underutilized in current RL pipelines for LLM agents.
AI.method: Alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Repurposes rollout data to train an action-conditioned next-observation predictor on a shared backbone. No extra expert data, sampling, or inference overhead. Plug-and-play with existing agent RL algorithms.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on WebShop and ALFWorld shows TAPO consistently improves task performance across foundation models of varying scales and different policy optimization algorithms.
AI.conclusion: TAPO provides a computationally lightweight, plug-in enhancement that leverages environmental transition dynamics to boost RL-based LLM agents without additional data or costs.

title: Diversifying Personalized Research Ideation against AI-Induced Homogenization
summary: AI-assisted research ideation has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating scientific discovery, with systems now capable of generating research directions conditioned on papers, topics, or lightweight researcher contexts. Yet current systems largely optimize individual suggestions in isolation. This leaves two blind spots. First, coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream directions that appear broadly feasible, but lack sufficient researcher-specific grounding. Second, independent recommendations can concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes. To address these blind spots, we propose DivAlign, a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization. DivAlign extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. On a benchmark we construct from 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, DivAlign reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/DivAlign.

AI.tldr: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization of AI research ideation, reducing community redundancy while preserving individual researcher-direction fit.
AI.motivation: Current ideation systems generate directions in isolation, leading to mainstream, potentially groundedless directions and homogenized portfolios. There's a need for finer-grained, researcher-specific representations and diverse, aligned directions across a community.
AI.method: Four-stage pipeline: (1) extract fine-grained researcher profiles; (2) generate profile-conditioned candidate directions; (3) score directions along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, Growth Potential); (4) surface researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. Benchmark on 95 AI researchers across five subfields.
AI.result: On the benchmark, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit: average pairwise similarity decreases from 0.331 to 0.294, and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608, compared with coarse single-shot ideation. Relative to an independent top-choice variant, nearest-neighbor similarity decreases from 0.663 to 0.608, while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score.
AI.conclusion: DivAlign effectively reduces redundancy in the community portfolio while maintaining alignment to individual researchers; code and data are available at the provided GitHub link.

title: Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness
summary: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

AI.tldr: Finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic-programming recursions; via a quantized, measure-valued DP formulation, with a DRO interpretation under Wasserstein distance.
AI.motivation: To obtain principled finite-sample guarantees for Transformer generalization when training can be modeled as a finite-horizon Markov decision process, and to connect to distributionally robust optimization.
AI.method: Develop doubly lifted, measure-valued Transformer dynamics; represent datasets as laws over pairs of empirical input-output measures; analyze a quantized surrogate by discretizing state, action, and measure-state spaces; derive concentration-based bounds for empirical laws on finite metric spaces and a Lipschitz stability bound for the value function; propagate bounds to the base model with explicit approximation error; extend to a distributionally robust control formulation (Wasserstein).
AI.result: Explicit finite-sample generalization bounds are obtained; explicit approximation error between the quantized surrogate and the base model; bounds derived via concentration inequalities and Lipschitz stability; framework yields a distributionally robust perspective via Wasserstein DRO.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides principled finite-sample generalization guarantees for Transformers under dynamic-programming-recursive training and connects Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, enabling robustness-aware training.

title: MonoVoc: Decoupling Geometry and Semantics for Lightweight Monocular Open-Vocabulary 3D Gaussians
summary: Open vocabulary 3D scene understanding is essential for next-generation interactive systems, empowering users to intuitively query and navigate reconstructed environments using natural language. However, current 3D Gaussian frameworks are often bottlenecked by restrictive multiview capture requirements, costly scene-specific optimization, and the massive memory overhead of storing dense language features. We present a novel, training-free pipeline that fundamentally reimagines this paradigm by explicitly decoupling 3D geometric reconstruction from semantic integration. Given a standard monocular video sequence as input, our method efficiently outputs a compact, highly interpretable, and fully searchable object-level semantic Gaussian map. Rather than entangling heavy language embeddings within the mapping loop, we extract geometry independently and ground semantics through a lightweight, modular post-processing framework. Extensive evaluations on the Replica dataset demonstrate that this decoupled architecture preserves strong rendering fidelity and competitive segmentation accuracy. Crucially, by replacing dense per-Gaussian storage with modular, object-level semantic embeddings, our approach delivers an order-of-magnitude reduction in memory usage compared to SOTA baselines. This provides a highly efficient, scalable, and practical solution for open-vocabulary 3D retrieval and question answering directly from everyday monocular video.

AI.tldr: A training-free, decoupled 3D scene understanding pipeline that extracts geometry from monocular video and grounds semantics via a modular post-processing step to produce an object-level semantic Gaussian map, achieving strong fidelity with order-of-magnitude memory reduction versus SOTA.
AI.motivation: Current 3D Gaussian frameworks rely on dense language features and heavy optimization, requiring multi-view captures and large memory; there is a need for open-vocabulary 3D retrieval and QA from monocular video.
AI.method: Decouple geometry extraction from semantic integration; use monocular video as input; produce compact object-level semantic Gaussian maps; apply lightweight post-processing to ground semantics; training-free; modular architecture.
AI.result: On Replica dataset, maintains rendering fidelity and competitive segmentation; memory usage reduced by an order of magnitude due to modular embeddings replacing dense per-Gaussian storage; enables open-vocabulary retrieval and QA from monocular video.
AI.conclusion: An efficient, scalable solution for open-vocabulary 3D retrieval and QA; practical for everyday monocular video; avoids embedding language features inside the mapping loop; enables modular extension.

title: PerturbMap: Cross-Context Transfer of Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
summary: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention in every cellular context: a query perturbation is often observed in one or more source contexts but missing in the recipient context where its effect is needed. Ignoring those measured responses discards query-specific experimental evidence, whereas copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal. We propose PerturbMap, which predicts a missing recipient-context effect by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations, with proposal weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1\% over a recipient-local low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It remains within $2.82\times10^{-6}$ MSE of our centralized token-matched pooled reference, which uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows the same direction: same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5\% for the low-rank base to 80.5\% for PerturbMap.

AI.tldr: PerturbMap improves cross-context transfer of perturbation effects in single-cell data by augmenting a recipient-local low-rank base with transport proposals based on trained ridge models; it uses route reliability from anchors to weigh proposals, yielding better MSE and retrieval metrics than several baselines and approaching a centralized reference.
AI.motivation: In single-cell perturbation atlases, query perturbations are often observed in some source contexts but missing in the recipient context where their effects are needed. Simply borrowing responses risks mis-signal transfer or discarding evidence; there is a need for a principled method to predict missing recipient-context effects while preserving perturbation-specific signals.
AI.method: Create a recipient-local low-rank base representation. For each perturbation, generate proposals that transport the measured source responses through ridge models trained on paired training perturbations (source-to-recipient). Weights for proposals are determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. Combine the base with weighted proposals to predict missing recipient-context effects.
AI.result: On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, the method reduces full-effect MSE by 4.1% over the recipient-local base and outperforms FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It achieves MSE within 2.82e-6 of a centralized token-matched pooled reference. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows same-recipient top-10 retrieval by cosine improves from 74.5% to 80.5%.
AI.conclusion: PerturbMap provides a robust mechanism to infer missing recipient-context perturbation effects by combining a local base with evidence-supported transport proposals, achieving improved accuracy and retrieval fidelity compared to multiple baselines.

title: It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations
summary:
Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

AI.tldr: Einx proposes a universal tensor operation notation derived from vectorization to unify and simplify tensor programming beyond existing numpy-like, einsum, and einops, with a Python-embedded implementation.
AI.motivation: Current tensor APIs (NumPy-like) are hard to read/write and error-prone due to inconsistent shape rules; existing alternatives (einsum/einops) are not general enough for a universal model of tensor programming.
AI.method: Reframe tensor operations as vectorization transformations, lift/lower-order operations via vectorization, and define einx as a declarative, loop-like, pointful notation that captures vectorization of tensor operations. Implement einx in Python and integrate with existing tensor frameworks.
AI.result: Introduction of einx as a universal notation with a Python-embedded implementation; reduces API surface to a small set of elementary operations and provides consistent rules, enabling readable/writable representations in code.
AI.conclusion: Einx offers a universal, readable, and integrable framework for tensor operations by grounding their vectorization, potentially unifying and simplifying tensor programming across frameworks.

title: ObjectStream: Latent Objects as Memory Anchors for Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video understanding requires models to continuously retain useful visual evidence before future questions are known. Existing approaches primarily manage the growing visual context according to token importance, temporal redundancy, or segment-level relevance, but rarely organize evidence around objects that persist and evolve over time. Thus, in this paper, we introduce ObjectStream, a training-free framework that treats latent objects as memory anchors for streaming video understanding. ObjectStream induces spatially coherent latent objects directly from frozen Video-LLM representations, links them across frames into persistent anchors, and maintains their histories under a bounded memory budget, without requiring external object detectors or segmentation models. Built on these anchors, ObjectStream preserves three complementary forms of evidence: persistent object histories, transient object changes, and recent visual context. This design enables existing Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) to reason over object identities, interactions, and state changes while leaving the underlying model unchanged. Extensive experiments on online streaming and offline long-video benchmarks demonstrate both effectiveness and efficiency. In online streaming evaluation, ObjectStream improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 10.0 points on OVO-Bench Real-Time Visual Perception, while reducing peak GPU mem-ory and TTFT by approximately 50%. On offline long-video benchmarks, it surpasses the full-token baseline while discarding 82.5% of visual tokens. These results highlight latent objects as a practical and effective organizing principle for compact streaming video memory.

AI.tldr: ObjectStream is a training-free, object-centric memory framework for streaming video understanding. It extracts latent, spatially coherent objects from frozen Video-LLMs to serve as persistent memory anchors, linking frames, maintaining limited histories, and preserving three evidence forms—persistent histories, transient changes, and recent context—without external detectors. It enables Video-LLMs to reason about object identities and state changes, achieving notable accuracy and efficiency gains on online and offline benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Streaming video understanding requires retaining useful visual evidence about objects over time. Existing approaches focus on token importance, temporal redundancy, or segment relevance but do not organize evidence around objects that persist and evolve. A latent-object memory could provide compact, object-centric context that improves reasoning without retraining or detectors.
AI.method: A training-free framework that induces spatially coherent latent objects directly from frozen Video-LLM representations, links them across frames into persistent anchors, and maintains their histories within a bounded memory budget. No external object detectors or segmentation models are used. Anchors preserve three evidence forms—persistent histories, transient changes, and recent visual context—and enable Video-LLMs to reason about object identities, interactions, and state changes while keeping the base model unchanged.
AI.result: Online streaming: Qwen2.5-VL-7B gains 10.0 points on OVO-Bench Real-Time Visual Perception; peak GPU memory and TTFT reduced by ~50%. Offline long-video benchmarks: surpasses the full-token baseline while discarding 82.5% of visual tokens.
AI.conclusion: Latent objects provide a practical, effective organizing principle for compact streaming video memory. The training-free latent-object memory enables accurate, efficient, object-aware reasoning with existing Video-LLMs without retraining or additional detectors.

title: An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale
summary:
This paper introduces a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape. AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. The framework structures policy analysis around multiple policy attributes, allowing users to surface priorities and tensions without prescribing outcomes. We use a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to inform the design of policy attribute rubrics. This quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives and presents them through comparative visualizations that support interpretability and cross-policy comparison. The paper also examines the use of commercial LLMs for rubric-based policy analysis, benchmarking their outputs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions. Rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability, the framework focuses on relevance and alignment across attributes. By making analytical assumptions explicit, including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes, the framework enables users to evaluate whether its embedded priorities align with the users' own normative commitments. The approach is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments.
  Contributions: (1) multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics that surface tradeoffs rather than resolving them; (2) a transparent hybrid methodology combining feedback from subject-matter experts with computational validation; and (3) use of domain-trained rubric-calibrated models as a benchmark for comparing different general-purpose large language models.

AI.tldr: A policy analysis framework for AI governance using multidimensional rubrics to surface tradeoffs, combining expert insights with computational analysis and benchmarking LLM outputs.
AI.motivation: Shed light on underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions in AI governance debates, avoiding binary positions; provide a transparent, interpretable, jurisdiction-agnostic tool for policymakers, analysts, and researchers.
AI.method: Mixed-methods: qualitative input from subject-matter experts; computational text analysis to design policy attribute rubrics; empirical weighting and visualizations for cross-policy comparison; rubric-based benchmarking of commercial LLMs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model; explicit analytical assumptions.
AI.result: A framework for multidimensional policy assessment that surfaces tradeoffs rather than resolving them; transparent hybrid methodology; benchmarking of general-purpose LLMs against domain-trained rubric-calibrated models; outputs include interpretable visualizations and explicit alignment with predefined attributes.
AI.conclusion: Enhances transparency, interpretability, and alignment with users' normative commitments; jurisdiction-agnostic; supports policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments; emphasizes relevance and alignment over effectiveness.

title: Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web
summary: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

AI.tldr: A self-supervised Transformer-based user representation model for open-web real-time bidding, leveraging masked language modeling and sequence-level contrastive learning on fragmented user histories, with an LLM-in-the-loop lifter-based optimization, yielding measurable gains in production bid win-rate and CTR ranking, plus live A/B improvements in CTR and eCPC.
AI.motivation: In open-web RTB, user identity is fragmented and non-persistent; historical signals are sparse and sessionly disjoint. There is a need to exploit sequential user behavior despite limited data to improve downstream production tasks like bid optimization and CTR ranking.
AI.method: Pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective on user browsing histories. Fine-tune on click prediction. Introduce an LLM-in-the-loop search over curated, reviewable edits (lifters) to optimize the pre-training pipeline, implementing an LLM-as-optimizer paradigm for industrial deployment. Apply the learned encoder to production tasks (bid win-rate model, CTR ranker) and evaluate via live A/B testing.
AI.result: +1.197% RIG on production bid win-rate model; +1.354% RIG on production CTR ranker. Seven-day live A/B test shows +2.13% CTR and -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excludes zero on both metrics).
AI.conclusion: The user encoder representations learned through self-supervised pre-training, augmented with LLM-guided optimization, are viable for open-web RTB deployments and yield consistent gains across critical production tasks, validating the applicability of user foundation models in environments with non-persistent identities.

title: AdaAnchor4D: Anchor-Conditioned Spatiotemporal Feature Aggregation for Monocular UAV 4D Reconstruction
summary: Monocular UAV videos provide valuable observations for dynamic reconstruction of complex urban scenes. However, such scenes exhibit pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity: different regions follow distinct temporal activity patterns, while the motion states of some dynamic regions may further evolve over time. Although dynamic Gaussian methods based on decomposed shared spatiotemporal feature fields have achieved efficient and accurate reconstruction in object-centric or relatively compact scenes, their commonly adopted fixed plane-wise feature combination mechanisms are less suited to the heterogeneous local dynamics of UAV scenes, often leading to ghosting artifacts and blurred dynamic details. To address this challenge, we propose AdaAnchor4D, an adaptive anchor deformation framework for monocular UAV dynamic scene reconstruction. At its core, Anchor-Conditioned Feature Aggregation (ACFA) adaptively aggregates shared spatiotemporal features using anchor-specific aggregation embeddings and temporal information, allowing different local units to obtain dynamic representations tailored to their local and temporal states. Decoupled Local Geometry Deformation (DLGD) separates anchor-state deformation from local Gaussian geometry deformation, while Density-Adaptive Coordinate Warping (DACW) reparameterizes feature-query coordinates according to the axis-wise anchor distributions, alleviating the mismatch between non-uniform geometric sampling and uniform grid parameterization. Experiments on UAV-Arc4D, VisDrone, and UAVDT show that AdaAnchor4D achieves higher rendering quality than representative dynamic Gaussian methods while maintaining real-time rendering performance. The code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: AdaAnchor4D proposes an adaptive anchor deformation framework to handle spatiotemporal heterogeneity in monocular UAV dynamic scenes, using anchor-conditioned feature aggregation, decoupled local geometry deformation, and density-adaptive coordinate warping to improve rendering quality while preserving real-time performance across UAV datasets.
AI.motivation: Dynamic UAV scenes exhibit region-specific temporal activity and evolving motion states. Fixed plane-wise feature aggregations in dynamic Gaussian methods cause ghosting and blur when local dynamics are heterogeneous, limiting reconstruction fidelity.
AI.method: 1) ACFA aggregates shared spatiotemporal features via anchor-specific embeddings and temporal cues to tailor dynamic representations per local unit. 2) DLGD decouples anchor-state deformation from local Gaussian geometry deformation for flexible geometry handling. 3) DACW reparameterizes coordinates according to axis-wise anchor distributions to align sampling with non-uniform geometry.
AI.result: On UAV-Arc4D, VisDrone, and UAVDT, AdaAnchor4D yields higher rendering quality than representative dynamic Gaussian baselines and operates in real time; code will be released.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, anchor-conditioned deformation effectively addresses heterogeneous local dynamics in monocular UAV scenes, improving rendering quality without sacrificing real-time performance; promising for scalable dynamic scene reconstruction.

title: SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring
summary: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

AI.tldr: Introduces Deep Scientific Data Exploration via SciDataSailor, an MCTS-based framework enabling LLM agents to navigate hierarchical scientific repositories, interpret heterogeneous files, execute analyses, and ground conclusions; accompanied by SciDataSailor-SFT-2K and SciDataSailor-Bench benchmarks spanning 27 datasets across life, earth, and physical sciences.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at planning and reasoning but lack interactive access to real scientific data assets; a tool-enabled, executable-environment paradigm is needed for reliable data-driven discovery.
AI.method: Modeling trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search with four mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds; dual-feedback first-play urgency; hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation; entropy-guided branching. Build SciDataSailor framework, produce SciDataSailor-SFT-2K (supervised fine-tuning) and SciDataSailor-Bench (evaluation): 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific QA tasks across 27 datasets in life, earth, physical sciences.
AI.result: Demonstrates the viability of trajectory-synthesis-based, tool-interactive data exploration; delivers two resources (SciDataSailor-SFT-2K and SciDataSailor-Bench) with broad cross-domain coverage for evaluating data-grounded agentic reasoning.
AI.conclusion: This paradigm enables agents to perform grounded, executable data exploration in scientific repositories and offers benchmarks to evaluate such capabilities across domains, representing a step toward autonomous, data-aware scientific inquiry.

title: Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts
summary: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

AI.tldr: Analyses evolving context supervision for open-ended LLM training via reverse KL decomposition, shows a student aligns with the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers and identifies a conflict term; introduces Flux-OPD to inject contextual corrections weighted by conflict, achieving improvements over prior OPD methods.
AI.motivation: Open-ended domains lack verifiable rewards, making task preferences hard to supervise. Contexts can express preferences but dynamic evolution with the student complicates supervision, necessitating stable targets and handling conflicting teachers.
AI.method: Decompose the reverse KL objective to reveal a geometric-mean distillation target across context-conditioned teachers and a conflict term. Propose Flux-OPD, which uses differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual correction signals, injected into a context-free anchor, with correction strength weighted by the conflict term.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on open-ended tasks shows Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, demonstrating the utility of combining evolving-context supervision with a conflict-aware correction mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Evolving contexts can meaningfully guide open-ended LLM training when framed via a reverse KL decomposition and a conflict-aware correction strategy, as instantiated by Flux-OPD.

title: Same Branches, Different Trees: A Bifurcation Connectedness Metric for Coronary Artery Segmentation and FFR-CT Decision Agreement
comment: Accepted at STACOM 2026 (MICCAI workshop). 11 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables
summary: Fractional flow reserve derived from CT angiography (FFR-CT) simulates flow through a patient-specific vessel model, so its accuracy depends on the connectedness of the segmented tree, not only on volumetric overlap: a segmentation can reach high Dice yet sever a bifurcation, dropping the downstream subtree and reversing the treatment decision. Topology-aware losses such as clDice and Skeleton Recall act on the global centreline and can miss localised breaks. We study the Bifurcation Connectedness Score (BCS), which scores connectedness at each ground-truth bifurcation, and soft-BCS, its differentiable training surrogate. BCS captures a property of segmentation quality the standard metrics miss: it responds strongly to breaks in connectedness while staying largely unchanged under connectedness-preserving narrowing. Higher BCS accompanies closer agreement between the FFR-CT decisions a solver makes on predicted versus ground-truth geometry, most clearly in severe disease (OR 2.16, CI [1.23, 4.18]). Both decisions come from the same solver, so this reflects geometric, not clinical, fidelity. In training, soft-BCS and Skeleton Recall recover the same branches but build different trees. Recovering branches and keeping them connected are separable properties, so we recommend reporting a measure of each.

AI.tldr: BCS/soft-BCS quantify bifurcation-level connectivity in vessel segmentation, capturing topology effects on downstream FFR-CT decisions beyond Dice. Report both branch recovery and connectedness for faithful geometry.
AI.motivation: Standard segmentation metrics (e.g., Dice) overlook topology critical for FFR-CT decisions. A topology-aware, differentiable surrogate (soft-BCS) targets downstream clinical decision fidelity.
AI.method: Define BCS to score connectedness at each ground-truth bifurcation; introduce soft-BCS as a differentiable training surrogate; compare with Skeleton Recall; assess impact on FFR-CT decision concordance (OR) in severe disease; analyze whether recovering branches and maintaining connectivity are separable.
AI.result: Higher BCS correlates with closer agreement between solver decisions on predicted vs ground-truth geometries (OR 2.16, 95% CI 1.23–4.18); soft-BCS and Skeleton Recall recover the same branches but yield different trees; recovering branches and preserving connectivity are separable.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware metrics reveal segmentation quality aspects missed by standard metrics; recovering branches and maintaining connectedness are distinct requirements. Recommend reporting both measures to fully characterize geometry fidelity for downstream FFR-CT decisions.

title: MIND: Lightweight and Effective Memory Injection Defense for LLM Agents via Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck
summary: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks: Agents may retrieve poisoned memory from attackers, which diverts their behavior from initial user intent and finally causes task failure. However, existing defense mechanisms either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. To address these challenges, we propose Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising(MIND), a lightweight defense framework for memory injection attack. Our preliminary analysis reveals that benign and poisoned trajectories exhibit distinguishable relationships between the initial user intent and subsequent behavior. Building on this observation, MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck(IB) to extract compact intent--behavior representations from the initial intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations. As such, MIND mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts while avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing. Extensive experiments show that MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. Notably, on ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

AI.tldr: MIND introduces an intent-aware neural denoising framework that uses an Information Bottleneck to extract compact intent-behavior representations and a lightweight detector to defend against memory injection in memory-augmented LLM agents, reducing attack success rates with minimal impact on accuracy and latency.
AI.motivation: Memory injection attacks can hijack LLM agents via poisoned memory, causing task failures. Existing defenses are computationally costly or rely on information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. A lightweight, effective defense that preserves task performance is needed.
AI.method: MIND (Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising) uses an intent-aware Information Bottleneck to derive compact representations from initial user intent and turn-level behavior, preserving intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering noise. A lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from these representations, reducing redundancy without repeatedly auditing the LLM.
AI.result: Experiments show MIND lowers attack success rates while maintaining task accuracy and inference efficiency. On ReAct-StrategyQA, mean ASR-r and ASR-a drop by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, with accuracy and latency matching undefended agents.
AI.conclusion: MIND effectively mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts, avoids repeated LLM auditing overhead, and provides a scalable defense against memory injection with substantial ASR reductions and preserved performance.

title: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation
summary: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

AI.tldr: CRPO reframes on-policy self-distillation as contrastive learning using predictive entropy to separate reflective exploration from exposure bias, enabling stable, fine-grained optimization signals and strong generalization across long-horizon reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Exposure bias in self-distillation with privileged self-teacher leads to degraded, biased search trajectories and convergent reasoning routes in multi-turn agentic LLMs; need a supervision signal that preserves diverse, informative gradients for long-horizon decisions.
AI.method: Introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO) by formulating OPSD as a contrastive objective. Use predictive entropy to identify positive (reflective exploration) and negative (exposure bias) positions; perform group-wise contrast to maintain fine-grained optimization signals, integrated into reinforcement learning policy optimization.
AI.result: CRPO achieves consistent improvements over RL and self-distillation baselines on 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks, with notable gains in training stability and generalization on long-horizon interactions.
AI.conclusion: CRPO effectively mitigates exposure bias and preserves reliable optimization signals through group-wise contrast, leading to better performance and robustness in agentic LLM settings; the approach shows promise for broader applicability in long-horizon decision-making tasks.

title: Capturing Token Tendencies for Training-Free Token Pruning in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: While visual token pruning is essential for efficient Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), existing training-free methods suffer from a critical limitation: they rely on static, instantaneous heuristics to perform irreversible filtering. This approach ignores the hierarchical nature of MLLMs, where token importance often evolves dynamically rather than remaining fixed across layers. Consequently, tokens essential for deep-layer reasoning are often prematurely discarded by shallow-layer estimates. To address this, we propose Trend-aware Pruning, a novel framework that elevates pruning from a local snapshot decision to a temporal trajectory modeling problem. Instead of relying on isolated scores, our method captures the momentum of attention flow. This enables a dynamic rectification mechanism that selectively reactivates "late-blooming" tokens, those initially undervalued but exhibiting rising semantic importance, thereby preventing the loss of critical visual cues. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves a superior efficiency-performance trade-off across diverse multimodal tasks. Notably, it reduces visual tokens by over 77.8%, retaining only approximately 23 tokens in the final layer while maintaining competitive performance, offering a robust and reversible solution for high-efficiency multimodal inference.

AI.tldr: We propose Trend-aware Pruning for Multimodal LLMs, modeling the temporal trajectory of token importance to selectively reactivate late-blooming tokens, achieving high efficiency with minimal performance loss.
AI.motivation: Training-free, static token pruning uses instantaneous scores and fails to capture dynamic cross-layer changes in token importance. This often discards tokens essential for deep-layer reasoning, hurting multimodal reasoning performance.
AI.method: Introduce Trend-aware Pruning that treats pruning as a temporal trajectory problem. It tracks the momentum of attention flow across layers and applies a dynamic rectification mechanism to reactivate undervalued tokens that gain importance later (late-blooming). This reverses earlier pruning decisions when warranted.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show a superior efficiency–performance trade-off across diverse multimodal tasks. Visual tokens are reduced by over 77.8%, leaving about 23 tokens in the final layer, with competitive performance and a robust, reversible approach for high-efficiency multimodal inference.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, trajectory-aware pruning offers a robust alternative to local snapshot pruning, preserving critical cues during deep reasoning and enabling efficient MLLM inference across tasks.

title: Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training
summary: Synthetic textbook data has improved language model pre-training, but prior work largely treats the benefit as a property of generated content or local rewriting style. We study a different factor: whether related content is organized into coherent book-level documents. We contribute both a scalable synthesis pipeline and controlled evidence that this organization matters. The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (our Full setting), yielding 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with this corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons then disentangle the relevant design factors. A content-matched Split condition holds generated text and tokens fixed but treats each section as an independent document; Full's +1.02 mean gain isolates document packaging. A length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length alone. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition independently rewrites individual retrieved documents under the same audience-by-style scheme, without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly; Full's +1.17 gain demonstrates the value of structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full likewise outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books, supporting book-level organization as a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design.

AI.tldr: Book-level, source-grounded synthetic data improves pre-training beyond content quality; organizing content into coherent books yields measurable gains.
AI.motivation: Test whether organizing related content into coherent book-level documents, as opposed to treating sections as independent or simply rewriting retrieved text, enhances pre-training benefits.
AI.method: Build a scalable synthesis pipeline: retrieve material, cluster into topical units, plan hierarchical TOCs, assemble sections into complete books (Full). Create 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15k+ disciplines. Compare Full with Split (sections as independent docs), RandomConcat (join sections from different books), and Rephrase (rewrite retrieved docs without book assembly) on Llama3-8B.
AI.result: Replacing natural books with the Full dataset yields +1.09 downstream performance on average. Full vs Split shows +1.02 gain from packaging. RandomConcat underperforms Full. Rephrase + Full difference is +1.17, indicating value of structured synthesis; results generalize to Llama3-8B.
AI.conclusion: Structured synthesis by packaging content into coherent book-level documents provides a tangible benefit for synthetic pre-training and is a useful design axis beyond content or length alone.

title: Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework
summary: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: A continuous-time Transformer-based framework for irregular multivariate time series that uses gap-aware continuous-time tokens and a simulation-free Residual Flow Matching training to enable accurate forecasting with limited rollouts.
AI.motivation: Irregular sampling, asynchronous observations, and the need to preserve continuous-time semantics; existing methods either discretize (losing information) or rely on ODE solvers (heavy).
AI.method: Continuous-Time Tokenization that encodes events and models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens; standard Transformer backbone; simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching that learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions without numerical solvers or backpropagation during training.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on multiple real-world datasets, demonstrating accurate and efficient forecasting.
AI.conclusion: WrapFlow integrates continuous-time representation with efficient training/inference (few rollout steps), enabling high-quality continuous forecasting for irregular time series.

title: ShadowDancer: Teaching Video World Models Any Action by Learning Unified Dynamics Representations from a Video and Its Shadow
summary: We present ShadowDancer, a novel approach to any-action, frame-level control of interactive video world models. The obstacle is representational: existing interfaces either encode an action loosely, leaving how it unfolds for the model to improvise, or encode it exactly through structured signals that serve one family and are hard to acquire, so precise control across diverse dynamics remains impractical. Demonstration videos are the natural remedy, specifying any dynamics frame by frame; yet a video shows its dynamics only through one particular appearance, a single shadow of the underlying dynamics, so actions learned from demonstrations transfer poorly to new scenes. ShadowDancer addresses this with two key innovations: (1) shadow pairs, video pairs that replay the same dynamics under independently resampled appearance, constructed at scale by our Shadow Library, so that a dynamics family becomes controllable exactly when such pairs can be constructed for it; and (2) cross-shadow prediction, which learns actions by predicting one shadow from the other, so that whatever the pairing resamples is discarded by construction and whatever it preserves becomes the action, yielding a unified dynamics representation that drives a block-causal world model. Any demonstrated clip thus becomes a reusable action asset, replayed in new environments without action labels, motion estimators, or fine-tuning. Experiments demonstrate improved action transfer and long action rollout over strong latent-action and interactive world model baselines across diverse dynamics families, with an average blinded win rate of 86% in rollout comparisons. We show video results at https://ShadowDancer-1.github.io

AI.tldr: ShadowDancer enables reusable, appearance-invariant action control for interactive video world models by learning from shadow pairs and cross-shadow prediction, enabling transfer across diverse dynamics without action labels or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Current interfaces either encode actions loosely and improvise, or rely on exact, hard-to-acquire structured signals, hindering precise, cross-dynamic control. Demonstrations carry dynamics but depend on appearance, causing poor transfer. A scalable, appearance-robust action representation is needed to control world models across varied dynamics.
AI.method: Two innovations. (1) Shadow pairs: video pairs that replay the same dynamics under independently resampled appearance, generated at scale via a Shadow Library, to cover a dynamics family. (2) Cross-shadow prediction: train the model to predict one shadow from the other, forcing the representation to discard appearance while retaining action information, yielding a unified dynamics representation to drive a block-causal world model. Demonstration clips become reusable action assets without action labels, motion estimators, or fine-tuning.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows improved action transfer and longer action rollout compared with strong latent-action and interactive world model baselines across diverse dynamics families. Reported average blinded win rate in rollout comparisons: 86%. Video results available at the given URL.
AI.conclusion: ShadowDancer provides a scalable, appearance-robust action control framework that reuses demonstrations as generalizable action assets, enabling precise cross-environment dynamics control without explicit action annotations or specialized signals.

title: BlueprintRepair: Typed Local Edits for Failed Lean Proof Blueprints
summary: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly organize a proof as a blueprint: a dependency graph of formal statements. We introduce BlueprintRepair, a repair interface that lets a model change this graph through ten schema-checked local operations. An operation names the node it edits, so the target theorem cannot be changed. Lean checks every applied change, and an accepted repair must declare every blueprint lemma its proof uses. We also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. We compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, one episode per state and interface. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the three interfaces solve almost the same number of the benchmark's localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching is 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x), and within 10,000 completion tokens per task it reaches almost all of its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces are well behind. A second model, Qwen3.6-Flash, solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, puts it ahead on the proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.

AI.tldr: BlueprintRepair proposes a schema-checked, node-local repair interface for LLM-generated proof blueprints in Lean, and BlueprintTrace as a diagnostic benchmark. Typed edits are most cost-effective; rewriting and patching are more expensive; free-form interfaces underperform; results are consistent across two models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Flash).
AI.motivation: LLM-based lean proving produces dependency graphs (blueprints) of formal statements. There is a need for reliable, low-cost repair mechanisms that preserve proof targets while allowing localized edits, enabling scalable proof-authoring under budget constraints.
AI.method: Introduce ten schema-checked local edits that target specific blueprint nodes (without changing the target theorem). Lean verifies each applied change; accepted repairs must declare all blueprint lemmas used. Build BlueprintTrace with 142 controlled failures and complete accepted/rejected repair trajectories. Compare three repair modalities—typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites—under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, evaluating one episode per state/interface. Evaluate across two models, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Flash.
AI.result: Across interfaces, repairs solve a similar number of localized failures. Typed repair is cheapest per solved state (patching >1.3x, rewriting >2.0x). With a 10k token per task budget, typed repair approaches near full final coverage, while free-form interfaces lag. Qwen3.6-Flash solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, leading on proof-authoring states and exhibiting the same localized repair pattern.
AI.conclusion: Typed repair offers a cost-effective, scalable approach for maintaining and repairing Lean proof blueprints in LLM-assisted theorem proving. It achieves strong coverage under token budgets and outperforms free-form interfaces, with consistent advantages across models, suggesting a practical direction for robust LLM-based proof systems.

title: Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers
summary: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

AI.tldr: A data-augmented, two-stage Newton initialization strategy that learns reduced representations from parameter-space sampling to accelerate nonlinear solves; it first predicts a surrogate solution and then applies a low-cost GMRES-based residual correction before a final high-fidelity Newton step, yielding speedups on large-scale PDEs.
AI.motivation: Improve convergence speed of Newton's method for large-scale nonlinear PDEs by providing high-quality initial guesses and low-cost corrections, reducing iteration counts and CPU time while remaining broadly applicable.
AI.method: Construct two complementary reduced spaces from discrete Newton trajectories: (1) a solution feature space from converged states and (2) a corrective search direction feature space from Newton increments. For a new parameter, train a regression model to predict a surrogate solution. Apply a residual-minimizing correction via a GMRES-based approach, then use the resulting state as the initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method. The corrective step requires only residual evaluations and solving a small least-squares problem; implementation is weakly intrusive with script-based interfaces.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems demonstrate quantifiable and significant speedups over using standalone surrogate initialization, driven by reduced iteration counts and lower CPU time.
AI.conclusion: The approach is generic and applicable to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems, offering a practical pathway to accelerate Newton-based solvers with data-driven initializations and cheap corrective steps.

title: Explaining Image Similarity with Automatically Extracted Concept Activation Vectors
summary: Image similarity underlies many computer vision applications, yet it is often unclear why two images receive a high or low similarity score. Existing explainability methods often rely on gradient-based attribution maps to provide local justifications for similarity. These approaches struggle to provide global insights into what specifically drives similarity in regions of an embedding space, such as texture, shape, or color. We introduce a model- and metric-agnostic framework that explains image similarity using Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) extracted automatically via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Given a pair of images, we perturb their embeddings along discovered concept directions and measure the resulting change in a chosen similarity function, yielding concept importances. For image pairs, we provide localization with concept attribution maps. We extend this procedure to group-level settings, explaining what drives similarity across a cluster of images rather than a single pair, and further, we introduce Exemplar Retrieval, aiming to recover samples with similar reasons contributing to similarity. Our experiments show that our latent perturbations are more faithful to the underlying data distribution than pixel-space baselines, and that concept importances linearly recover the true similarity score. Qualitative results further confirm the usefulness of our methods in understanding a model's individual and group similarity judgments.

AI.tldr: A model- and metric-agnostic framework explains image similarity via latent concept directions (CAVs) learned by Sparse Autoencoders, perturbing embeddings to yield concept importances for pairs, groups, and exemplars, outperforming pixel-space baselines.
AI.motivation: Current gradient-based attribution methods struggle to provide global, embedding-space insights into what drives image similarity (texture, shape, color). There is a need for concept-level explanations that generalize across pairs and groups.
AI.method: Learn Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) automatically from Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Perturb image embeddings along discovered concept directions, measure changes in a chosen similarity function to obtain concept importances. Provide pairwise attribution maps (concept attribution maps) and extend the approach to group-level similarity explanations and Exemplar Retrieval.
AI.result: Latent perturbations better align with the data distribution than pixel-space baselines. Concept importances linearly recover the true similarity score. Qualitative results validate usefulness for understanding both individual and group similarity judgments.
AI.conclusion: The framework delivers model- and metric-agnostic, concept-based explanations of image similarity across multiple levels (pair, group, exemplar), enabling global interpretability of what drives similarity in embedding spaces.

title: ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory for Long-Horizon Manufacturing Inspection Logs
summary: Long-horizon steel-equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records accumulated across repeated inspection cycles. Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk. To this end, we propose ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, supporting a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system. Specifically, our ConMem first segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, then estimates each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis through a Shapley-style estimation, and finally retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. In experiments, we evaluate ConMem on real-world dataset and ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, exceeding the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to the naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces the average number of input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies also show that the functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation are helping prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection. Practical deployments further confirm that ConMem retains the weak early signal across three inspection cycles, providing an early-stage seal-wear alert targeted for on-site inspectors.

AI.tldr: ConMem is a contribution-aware, memory-augmented framework for long-horizon equipment inspection that segments logs into functional evidence, uses Shapley-style valuation to estimate each unit's diagnostic contribution, and retains high-value evidence under a budget, enabling patient early-risk detection with significant efficiency gains.
AI.motivation: Tackling the challenge of reasoning over heterogeneous, temporally distributed inspection records where treating logs as a static corpus neglects early diagnostic value and delays risk detection.
AI.method: Segment logs into functional evidence units; estimate each unit’s contribution via a Shapley-style valuation; enforce a memory budget to store only high-value evidence; enable human-in-the-loop early-risk screening, with ablation studies to validate components.
AI.result: On real-world data, achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline. Reduces input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6% relative to naive 8K-context LLMs. Ablations show functional segmentation and valuation are key; deployments demonstrate retention of weak early signals across three inspection cycles and early seal-wear alerts for on-site inspectors.
AI.conclusion: ConMem effectively prioritizes high-value, early-risk signals in long-horizon inspection logs, enabling efficient, human-in-the-loop diagnostics and timely field interventions.

title: ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents
summary:
As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

AI.tldr: ClawTrack introduces a dual-assessment benchmark for LLM agents in long-horizon tasks, jointly measuring Task Score (outcome) and Process Score (reasoning process) with 320 tasks across 8 domains, 25+ mock services, and a 12,541-item rubric. Evaluations show process scores diagnose failures, complement outcome metrics, bottleneck in result verification, robustness to evaluator choice, and improvements via trajectory filtering across model scales.
AI.motivation: To address the evaluation gap where outcome-only metrics fail to diagnose the quality of reasoning in long-horizon tasks and to enable attributing successes/failures to specific process deficiencies.
AI.method: Dual scoring framework: Task Score (outcome), Process Score (per-turn reasoning). A Process Grader assesses four dimensions—goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification—using 12,541 rubric items across 320 tasks in 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. 21 models evaluated over 16,000+ trials.
AI.result: Process scores effectively attribute success/failure to reasoning dimensions, defeating luck-based success not captured by outcome-only metrics. The four dimensions are complementary; result verification is the bottleneck. Framework shows robustness to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs. Process-based trajectory filtering yields post-training improvements across model scales.
AI.conclusion: Process-based evaluation provides rich, actionable diagnostics for long-horizon reasoning, enabling targeted improvements and more reliable performance; the approach can augment or replace outcome-only benchmarks and can be extended to real-world tasks with scalable rubric design.

title: Hand-Object Interaction in the Age of Large Foundation Models:Reconstruction, Generation, and Embodied Transfer
summary: Hand-object interaction (HOI) modeling remains challenging because it requires joint reasoning about hand articulation, object geometry, contact, semantics, and dynamics under severe visual uncertainty. Foundation models introduce transferable prior knowledge learned from large-scale cross-domain data, offering new ways to address these challenges beyond task-specific data and models. However, the rapidly growing literature remains fragmented, and existing studies typically describe these methods simply as ``using large models'' without systematically characterizing what knowledge is introduced, where it enters the HOI pipeline, or which HOI uncertainty it helps reduce. This survey presents the first systematic review of foundation-model priors for HOI. We organize the literature into six HOI tasks spanning reconstruction and generation. More importantly, we establish a taxonomy of eight foundation-model sub-priors grouped into geometric, semantic, and visual families. Geometric priors encompass shape retrieval, shape reconstruction, and spatial reconstruction; semantic priors include semantic grounding and language reasoning; and visual priors cover visual representation, image generation, and video generation. Based on this taxonomy, we systematically analyze how different priors are represented, injected, and adapted across HOI pipelines and tasks. Beyond how foundation models empower HOI, we further examine how HOI-derived knowledge is used in robot learning, including human-data pretraining, human-to-robot skill transfer, and HOI-to-robot data generation. Finally, we summarize datasets and evaluation protocols, and discuss limitations and future directions toward more generalizable HOI systems. To support long-term progress, we curate a live repository that continuously aggregates emerging methods and benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A systematic survey of foundation-model priors for hand-object interaction (HOI), proposing a taxonomy of eight sub-priors across geometric, semantic, and visual families, and analyzing their integration in HOI pipelines, with implications for robot learning and a live benchmark repository.
AI.motivation: HOI modeling is challenging due to joint reasoning about hand articulation, object geometry, contact, semantics, and dynamics under visual uncertainty. Foundation models offer transferable priors, but the literature is fragmented and lacks a systematic characterization of what knowledge is introduced and where it enters HOI pipelines.
AI.method: Literature review across six HOI tasks (reconstruction and generation). Propose a taxonomy of eight foundation-model sub-priors: geometric (shape retrieval, shape reconstruction, spatial reconstruction), semantic (semantic grounding, language reasoning), visual (visual representation, image generation, video generation). Analyze how priors are represented, injected, and adapted across HOI pipelines and tasks; examine how HOI knowledge informs robot learning (human-data pretraining, human-to-robot skill transfer, HOI-to-robot data generation). Summarize datasets/evaluation protocols and discuss limitations/future directions. Curate a live repository aggregating methods and benchmarks.
AI.result: A structured taxonomy linking eight sub-priors to six HOI tasks, with cross-task analysis of how priors are represented, injected, and adapted; guidance on exploiting HOI-derived knowledge in robot learning; an overview of datasets/evaluation and a plan for a live, evolving benchmark repository.
AI.conclusion: The survey lays groundwork for generalizable HOI systems by clarifying what foundation-model priors bring to HOI, identifying gaps and limitations, and outlining directions for future research and community resources.

title: AgenticASR: Refining Speech Recognition in Real-World Scenarios via an Agentic Approach
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved substantial gains in transcription accuracy, yet verbatim transcription does not necessarily produce readily usable text. It retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure the speaker's final intent, and propagate unresolved or abandoned content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio or transcripts but cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted. We therefore formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), an audio-to-clean-text task that removes disfluencies, resolves self-corrections, and normalizes written form while preserving the speaker's final intent.
