We formulate this post-selection stage as a latent evidence interface and instantiate it with GenEvA ($\textbf{Gen}erative$ $Latent$ $\textbf{Ev}idence$ $\textbf{A}ggregation$), a distribution-guided latent evidence aggregation framework. Specifically, GenEvA uses a query-conditioned evidence distribution to focus aggregation on relevant frames, forming compact cross-frame latent evidence from their frame-specific information. Since cross-frame integration is not always needed, the same distribution determines whether to insert this latent complement. Across four benchmarks and two Video-MLLM backbones, GenEvA consistently improves matched-frame baselines. At 8 frames, it raises the four-benchmark LLaVA-Video average by $+5.2$ points and Qwen2.5-VL accuracy on LVBench by $+10.1$ points. These gains require only $0.11\%$--$0.40\%$ average video-token overhead; analyses further show task-aware allocation and benefits from Adaptive Evidence Invocation.

AI.tldr: GenEvA introduces a latent evidence aggregation mechanism to form cross-frame, query-relevant evidence for video question-answering, achieving consistent gains with minimal token overhead.
AI.motivation: Evidence from multiple moments is not automatically integrated; a mechanism is needed to fuse complementary cues across frames to improve answer generation.
AI.method: A post-selection latent interface is used to generate cross-frame latent evidence. GenEvA employs a query-conditioned evidence distribution to guide aggregation of frame-specific information into compact, cross-frame latent evidence, with a decision mechanism to insert the latent complement as needed. Evaluated with two backbones and four benchmarks, using 8-frame inputs, while maintaining very low video-token overhead and enabling adaptive evidence invocation.
AI.result: GenEvA consistently improves matched-frame baselines, e.g., +5.2 on average across four LLaVA-Video benchmarks and +10.1 on LVBench (Qwen2.5-VL). Overhead is only 0.11%–0.40% of video tokens. Analyses show task-aware allocation and benefits from Adaptive Evidence Invocation.
AI.conclusion: Cross-frame, query-guided latent evidence aggregation effectively enhances long-video understanding with minimal overhead, validating the utility of a latent, post-selection interface for evidence integration.

title: One Human, $N$ Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence
summary: A single human must audit $N$ LLM agents under a budget of $B \ll N$ audits per round, guided by self-reported confidence that may be adversarially miscalibrated and by correlated errors. We model this as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula and locate the miscalibration threshold $δ^*$ past which confidence-ranked auditing is \emph{worse} than random. Two a-priori expectations reverse: $δ^*$ \emph{rises} as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is not low---shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs show operationally useless (near-constant) confidence, point estimates at or beyond the flip though CIs straddle it; a proprietary model is informative and lands below it. We give a quantitative criterion for \emph{vacuous} oversight, and replaying policies on recorded traces confirms the ordering.

AI.tldr: Budgeted, confidence-guided auditing of LLM agents under miscalibration and correlated errors can become worse than random past a threshold; many models show near-constant confidence; a threshold δ* grows as budget shrinks; cross-family correlations matter; a criterion for vacuous oversight is proposed; empirical validation supports the ordering.
AI.motivation: Assess reliability of using self-reported confidence to audit multiple LLM agents under budget constraints, especially when confidence is miscalibrated and errors are correlated; determine when such auditing is informative vs vacuous.
AI.method: Model the problem as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula, derive miscalibration threshold δ*, analyze how δ* depends on budget and correlations, and perform experiments on five open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model; replay policies on traces to validate ordering.
AI.result: Identified miscalibration threshold δ* above which confidence-ranked auditing under budget becomes worse than random; δ* increases as budget B decreases; cross-family correlation is strong; five open-weight models show near-constant confidence with CIs crossing δ*; proprietary model is informative and lands below threshold; provided a quantitative criterion for vacuous oversight; replay confirms the predicted ordering.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-based auditing under tight budgets and correlated errors can be vacuous for some models, necessitating alternative oversight strategies; the δ* criterion and experimental results help detect vacuity and guide auditing design.

title: HARGO: Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization for RL Post-Training of LLMs on HPC Tasks
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge for high-performance computing (HPC) tasks such as data race detection and benchmark question answering. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior: the same SFT model that correctly classifies 88.65\% of C/C++ data race samples produces verbose, imprecise answers to factual queries, with 65.9\% of MLPerf responses exceeding 40 characters. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training addresses this gap by optimizing for task-specific rewards rather than token-level imitation. Yet HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy. This makes uniform-weight RL methods such as GRPO suboptimal. We propose HARGO, Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization, which introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage: computing a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulating the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels. Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62\%, Data Race F1 91.30\%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals. HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

AI.tldr: HARGO (Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization) is proposed for RL post-training in heterogeneous HPC tasks to address varied task types and reward distributions. It introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage, using a group-level reward contrast and a reference-model log-probability signal, without requiring task-type labels, improving alignment across tasks.
AI.motivation: SFT alone yields task-appropriate behavior inconsistencies in HPC tasks due to extreme heterogeneity (binary classification, factual QA, semantic generation) and uneven reward distributions. RL post-training can help but standard uniform-weight methods underperform across such diverse tasks; a heterogeneity-aware approach is needed.
AI.method: HARGO computes two signals: a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrasts and a confidence signal from reference-model log-probabilities. These are used to modulate the advantage and compute per-response weights, enabling heterogeneity-aware reward-guided optimization without task-type labels.
AI.result: Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves top performance on WinRate (54.62%), Data Race F1 (91.30%), and PLP Similarity (0.8558). Ablation studies show the two signals contribute complementarily, and HARGO provides the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.
AI.conclusion: HARGO effectively handles heterogeneity in HPC tasks during RL post-training, delivering superior task alignment and decision quality without requiring task-type annotations.

title: What to Remove, What to Preserve: Dual-Ambiguity Rectification for All-in-One Image Restoration
summary: All-in-one image restoration aims to handle diverse degradations within a unified framework. Existing methods commonly encode heterogeneous degradation conditions in a shared latent space, where degradation-related cues and scene content can remain entangled. We characterize the resulting challenge as dual ambiguity: semantic ambiguity in channel-wise modulation and spatial ambiguity in restoration responses, which can lead to content corruption and residual artifacts. To mitigate this issue, we propose DAR-Net, a Dual-Ambiguity Rectification Network for all-in-one image restoration. DAR-Net first introduces a Degradation Archetype Representation (DAR) module to construct a structured degradation state through simplex-constrained archetype mixture modeling. Based on this state, a Semantic Ambiguity Rectification (SeAR) module generates degradation-aware prompts to improve channel-wise conditioning in the decoder. A Spatial Ambiguity Rectification (SpAR) module further regularizes degradation-aware and complementary features toward orthogonal response subspaces, reducing spatial interference between removal and preservation cues. Extensive experiments on standard all-in-one restoration benchmarks show that DAR-Net achieves the best overall performance under both three-degradation and five-degradation settings, improving the average PSNR over the strongest competitor by 0.14 dB and 0.34 dB, respectively; it additionally shows superior performance on CDD-11 and WeatherBench.

AI.tldr: A dual-ambiguity rectification framework (DAR-Net) for all-in-one image restoration that decomposes degradations into a structured archetype space and uses semantic/spatial rectification to reduce content corruption and artifacts, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple degradation settings.
AI.motivation: All-in-one restoration methods often encode heterogeneous degradations in a shared latent space, causing semantic ambiguity in channel-wise conditioning and spatial ambiguity in restoration responses, which can corrupt content and leave artifacts.
AI.method: Propose DAR-Net with three components: (1) Degradation Archetype Representation (DAR) to construct a structured degradation state via simplex-constrained archetype mixtures; (2) Semantic Ambiguity Rectification (SeAR) to generate degradation-aware prompts that improve channel-wise conditioning in the decoder; (3) Spatial Ambiguity Rectification (SpAR) to regularize degradation-aware and complementary features toward orthogonal response subspaces, reducing spatial interference between removal and preservation cues.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on standard all-in-one restoration benchmarks show DAR-Net achieves the best overall performance under three- and five-degradation settings, with average PSNR gains of 0.14 dB and 0.34 dB over the strongest competitors, respectively; it also shows superior performance on CDD-11 and WeatherBench.
AI.conclusion: DAR-Net effectively mitigates dual ambiguity in all-in-one restoration and yields improved restoration quality across diverse degradations.

title: PathView-Bench: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Achieve Fine-grained Multiscale Understanding of Pathology Images?
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to analyze pathology images. However, dominant multimodal benchmarks in pathology mainly score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports. These evaluations provide limited insight into whether a model understands the multiscale visual content needed for pathology reasoning and decision-making. We introduce PathVU, a vision-anchored benchmark for fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology. Built from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations, PathVU evaluates MLLM understanding in two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. By converting raw annotations into deterministic task targets, PathVU enables programmatic scoring of region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. The benchmark contains 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, we observe substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images. PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding.

AI.tldr: PathVU is a vision-anchored, multiscale pathology benchmark enabling fine-grained evaluation of multimodal LLMs on region- and slide-level tasks across 23 datasets, revealing gaps in current models' multiscale pathology understanding.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal pathology benchmarks emphasize final outputs (diagnoses, captions) and overlook fine-grained multiscale visual reasoning essential for pathology decisions; there is a need for deterministic, scalable, region- and scale-aware evaluation.
AI.method: Assemble PathVU from 23 public pathology datasets with human labels and spatial annotations; define Region FOV (high-resolution local regions) and Slide FOV (macro whole-slide views); convert annotations into deterministic task targets; provide 14 VQA-style tasks; 61,673 images and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations; enable programmatic scoring for region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment; evaluate 18 MLLMs spanning general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-specific.
AI.result: 18 representative MLLMs show substantial limitations on fine-grained, multiscale pathology tasks; advanced models still struggle with precise region localization, quantity estimation, and spatial reasoning across multiscale pathology images.
AI.conclusion: PathVU provides a reproducible, scalable framework for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus
summary: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.

AI.tldr: Ensemble-consensus semi-supervised learning improves molecular property prediction across datasets, tasks, and GNNs, with robustness and calibration benefits; an individual ensemble member can outperform a supervised full ensemble, suggesting a distillation-like effect.
AI.motivation: In molecular ML, labeled data is expensive and time-consuming to obtain, while unlabeled data are abundant. Designing label-preserving augmentations is difficult because small molecular changes can drastically alter properties. There is a need for SSL methods that do not rely on augmentation but leverage unlabeled data effectively.
AI.method: Train with an ensemble-consensus objective across unlabeled data, leveraging predictions from multiple models to enforce consensus. This approach yields robustness and distillation-like benefits, and is evaluated across diverse molecular datasets, tasks, and graph neural network architectures; comparisons include traditional supervised training.
AI.result: The ensemble-consensus SSL method yields higher predictive accuracy across varied molecular datasets, tasks, and GNNs. An individual ensemble member often outperforms a full ensemble trained in supervised fashion. The method also reduces calibration error, indicating improved probability estimates.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble-consensus semi-supervised learning is a robust, data-efficient strategy for molecular ML that mitigates reliance on label-intensive data and challenging augmentations, while producing distillation-like benefits and better-calibrated models.

title: MarkushGlyph and OCSRGlyph: Improved Chemical Structure Recognition
summary: Chemical structures appear in patents and the scientific literature as images. For programmatic usage, such as indexing in databases or constructing machine learning model training sets, they must be transformed into line notations. The two common forms of this task are translating an image of a single molecule (optical chemical structure recognition - OCSR) and translating a Markush structure that represents a family of molecules. While prior work in the former case is quite mature, Markush structure parsing remains a challenging task. In this work, we treat both tasks as an image-to-text translation problem. We then propose OCSRGlyph, a state-of-the-art OCSR model, improving performance over prior methods by carefully considering stereochemistry. For the Markush task, we introduce MarkushGlyph, a vision-language model that reads the entire Markush structure as an image. This contrasts with prior systems, which often use multiple stages to separately process visual and text input content. Finally, we introduce a new metric for determining the accuracy of Markush structure translations, handling failure modes present in prior metrics.

AI.tldr: Treats both single-molecule OCSR and Markush parsing as image-to-text; introduces OCSRGlyph (state-of-the-art, stereochemistry-aware) and MarkushGlyph (vision-language, single-stage); proposes a new metric for Markush translation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Chemical structure images (patents, literature) must be converted to text for indexing and ML training; Markush parsing is particularly challenging; unifying the tasks under image-to-text can streamline pipelines.
AI.method: Develop OCSRGlyph for optical chemical structure recognition with enhanced stereochemical handling; develop MarkushGlyph as a single-stage vision-language model that reads full Markush structures; introduce a new evaluation metric addressing failure modes of prior metrics.
AI.result: OCSR performance is advanced beyond prior methods; MarkushGlyph demonstrates the viability of a unified image-to-text approach for Markush structures; a new metric more robustly evaluates Markush translations.
AI.conclusion: A unified image-to-text framework effectively handles both standard molecule images and Markush structures; improved evaluation metrics enable better assessment and progress; potential benefits for database indexing and data-driven chemistry.

title: Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly act as autonomous merchants that write their own product listings, and under competitive pressure, they fabricate attributes to win sales. Even under instructions to be honest, they fabricate attributes in a majority of listings across models. A platform's obvious remedy---verifying each claim against the truth---is unavailable, because it observes only a noisy, biased complaint signal, never the ground truth. We design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic gaming. CARP protects consumers by suppressing the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, without ever accessing the truth. It also achieves the best welfare of the policies we compare. We further show that this felt penalty becomes behaviorally binding through SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales, a self-interested response rather than compliance. We trace this distinction to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, and observe the binding across models, with supporting confidence intervals.

AI.tldr: CARP is a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband and state-dependent severity to deter deceptive product listings by LLM merchants without requiring ground-truth checks; paired with SPARC, it improves consumer welfare close to a perfect oracle and exploits penalty-gated self-correction to induce honest behavior.
AI.motivation: Address the gap where LLM-driven marketplaces feature sellers fabricating attributes to win sales, while truth verification is noisy or unavailable. Need a mechanism robust to gaming that protects consumers without ground truth.
AI.method: Introduce CARP: a reputation-based penalty with a deadband to absorb complaint noise and a state-dependent severity to counter reputation erosion. It does not require product-level ground truth. Pair with SPARC, a reflection mechanism that makes fabrication costly and self-correcting when penalties are present.
AI.result: CARP suppresses sales of low-rated liars and spares honest sellers; paired with SPARC, it substantially closes the consumer-welfare gap relative to an oracle, achieving best welfare among policies tested. Findings reported as across-model robustness with confidence intervals.
AI.conclusion: The combination yields a robust, ground-truth-free approach to deter deception in AI-enabled marketplaces, leveraging penalty-gated self-correction reasoning to induce self-enforcement of honesty and higher welfare.

title: Beyond Geometric Complementarity: Coherent Overlap in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route each token to multiple experts, suggesting a geometric account of their benefit: co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions. Existing evidence often conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. We distinguish these quantities using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled $2\times2$ factorial; frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-$k$ study assess functional value. Three paired contrasts organize the findings. First, across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Second, across the 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, the selected candidate explains more of the residual representation than the strongest unselected rival in every cell, yet the actual prefix narrows this advantage throughout: all interactions are negative, and every 95% confidence interval lies below zero. Third, this geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons, while the other 15 estimates are inconclusive; a controlled training study also favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds. We call this joint pattern coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Separating these quantities clarifies why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.

AI.tldr: Coherent overlap in sparse MoE expert subspaces coexists with functional benefits from routing; geometry alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.
AI.motivation: Disentangle what geometric similarity among expert subspaces implies for MoE performance by separating route coherence, candidate quality, and context interaction.
AI.method: Introduce ESSI (Expert Subspace Separation Index), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled 2x2 factorial; use frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-k study; three paired contrasts across six MoE architectures and 39 factorial cells; supplemented by a controlled training study.
AI.result: Subspaces overlap across architectures, but actual routes better explain token representations than matched substitutes. In 39 factorial cells, the selected candidate explains more of the residual than the strongest unselected rival, yet the prefix narrows this advantage (negative interactions; all 95% CIs < 0). Adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24/39 frozen-route comparisons; 15 inconclusive. Across seeds, Top-2 outperforms Top-1. This supports coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood; multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage.
AI.conclusion: Geometric similarity and overlap do not imply redundancy; optimal MoE functioning arises from selecting token-relevant experts within a shared geometry, and separating these quantities clarifies that geometry alone cannot determine pruning value or redundancy.

title: ScaFE: Data-Efficient Scar Classification with LLM-Generated Clinical Feature Programs
summary: Classifying pathological scars from clinical photographs requires distinguishing keloids from hypertrophic scars despite limited expert-labeled data and substantial acquisition variation across hospitals. End-to-end image models remain data-dependent, whereas sending photographs to a hosted vision-language model (VLM) may conflict with local data-governance requirements and yields decisions that are difficult to reproduce and audit. We introduce ScaFE (Scar Feature Engineering), which transfers clinical knowledge from a large language model (LLM) into deterministic, executable feature programs instead of asking the model to diagnose images. A web-enabled LLM retrieves clinical evidence and synthesizes programs that measure visually assessable scar attributes. Candidate programs execute in a restricted local environment, and only aggregate validation statistics and feature-level SHAP summaries are returned for iterative repair and refinement; raw images and patient-level outputs remain local. A lightweight Random Forest then operates on the resulting structured representation. On 600 photographs from three hospitals under leave-one-site-out evaluation, ScaFE achieves 81.0% site-macro balanced accuracy, exceeding the strongest baseline, BiomedCLIP, by 10.0 percentage points. With only 10% of the development data, ScaFE retains 72.0% balanced accuracy and an 11.8-point lead. Iterative refinement also raises the executable-program rate from 66.7% to 95.0%, with verified evidence for 91.7% of the final features. These results show that LLM knowledge can support data-efficient, cross-site medical image classification through local and auditable feature programs rather than direct VLM decisions.

AI.tldr: ScaFE uses an LLM to generate executable feature programs for scar classification, enabling data-efficient, auditable image diagnosis with local privacy. It outperforms a strong baseline and maintains performance with limited data.
AI.motivation: Classifying keloids vs hypertrophic scars from clinical photos is data-limited and sensitive to data governance. End-to-end vision models require large datasets; hosted VLMs raise privacy/audit concerns. A transparent, executable feature-based approach can improve data efficiency and reproducibility while staying local.
AI.method: LLM-assisted generation of deterministic feature programs that quantify clinically observable scar attributes from images. Programs run in a restricted local environment; only aggregated statistics and SHAP explanations are shared for iterative refinement. A lightweight Random Forest consumes the structured feature representation.
AI.result: Leave-one-site-out evaluation on 600 photos across three hospitals yields site-macro balanced accuracy of 81.0%, 10.0 percentage points higher than BiomedCLIP. With 10% of development data, accuracy is 72.0% and the performance gap remains (11.8 points). Executable-program rate improves from 66.7% to 95.0% through iteration; 91.7% of final features have verified evidence.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge from LLMs can be harnessed to create auditable, data-efficient medical image classifiers via executable feature programs, enabling cross-site generalization while preserving data locality and interpretability.

title: Correcting What You Cannot See: Credit Assignment for Perception Distillation in Multimodal Reasoners
summary: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but its trajectory-level reward cannot determine whether a failed answer arose from perception or subsequent reasoning. Perception Success Rate (PSR), estimated from multiple reasonings sharing one perception, remains ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty. We introduce \textbf{Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD)}, a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher--student disagreement as complementary witnesses. Their product, , forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. We motivate this rule through Bayesian evidence combination and show that multiplication is the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception--reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged. Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B 2B macro average from 44.50 with OPD to 47.28 and the 32B 8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively. Effective multimodal distillation therefore depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction.

AI.tldr: Introduces Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD), a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures by combining downstream failures and teacher–student disagreement via a multiplicative soft AND gate, improving multimodal distillation performance across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Trajectory-level rewards cannot distinguish whether failures arise from perception or subsequent reasoning; perceptions-based success rate (PSR) is ambiguous; a principled method is needed to identify when perception is the appropriate target of correction to improve distillation.
AI.method: PCD uses separated perception–reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights. It uses two witnesses—downstream failure and teacher–student disagreement—as complementary signals; their product forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both signals are present. The approach is motivated by Bayesian evidence combination and yields a unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes if either witness is absent.
AI.result: Across eight benchmarks, PCD raises macro 8B 2B average from 44.50 (OPD) to 47.28 and 32B 8B from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD reduces held-out average by 2.22 points, and removing separated rollout reduces by 0.88 points.
AI.conclusion: Effective multimodal distillation requires not only accurate teacher predictions but also correct identification of perceptual failures; PCD provides a principled, label-free mechanism to target perception corrections and yields measurable performance gains.

title: Measuring Distortion in the Empty Regions of Dimensionality Reduction Scatterplots with the Gap Index
summary: Quality metrics play a crucial role in the proper use of dimensionality reduction projections for visual analysis of high-dimensional data. They quantify the degree of distortion of a projection compared to the high-dimensional data and provide a reliable indication of how confident users can be in the structures they see in the resulting layouts. However, most popular metrics focus on capturing direct relationships between points (e.g., distances or neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these often compose visually relevant features of a 2D layout. In this paper, we introduce the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that captures visual distortion by measuring spatial distortion in empty areas of a projection. It does so by decomposing the space into empty triangles, which are then compared to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute the deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or overlaid on a projection to visualize regional distortion patterns. Results show that, contrary to popular quality metrics, the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

AI.tldr: Introduces Gap Index (GI), a 2D projection quality metric that targets distortions in empty space by triangulating the projection’s empty regions and comparing each triangle to its high-dimensional counterpart, yielding per-triangle deformations that can be aggregated into a scalar or visualized as a distortion map.
AI.motivation: Existing quality metrics focus on direct point relationships (distances, neighborhoods) and largely ignore distortions in empty areas, which can strongly affect perceived structure in a layout.
AI.method: Construct a triangulation of the projection’s empty space into empty triangles, measure deformation by comparing each triangle to its high-dimensional counterpart, and aggregate per-triangle distortions (or overlay them on the projection for visualization).
AI.result: GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact, unlike some popular metrics; it is fast to compute and interpretable, and supports both a scalar score and regional distortion visualization.
AI.conclusion: GI provides a complementary, perceptually oriented quality metric for 2D projections by focusing on distortions in empty regions, enabling both quantitative assessment and visual diagnosis of projection quality.

title: MIND: Multimodal Intent-Driven Network via Diffusion Transformers for Medical Image Fusion
summary: Medical image fusion aims to integrate complementary information from diverse imaging modalities to support clinical diagnosis. Existing methods typically apply uniform fusion rules globally, lacking a deep understanding of diagnostic intents and pathological structures. To address these limitations, we propose MIND, a Multimodal Intent-Driven Network via Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for medical image fusion. Specifically, we utilize BioMedGPT to generate intent-driven fusion texts from source images, guiding the fusion process with pathology-aware diagnostic intents. To combat the loss of 2D spatial continuity caused by 1D sequence flattening in DiTs, we design a Multi-scale Latent Adapter. This module explicitly extracts source image features before serialization, injecting them into the network via strict dimensional alignment to effectively supplement image features. To resolve the semantic shift caused by decoupling image outputs from diagnostic intents, we design a medical semantic consistency loss. This loss ensures deep semantic locking between fused images and fusion texts while maintaining the stability of the underlying physical manifold reconstruction. Comprehensive experiments on the Harvard, BraTS, and GFP datasets reveal that MIND delivers superior fusion quality, significantly improves downstream brain tumor segmentation accuracy, and enables flexible interactive fusion, holding significant promise for intent-driven intelligent clinical decision support systems.

AI.tldr: MIND introduces an intent-driven diffusion-transformer framework for multimodal medical image fusion with a multi-scale latent adapter and semantic consistency loss, guided by BioMedGPT-generated fusion texts to improve fusion quality and downstream segmentation.
AI.motivation: Current fusion methods apply uniform, global fusion rules and ignore diagnostic intents and pathology structures; 2D spatial continuity is degraded by 1D sequence flattening in diffusion transformers; semantic shift between fused outputs and clinical intents degrades decision support.
AI.method: MIND describes a Multimodal Intent-Driven Network via Diffusion Transformers. It uses BioMedGPT to generate intent-driven fusion texts from source images, guiding the fusion with pathology-aware intents. A Multi-scale Latent Adapter extracts source features before serialization and injects them with strict dimensional alignment to supplement image features. A Medical Semantic Consistency Loss aligns the fused images with fusion texts while preserving the underlying physical manifold reconstruction.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments on the Harvard, BraTS, and GFP datasets show that MIND achieves superior fusion quality, significantly improves downstream brain tumor segmentation accuracy, and enables flexible interactive fusion.
AI.conclusion: MIND demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of intent-driven medical image fusion for interactive clinical decision support, with strong potential to enhance diagnostic workflows and personalized treatment planning.

title: How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents (CUA) are being deployed to browse the web and operate desktop software, yet their benchmark scores are still commonly produced by brittle scripted oracles. A score is the output of a pipeline in which tasks can be stale, trajectories can omit decisive visual evidence, evaluators can reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports can hide the cause of failure. We organize these problems into a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. We then audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control benchmarks, find that 15.3\% of FAIL verdicts are wrong: 10.7\% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7\% are broken tasks. For genuine failures, a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy shows that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors, while a single scalar success rate can not explain. We connect these findings to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation.

AI.tldr: Audit of 150 failure-scored trajectories across five benchmarks reveals 15.3% incorrect FAIL verdicts (10.7% evaluator false negatives; 4.7% broken tasks). Proposes a reliability framework across task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting, plus a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy showing verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors. Argues a single scalar success rate is insufficient and derives stage-specific evaluation rules for CUA benchmarks, with links to long-horizon tasks.
AI.motivation: Current CUA benchmark evaluation relies on brittle scripted oracles and coarse, opaque scoring pipelines that can mislabel failures and hide root causes. There is a need for reliable, diagnostic evaluation to improve benchmarking for long-horizon, web/enterprise/desktop tasks.
AI.method: Audit 150 publicly failure-scored trajectories from five benchmarks spanning web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control domains; categorize incorrect FAIL verdicts and analyze error taxonomy; develop a reliability framework across task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting; derive stage-specific design rules.
AI.result: Found 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are wrong (10.7% evaluator false negatives; 4.7% broken tasks). Identified a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy: verification/feedback failures and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors. A single scalar success rate cannot explain performance. Established stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation and connected findings to long-horizon benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware evaluation with diagnostic taxonomy and stage-specific rules is needed for CUA benchmarks, especially for long-horizon tasks; results guide improvements in task construction, observation, scoring and reporting to reduce mislabeling and illuminate failure causes.

title: Encryption-Compatible Clustered Federated Learning via Distributed Expectation-Maximization over Metadata
summary: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

AI.tldr: FLAMECHE is a privacy-friendly, EM-based method for metadata-driven clustered federated learning (CFL) that uses additive server updates to enable encryption-compatible clustering and improves client model performance.
AI.motivation: CFL combats data heterogeneity by clustering clients with similar distributions but faces a trilemma between privacy, communication, and computation. Metadata-based clustering helps efficiency but clashes with standard FL privacy guarantees.
AI.method: Reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization procedure with server updates restricted to additive operations, enabling compatibility with secure FL schemes while maintaining efficiency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and heterogeneous scenarios show that FLAMECHE improves client model effectiveness and enables encryption-compatible clustering, strengthening its position within the CFL trilemma.
AI.conclusion: FLAMECHE demonstrates a practical, privacy-preserving approach to metadata-based CFL, achieving improved performance and compatibility with encryption-based FL, and suggesting directions for scaling and privacy-utility tradeoff exploration.

title: Finding Change in Satellite Archives from Text: How to Combine Before-and-After Images Efficiently
summary: Operational Earth observation increasingly calls for answering queries such as ``find the image pairs where a new building appeared.'' This means searching an archive of before-and-after (bi-temporal) satellite image pairs and ranking each pair by how well it matches a natural-language description of the change. The component that performs this match, the fusion module that combines the ``before'' and ``after'' views, must be run at query time across many candidate pairs, so its speed largely sets the cost of every search. We present a controlled comparison of how to build that module. Using one fixed image encoder (a frozen CLIP model) and one training recipe for all variants, we evaluate eight designs drawn from three families: attention, state-space models (Mamba), and learned compression (our Temporal Bottleneck Fusion, TBF). Each design is tested on two benchmarks (LEVIR-CC and Dubai-CC) with ten random seeds, so the reported differences are statistically grounded. We outline three findings: first, a training-free two-stage search (a cheap difference model that shortlists candidates, followed by attention fusion that re-ranks them) matches or exceeds full-fusion recall on LEVIR-CC while cutting query cost $10$-$15\times$, with comparable R@1/R@5 on Dubai-CC; second, the linear-time scan of Mamba, attractive on paper, gives no speed benefit at the patch counts typical of vision transformers ($L{=}196$): the scan is limited by memory bandwidth, whereas attention maps cleanly onto parallel hardware; and third, compressing the fused representation (TBF) reduces parameters by $2.3\times$ and latency by $1.6\times$ for a change-only BLEU-1 cost of $0.007$, although more aggressive compression quietly discards change-relevant detail that aggregate metrics fail to reveal.

AI.tldr: Eight fusion designs for bi-temporal EO search are evaluated under a fixed CLIP encoder and training recipe. A two-stage cheap+attention approach matches/exceeds full fusion with substantially lower query cost; Mamba offers no speed benefit at typical ViT patch counts; compressing fused representations (TBF) reduces size and latency but may sacrifice change-relevant details not captured by aggregate metrics.
AI.motivation: To enable fast, query-time matching of before–after satellite image pairs to natural-language queries by rigorously comparing fusion architectures under controlled conditions.
AI.method: An empirical study using one fixed image encoder (frozen CLIP) and a single training recipe to evaluate eight fusion designs drawn from three families (attention, state-space Mamba, and Temporal Bottleneck Fusion, TBF). The evaluation uses two benchmarks (LEVIR-CC and Dubai-CC) with ten random seeds to ensure statistical reliability, and compares a cheap two-stage search (difference model + re-ranker) against full-fusion baselines.
AI.result: Findings: (1) Training-free two-stage search with a cheap differencing step followed by attention fusion achieves recall comparable to or better than full fusion on LEVIR-CC while reducing query cost by 10–15×, and matches R@1/R@5 on Dubai-CC. (2) Mamba’s linear-time scan yields no practical speed benefit at ViT-like patch counts (L=196) due to memory bandwidth limits; attention fusion maps scale well on parallel hardware. (3) Temporal Bottleneck Fusion reduces parameters by ~2.3× and latency by ~1.6× for a change-only BLEU-1 cost of 0.007, but more aggressive compression can discard change-relevant details not captured by aggregate metrics.
AI.conclusion: Practical guidance: a two-stage cheap-difference then attention fusion is a strong, cost-efficient default; Mamba offers no speed advantage at typical patch counts; compression via TBF can greatly reduce resources at the risk of losing change-specific information, underscoring the need for metric selection that reflects change-grounded tasks.

title: HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection
summary: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

AI.tldr: HyperClaim uses a discriminative temporal hypergraph to model higher-order cross-modal cues for video misinformation detection, outperforming baselines on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV with a lightweight, rationale-free framework.
AI.motivation: Global multimodal fusion and pairwise graphs under-represent localized, higher-order cues arising from interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal frame spans. Hypergraphs enable capturing multi-way cross-modal dependencies.
AI.method: Construct a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; apply confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; perform adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregate textual, visual, and hyperedge states via a discrepancy-aware readout.
AI.result: Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, accuracies are 83.7% (FakeSV), 82.0% (FakeTT), and 87.3% (FakeVV), surpassing strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights reveal token- and frame-level structure.
AI.conclusion: HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten, without relying on generated rationales or external tools, and offers interpretable incidence/attention patterns while achieving strong detection performance.

title: LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger
summary: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. We propose to treat a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine: tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as the trajectory state, downstream reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries, grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level, and repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. We instantiate this design as LedgerMind (Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger), augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. We use LedgerMind to target four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.

AI.tldr: LedgerMind introduces a provenance-constrained, ledger-based reasoning framework for multimodal VQA agents to increase faithfulness and accuracy by constraining outputs to tool-backed evidence and enabling recovery from errors.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of multimodal reasoning (final-answer accuracy) obscures whether reasoning is grounded, language-prior driven, or affected by error cancellation. A structured provenance mechanism is proposed to make reasoning traceable and repairable.
AI.method: Propose a Structured Evidence Ledger as the normalized trajectory state; implement an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher and a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol; enable Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair with provenance non-amplification guarantees; differentiate by repair as typed state transitions that only incorporate tool-produced provenance.
AI.result: Across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs, LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness, targeting failure patterns such as unsupported intermediate reasoning, phantom grounding, over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification.
AI.conclusion: A provenance-constrained, ledger-based approach effectively increases faithfulness and accuracy in multimodal agent reasoning, with practical mechanisms to verify grounding, prevent hallucinations, and repair trajectories without amplifying erroneous content.

title: ROAD: Reciprocal-Objective Alignment of Discriminative Semantics for 3D Shape Generation
summary: High-fidelity 3D generation predominantly relies on scaling model capacity and data, which incurs prohibitive computational costs. This paradigm typically requires learning geometry from scratch and overlooks the rich semantic and structural priors already encapsulated in discriminative 3D foundation models. We contend that leveraging the profound understanding of the 3D world possessed by these discriminative models can significantly reduce generative cost. To this end, we propose ROAD, a framework that reduces the training cost of 3D generation by transferring these rich discriminative priors into diffusion transformers. To address the inherent semantic-structural heterogeneity between generative and discriminative latents, we introduce a reciprocal-objective alignment strategy. This method synergizes Holistic Semantic Condensing to enforce global semantic coherence and Structural Optimal Alignment, which is formulated as a bipartite matching problem to rigorously align microscopic geometric details between disparate latent spaces. The 3D foundation model is only used for training-time supervision of alignment and is not used at inference, incurring no additional inference cost. Compared with the industrial baseline Step1X-3D, the proposed ROAD achieves highly competitive generation performance with only 1.5% of the training data and significantly reduces training costs, effectively reducing the computational overhead of high-fidelity 3D generation. Code is available at https://github.com/H-EmbodVis/ROAD.

AI.tldr: ROAD reduces 3D generative training cost by transferring priors from discriminative 3D foundation models into diffusion transformers, using reciprocal-objective alignment with Holistic Semantic Condensing and Structural Optimal Alignment; achieves competitive results with only 1.5% of training data and no inference cost increase.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity 3D generation is computationally expensive due to scaling of model capacity and data requirements. Discriminative 3D foundation models encode rich semantic and structural priors that current generative approaches do not leverage, leading to high training costs.
AI.method: Introduce ROAD: transfer discriminative priors into diffusion transformers with reciprocal-objective alignment. Use Holistic Semantic Condensing to enforce global semantic coherence and Structural Optimal Alignment, formulated as bipartite matching to align microscopic geometric details across latent spaces. The 3D foundation model provides training-time supervision for alignment but is not used at inference, avoiding extra inference cost.
AI.result: ROAD achieves highly competitive generation performance with only 1.5% of the training data and significantly reduces training costs against the industrial baseline Step1X-3D. Code is available at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging discriminative 3D priors via ROAD enables cost-efficient high-fidelity 3D generation without incurring extra inference overhead; demonstrates effective cross-domain latent alignment between generative and discriminative models.

title: When Specifications Conflict: A Symmetry-Based Framework for Measuring LLM Preferences
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to integrate multiple sources of information that may be inconsistent or conflicting. However, there is still a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying model preferences under conflicting specifications. By constructing specifications with explicit conflicts, the framework enables model choices between competing specifications to be directly observed and analyzed. A symmetry-based design further reduces confounding factors, allowing preferences across representation types to be compared systematically.
  We evaluate the framework on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances spanning 11 function families, comparing four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input--output examples. Results show systematic preference patterns rather than random behavior, with a consistent ordering: $ \text{Formal} \approx \text{Naturalized Formal} > \text{Pure Natural Language} > \text{Input--Output Examples} $. Example effects further depend on model capability and function family.
  We extend the framework to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and the clinical domain, demonstrating its applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms. The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information.

AI.tldr: A symmetry-based, controllable experimental framework to study how LLMs resolve conflicting specifications, demonstrated on a 550-instance executable math benchmark across 11 function families with four representation types; results show formal representations are preferred; framework extends to diverse tasks, providing a unified method to measure conflict resolution in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Addresses the lack of controllable, attributable methods to analyze how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing specifications and to quantify model preferences across representation types.
AI.method: A controlled experimental design with explicit specification conflicts and a symmetry-based design to reduce confounds. Evaluation on an executable mathematical benchmark (550 conflict instances, 11 function families) across four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input–output examples. Extended to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and clinical domain to demonstrate generalizability.
AI.result: Found systematic, non-random preferences with a consistent ordering: Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input–Output Examples. Effects depend on model capability and function family. Demonstrated applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information and can be extended to varied tasks and specification types to analyze model preferences and reasoning under conflicting constraints.

title: Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs
summary: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

AI.tldr: Introduces a hierarchical MLMC neural critic to debias estimates in average-reward CMDPs, enabling first-order optimal convergence guarantees for neural-critic primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic with tilde O(T^-1/2) rates, without knowledge of mixing time.
AI.motivation: Enable safe reinforcement learning in constrained Markov decision processes with neural critics by addressing the fundamental bias-cost trade-off under Neural Tangent Kernel analysis, which hinders order-optimal convergence.
AI.method: Develop a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that debiases across both trajectory sampling and critic optimization, yielding an estimator with logarithmic sample cost. Integrate this estimator into a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm.
AI.result: The MLMC estimator achieves the bias of a long critic optimization with only a logarithmic (polylog) sample cost. The resulting algorithm attains an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order ~O(T^{-1/2}) (up to logarithmic factors) for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, without requiring knowledge of the mixing time.
AI.conclusion: First-order optimal convergence guarantees are established for neural-critic CMDPs in the infinite-horizon average-reward setting, with novelty even in the unconstrained case; this advances sample efficiency and removes separation assumptions on mixing time while enabling general policy parameterizations.

title: MixFrag: Fragility-Guided Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization for Vision Transformers
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has emerged as an effective solution for deploying Vision Transformers (ViTs) on resource-constrained devices. However, existing PTQ methods typically employ uniform bit-widths across transformer components, overlooking their heterogeneous sensitivity to quantization and leading to inefficient precision allocation. In this paper, we propose {MixFrag, a fragility-guided mixed-precision PTQ framework for Vision Transformers. MixFrag first estimates component-level quantization fragility by measuring the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence between full-precision and isolated quantized output distributions using a small calibration set. It then formulates bit allocation as a Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem (MCKP), enabling adaptive layer-wise precision assignment under a target bit budget. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K across multiple Vision Transformer architectures demonstrate that MixFrag achieves competitive classification performance under practical mixed-precision settings. Furthermore, evaluations on COCO object detection and instance segmentation show that MixFrag achieves state-of-the-art performance among existing mixed-precision PTQ methods, improving the previous best method by up to 9.6 AP under the challenging MP3/MP3 setting. Additional analyses validate the proposed fragility metric and demonstrate its strong correlation with the learned bit allocation. These results establish MixFrag as an effective framework for mixed-precision post-training quantization of Vision Transformers.

AI.tldr: MixFrag is a fragility-guided mixed-precision post-training quantization framework for Vision Transformers. It quantifies per-component quantization fragility via KL-divergence between full-precision and isolated quantized outputs on a small calibration set, and allocates per-component bit-widths by solving a Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem under a target bit budget. It achieves competitive ImageNet performance across ViTs and state-of-the-art gains on COCO object detection/segmentation under mixed precision, with up to 9.6 AP improvement over previous methods; fragility correlates with the learned bit allocation.
AI.motivation: Vision Transformers exhibit heterogeneous sensitivity to quantization, making uniform-precision PTQ inefficient. A data-driven fragility metric can guide adaptive bit allocation to maintain accuracy under a fixed bit budget.
AI.method: Estimate component-level fragility by computing KL divergence between full-precision and isolated quantized outputs using a small calibration set. Formulate bit allocation as a Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem (MCKP) to assign per-component bit-widths within a total bit-budget, yielding an adaptive layer-wise precision plan.
AI.result: On ImageNet-1K, MixFrag delivers competitive accuracy across multiple ViT architectures under mixed-precision PTQ. On COCO, it achieves state-of-the-art performance among mixed-precision PTQ methods, with up to 9.6 AP improvement under MP3/MP3. Analyses show the fragility metric correlates strongly with the learned bit allocation.
AI.conclusion: MixFrag provides an effective framework for fragility-guided mixed-precision PTQ of Vision Transformers, enabling efficient precision allocation that preserves accuracy under budget constraints and surpasses prior mixed-precision PTQ methods on challenging detection/segmentation tasks.

title: GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

AI.tldr: A graph-language-model (GLM) retriever for retrieval-augmented generation over knowledge graphs is proposed and evaluated against GNN-based and vector-search retrievers across single- and multi-hop tasks, showing strong out-of-domain generalization and SOTA performance on two multi-hop benchmarks, with GNNs offering higher graph coverage and vector search excelling in single-hop tasks.
AI.motivation: To develop retrievers that capture both graph structure and semantic information in RAG over knowledge graphs, and to assess how GLM-based retrievers compare with GNN-based and traditional vector-search retrievers, especially in transferability to unseen domains.
AI.method: Introduce and finetune a GLM-based retriever for RAG over knowledge graphs; conduct comparative experiments against GNN-based and vector-search retrievers on single- and multi-hop RAG tasks; evaluate in-domain performance and transferability to unseen domains; analyze scaling effects with parameter count and subgraph coverage.
AI.result: Finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out-of-domain, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets, GLM retrievers remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with efficient training, whereas the vector-search baseline excels on single-hop datasets.
AI.conclusion: GLM-based retrievers are a promising direction for RAG over knowledge graphs, offering superior cross-domain transferability and competitive multi-hop performance; GNNs emphasize graph coverage with efficient training, and vector-search remains strong for simpler, single-hop scenarios. Future work may explore hybrid approaches, scaling, and broader transfer to unseen domains.

title: Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees
summary: Computer-use agents often fail on transient GUI events because they produce the correct action only after the relevant window has already closed. We identify the main cause as expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path. We propose Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees (AAPT), which eliminates this delay without modifying the underlying model. During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree is sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text. In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves the success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window ($p=1.8\times10^{-3}$), while producing no incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success because they still decode during execution. A preparation-time sweep shows that the gain emerges where the latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts, and ablations reveal three key requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. A pre-registered oracle probe rejects our initial hypothesis and instead points to branch routing as the causal bottleneck. We further reproduce the effect on an independent general-purpose multimodal model over 126 paired trials ($p=4.9\times10^{-13}$). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the overall performance of a reactive baseline, although the two methods exhibit complementary strengths. Together, these results suggest that AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

AI.tldr: AAPT precomputes a bounded decision policy tree during idle periods to bypass slow autoregressive decoding, enabling immediate actions on transient GUI events without text generation; it significantly improves success rates while avoiding incorrect actions, outperforming baselines that decode at execution.
AI.motivation: GUI-based agents suffer from latency due to autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path; reducing this latency without altering the underlying model can improve performance during transient events.
AI.method: During idle periods, freeze the multimodal model and construct a bounded conditional policy tree with guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. An observer on event-time matches current frames to a prepared branch and executes the corresponding action immediately, avoiding new text generation. Evaluated via paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests across two models; ablations identify fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing as key components; an oracle probe shifts focus to branch routing as the bottleneck.
AI.result: AAPT raises success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window (p=1.8×10^-3) with no incorrect actions in paired trials. Open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines fail (0 success) due to decoding during execution. A latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts the gain; results replicate on a second general-purpose model (p=4.9×10^-13) across 126 paired trials. On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the reactive baseline overall, with complementary strengths.
AI.conclusion: AAPT is most effective when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance; reactive execution remains stronger when such enumeration is infeasible. Key requirements are fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing; branch routing is the identified causal bottleneck, and the method generalizes across models.

title: VAD: Attributing Visual Evidence for Target Reconstruction in Multimodal On-Policy Distillation
summary: Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers fine-grained visual knowledge by supervising student-generated trajectories with a privileged-view teacher. Yet its next-token corrections are source-mixed, combining visual signals with linguistic priors and teacher-specific effects. The key challenge is to estimate which corrections are supported by visual evidence, not merely where or how strongly to distill. We introduce Visual Attribution Distillation (VAD), a counterfactual target-reconstruction algorithm that estimates the visually attributable part of a teacher correction. At each student-generated prefix, VAD evaluates the same fixed teacher with the relevant evidence present and removed. The corresponding change in centered log-probabilities defines ut, a signed proxy for the visual evidence direction that estimates how revealing the evidence supports or refutes candidate tokens. VAD projects the original correction onto this proxy to obtain an intervention-aligned component and a proxy-unexplained residual, then reconstructs a student-anchored target from the former. During training, this reconstructed target supplies the primary supervision signal, while the privileged teacher contributes a weak regularizer. Across six fine-grained visual benchmarks at 4B and 9B scales, VAD outperforms direct privileged-view distillation and visual-advantage weighting. Token- level and controlled-target analyses show that the proxy-aligned component is enriched in task-relevant visual corrections and yields stronger target shifts, especially when evidence refutes a mistaken answer. These results support counterfactual target reconstruction as an effective alternative to source-mixed supervision.

AI.tldr: Visual Attribution Distillation (VAD) introduces counterfactual target reconstruction to isolate visually grounded corrections in multimodal on-policy distillation, aligning targets with evidence and improving supervision over prior methods.
AI.motivation: In multimodal on-policy distillation, next-token corrections mix visual evidence with linguistic priors and teacher biases. A key problem is identifying which corrections are truly supported by visual evidence rather than being driven by priors or teacher-specific effects.
AI.method: For each student prefix, evaluate the teacher with and without the relevant visual evidence. Compute ut as the change in centered log-probabilities to capture the direction of visual support/refutation. Project the original correction onto this proxy to obtain an intervention-aligned component and a proxy-unexplained residual. Reconstruct a student-anchored target from the aligned component and use it as the primary supervision signal; the privileged teacher serves as a weak regularizer. Evaluated on six fine-grained visual benchmarks at 4B and 9B scales.
AI.result: VAD outperforms direct privileged-view distillation and visual-advantage weighting across six benchmarks. The proxy-aligned component is enriched for task-relevant visual corrections and yields stronger target shifts, particularly when visual evidence refutes a mistaken answer.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual target reconstruction is an effective alternative to source-mixed supervision in multimodal on-policy distillation, enabling better isolation of visually grounded corrections and stronger supervision signals.

title: QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, but their iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are poorly suited to WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect deployment. We present QuantWAMs, a PTQ framework that aligns quantization decisions with the calibration context defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective. QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video--action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget. We evaluate QuantWAMs on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under a W4A4-dominant setting, the reported simulation means differ from FP16 by 0.2--0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials further establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For the targeted video and action blocks, QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29\% of FP16 and provides 1.4--1.6$\times$ block-level speedups.

AI.tldr: QuantWAMs: a post-training quantization framework for World Action Models that aligns quantization with the calibration context (model structure, rollout distribution, task objective).
